hl_en: State approves $2.5 million for Goleta Community Center and Goleta Valley Library improvements
text_en:
GOLETA, CA, October 9, 2026 – The City of Goleta is pleased to announce that it has secured $2.5 million in state funding to support improvements to two important community facilities: $2 million to improve the child care and preschool education facilities at the Goleta Community Center (GCC) and $500,000 to renovate the Goleta Valley Library.

The funds are included in Bill AB 113, the 2026 Budget Act, authored by State Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and signed into law by the governor on September 18, 2026. The funding was secured with the support of Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón, State Assemblymember Gregg Hart and Governor Gavin Newsom. It will help improve these facilities, which serve Goleta residents and community members of all ages.

Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón stated: "The Goleta Community Center and the Goleta Valley Library are essential spaces that community members rely on for services such as child care and after-school activities. I am proud to have secured funding to help modernize our library and our community center, which serve hundreds of Goleta children every year. By making the Goleta Valley Library more accessible, updating interior spaces with technology and replacing the community center's outdated classrooms, we are investing in the future of our children."

"We are grateful to Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assemblymember Gregg Hart for recognizing the importance of these facilities and supporting these projects," said Goleta Mayor Paula Perotte. "The Community Center and the Library mean a great deal to our community, and these funds will help ensure that they remain welcoming and accessible places for Goleta residents and community members for many years to come."

$2 Million for Child Care Facilities at the Goleta Community Center

The Goleta Community Center, located at 5679 Hollister Avenue, is a gathering place for community programs and services. Various organizations are based at the facility, and activities are held there that benefit residents of all ages and backgrounds. Two organizations that have occupied space at the GCC for many years, Rainbow School and CommUnify, provide early childhood education and Head Start programs to local families. Their programs currently operate in portable buildings that have reached the end of their useful life and need to be replaced.

The $2 million in state funding will help finance the demolition and replacement of the two portable buildings, providing improved facilities for early childhood education and Head Start programs in the Goleta community.

$500,000 for Improvements to the Goleta Valley Library

The Goleta Valley Library, located at 500 N. Fairview Avenue, has served the community for more than 50 years, since it opened in 1972. The building is currently receiving its first major improvements in several decades as part of the Goleta Valley Library Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Accessibility, Safety and Building Improvement Project.

The $500,000 in state funding will help finance renovations so that the building meets current building code standards and improves its accessibility, safety and sustainability. These improvements are part of the City's broader efforts to preserve and modernize the library for current and future generations. The infrastructure improvements at the Goleta Valley Library are also complemented by the community-backed infrastructure fundraising campaign Writing the Next Chapter, launched in 2026 to fund the renovation of interior furnishings and other improvements.

hl: Dos nuevas demandas reabren el debate por el arte saqueado por los nazis en los EE.UU.
twhy: News on Nazi-looted art lawsuits presents Gabriel's AB 2867 as strengthening heirs' claims; he is quoted urging museums to be on history's right side.
hl_en: Two new lawsuits reopen the debate over Nazi-looted art in the U.S.
text_en:
Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California to press their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.

Works by the Austrian Expressionist artist Egon Schiele are displayed at the Manhattan District Attorney's Office and returned to the heirs of Fritz Grünbaum, a well-known cabaret performer who was arrested in 1938 and later died in the Dachau concentration camp. (AP Photo/Bobby Caina Calvan) These lawsuits are the first filed since the recent passage of laws by California and Congress that strengthen U.S.-based claims to artworks forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.

One of the suits was filed Monday in Los Angeles Superior Court by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair, Daniel Gryczman, against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, seeking the return of "Adam and Eve." The works are two masterful, life-size oil-on-panel paintings created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.

The other suit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held at Auschwitz. It demands the return of watercolors of other prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi doctor who earned the nickname "Angel of Death."

Spokespeople for both museums say the institutions legally hold title to the works and intend to keep exhibiting them to the public. The lawsuits do not specify the monetary value of the paintings.

Families versus museums The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional one, laden with legal and ethical implications, that pits Jewish families who have suffered intergenerational trauma against museums that, in their view, are trying to preserve a painful but important chapter of history.

A photo from the Technisches Museum Wien shows the books of Leopold Singer, an Austrian engineer whose library was looted by the Nazis. (Technisches Museum Wien via The New York Times) Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing more than 600,000 artworks across Europe belonging to Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces hang in prominent museums around the world, which makes the push to recover them more complex than a simple ownership dispute.

Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, the sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has assigned her rights. The paintings were confiscated from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler's second-in-command, and passed through several hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Art Museum, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.

Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from recovered art to provide aid to the roughly 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area who urgently need it.

"These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces, stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and finance the machinery of war and death against people," he said. "It is an honor for us to take on this role on behalf of the community and to use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live the last years of their lives with dignity, comfort and peace, something their relatives were denied during the Holocaust."

Marei von Saher said in a statement that she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family's cause.

Photograph provided by the Louvre Museum of 31 paintings taken by Nazi Germany, released to help connect them with their rightful descendants. EFE "This effort represents an important step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and the victims of Nazi-era atrocities," she said. New legislation Jesse Gabriel, a Democratic Assemblymember from Woodland Hills, California, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that state law apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art confiscated during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution.

Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling that allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep an Impressionist masterpiece by Camille Pissarro worth several million dollars. That painting was taken from the Cassirer family by the Nazis in 1939. The case that prompted the new law is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.

Gabriel said it is time for museums to "do some deep soul-searching about whether they want to be on the right side of history."

The Norton Simon Museum issued a statement noting that a federal court unanimously determined in 2018 that the museum held valid title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up the case, leaving the lower-court rulings in place. The museum said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union at an illicit auction in Berlin, where they were acquired by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a descendant of the Stroganoff family. The museum subsequently restored and preserved the pieces.

Photograph provided by the Louvre Museum of 31 paintings taken by Nazi Germany, released to help connect them with their rightful descendants. / AFP PHOTO / ALAIN JOCARD "For nearly 50 years, they have been displayed at the Norton Simon Museum and they will remain accessible to the public for many years to come," the statement said.

Pawel Sawicki, a spokesman for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced by Mengele to paint to document his horrific experiments and racial research "must remain at the Memorial" to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings should not be mischaracterized as "Nazi-looted art" because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore did not own the watercolors.

While he understands the family's feelings, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele's criminal experiments and must be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp. "While fully respecting the rights of the people who created some of the documents we have here, we believe that any loss to the Memorial's collections will constitute irreparable damage," he said. "... The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and a stain on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz."

Case-by-case analysis Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families trace and recover Nazi-looted art, said that in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed an update to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act in 2025.

That new law permanently eliminated the expiration date, allowing Holocaust survivors and their heirs to pursue recovery of these artworks indefinitely. Photograph provided by the Louvre Museum of 31 paintings taken by Nazi Germany, released to help connect them with their rightful descendants. / AFP PHOTO / ALAIN JOCARD Greenberg explained that the new federal law gave families the right to claim their art for up to six years from the time they learn who holds it.

"These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer succeed in court," he said. "Every case will be heard on its merits."

He added that the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families are heard in court and have a fair process to determine ownership of stolen art.

"It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry are not lost or forgotten," he said. "Art can still be returned to its rightful owner."

With information from AP.

hl_en: Newsom confronts ICE with a new law protecting California migrant families
text_en:
Newsom takes on ICE with a new law that protects California's immigrant families

The governor signed AB 1655; it changes CalWORKs rules so that households' assistance is not automatically reduced

October 5, 2026 · LA NACION

California has added a new measure in response to federal immigration policies. AB 1655 changes CalWORKs rules so that an immigration detention does not reduce the cash aid going to a household, with the goal of keeping families from losing part of their assistance when one of their members is taken into custody.

California changes CalWORKs rules in response to ICE detentions

Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 29 signed AB 1655, authored by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, which changes the rules of the California Work Opportunity and Responsibility to Kids program, known as CalWORKs.

The legislation provides that a child or other member of the family unit who is detained in a federal immigration detention facility may be considered temporarily absent from the home for the entire period of detention.

CalWORKs provides cash aid and other services to low-income families through a combination of federal, state and county funds. Until now, the rules covered situations of temporary absence, including a child's hospitalization, but the new legislation expressly adds federal immigration detention to those exceptions.

The key points of AB 1655:

- A child or any other member of the assistance unit who remains detained in a federal immigration detention facility will be considered temporarily absent from the home for as long as the detention lasts.
- The family may be eligible to receive CalWORKs assistance and services, provided it meets the conditions set by law.
- The other members of the family unit must meet the applicable eligibility requirements.
- If the detained person is outside California, they must intend to return to the state once released.
- The detained person must be legally eligible for CalWORKs benefits under all other criteria, regardless of their detention status.
- A written, sworn statement submitted by the applicant or recipient may be sufficient to establish that a member of the family unit is being held in an immigration facility.
- The state Department of Social Services may begin implementing these provisions through all-county letters or other written instructions while the corresponding regulations are adopted.

In this way, the detention of a family member will not automatically mean that their share of the cash assistance disappears while they remain in federal custody.

California sets when the new protection will take effect

AB 1655 does not take effect immediately. The new provisions will begin to apply on July 1, 2027, or on the date the Department of Social Services reports that the state system can implement the necessary automation, whichever is later.

The reference to the automated system is important because applying the new rule requires changing the way CalWORKs assistance is determined. For that reason, the legislation ties its effective date to the state system's technical capacity to process the new status of detained members.

While the final regulations are being adopted, the Department of Social Services may administer and implement the rule through written instructions to the counties. These will have the same force and effect as regulations until the corresponding rules are approved.

The laws Gavin Newsom signed along with AB 1655

The package announced by the governor included the following laws:

- AB 1627, by Assemblymember Anamarie Ávila Farías: public employment and disqualifications.
- AB 1633, by Assemblymember Matt Haney: taxation of private detention facilities.
- AB 1650, by Assemblymember Jessica Caloza: rented vehicles used by law enforcement.
- AB 1655, by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan: CalWORKs, temporary absence and immigration detention.
- AB 1801, by Assemblymember Alex Lee: approval of detention facilities by public agencies.
- AB 1806, by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel: Department of Justice.
- AB 1807, by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel: use of state property for immigration enforcement.
- AB 1994, by Assemblymember David Alvarez: Defending Immigrant Victims Act.
- AB 2318, by Assemblymember Sade Elhawary: law enforcement and medical assistance.
- AB 2495, by Assemblymember Ash Kalra: unlawful immigration-related practices.
- AB 2760, by Assemblymember Dr. LaShae Sharp-Collins: handheld electroshock devices used by law enforcement.
- SB 420, by Sen. Steve Padilla: property tax and exemption for detention facilities.
- SB 423, by Sen. Lena Gonzalez: California Public Records Act and private detention centers.
- SB 747, by Sen. Scott Wiener: civil rights and deprivation of federal constitutional rights, privileges and immunities.
- SB 873, by Sen. Eloise Gómez Reyes: protection from civil arrests at courthouses.
- SB 937, by Sen. Lena Gonzalez: flash-bang grenades and breaching charges.
- SB 942, by Sen. Anna Caballero: people held in civil custody.
- SB 957, by Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez: civil detention facilities.
- SB 1004, by Sen. Scott Wiener: use of masks by law enforcement.
- SB 1367, by Sen. Sabrina Cervantes: planning and zoning of detention facilities.
- SB 1399, by Sen. María Elena Durazo: reviews of locked civil immigration detention facilities.

hl_en: California tightens rules on private detention and federal immigration operations
text_en:
Los Angeles — California is tightening the rules for private immigration-detention companies and placing new limits on certain federal operations. The change follows Gov. Gavin Newsom's signing of three new laws.

The measures, AB 1633, AB 1806 and AB 1807, address three different areas: the revenue of private detention companies, investigations of fatal shootings involving federal immigration agents, and the use of state property during immigration operations.

The laws are part of a broader package of immigration-related measures that Newsom signed in late September.

A new tax on detention companies

AB 1633, introduced by Assemblymember Matt Haney, establishes a 25% tax on the gross receipts of for-profit corporations that operate private immigration detention centers.

The money raised will go to the new Due Process for All Fund, created to pay for immigration-related services.

The measure puts California in an unusual position toward the private immigration-detention industry. A legislative fiscal analysis estimated the tax could raise about $177 million.

The initiative aims to direct part of the revenue from these facilities to services for people and families going through immigration proceedings.

Independent investigation after fatal shootings

AB 1806, by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, creates a new oversight mechanism when a federal immigration agent shoots and kills an unarmed civilian in California.

The law directs the state attorney general to conduct an independent investigation of these cases. If grounds to bring charges are found, the attorney general must start a criminal prosecution. The findings must also be made public.

The measure seeks to establish independent state review of incidents involving federal agents, expanding the role of California authorities in such cases.

The law's authors also cited several recent cases to explain the need for an independent investigation, among them those of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis and of Keith Porter Jr., who died after being shot by an off-duty immigration agent in Northridge.

"These new laws will strengthen the rule of law and protect the people who call our state home," said Assemblymember Gabriel.

State property kept out of immigration operations

The third measure, AB 1807, also introduced by Gabriel, restricts the use of state-owned property.

The law bars using state land and facilities, including parking lots and garages, to stage, process or detain people during immigration enforcement operations; it requires state agencies to identify vulnerable properties, post signs, set access limits and develop procedures to prevent unauthorized federal immigration activity on state land.

The legislation also sets procedures for documenting attempts to use, or uses of, state property connected with these operations and provides certain exceptions.

The two measures, AB 1806 and AB 1807, were backed by a coalition of more than 100 immigrant-rights organizations, unions, legal-aid groups, civil-rights organizations and faith communities.

A new stage in the immigration standoff

The three laws represent different fronts in California's strategy toward federal immigration operations: a tax measure aimed at private detention companies, a new route for state investigation, and restrictions on the use of state resources and property.

The California Immigrant Policy Center, one of the organizations that backed the measures, welcomed Newsom's decision and highlighted the role of the families, workers, faith leaders, unions and community organizations that took part in the campaign for the laws.

"This year, California made clear that no one is above the law and took direct action against the profits of corporations that separate families," said Masih Fouladi, executive director of the California Immigrant Policy Center.

"With AB 1633, California became the first state in the country to impose a tax on private immigration-detention corporations, and that money will go to guaranteeing due process for immigrant families," Fouladi said.

The activist added that with AB 1806, families who lose a loved one at the hands of a federal immigration agent will be entitled to an independent investigation and clear answers.

"And with AB 1807, our state buildings and land, spaces that belong to all of us, can no longer be used to stage operations against our neighbors," he said.

The measures come amid a broader confrontation between California and the federal government over immigration policy and how federal operations are carried out within the state.

With these new laws, California adds state tools to oversee different aspects of private detention and federal immigration operations, while the national debate continues over the scope of federal authority and the role of the states.

Shiu-Ming Cheer, deputy director of the California Immigrant Policy Center, said no one should die at the hands of a government official or while in government custody.

"The enactment of AB 1806 and AB 1807 sends a clear message: California will ensure that state resources are used to protect the safety and rights of all Californians, not to facilitate dangerous immigration operations, detentions and deportations," she said.

hl_en: Newsom signs two immigration bills co-sponsored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
text_en:
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Tuesday signed two bills co-sponsored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) aimed at restricting the use of state facilities for federal immigration enforcement operations and requiring state investigations into fatal shootings of unarmed civilians by immigration agents.

Assembly Bills AB 1806 and AB 1807 were among several immigration-related measures that Newsom signed on Tuesday.

AB 1806 requires the California Attorney General's Office to conduct an independent investigation into fatal shootings of unarmed civilians by immigration agents, according to Gabriel's office.

The measure expands a state law enacted in 2020 that requires the Attorney General to investigate fatal shootings of unarmed civilians by police officers. Under AB 1806, if an investigation determines that an immigration agent violated state law, the state's attorney general is empowered to prosecute the case, and the findings must be made public in a written report.

AB 1807, which is also co-authored by Assemblymember Juan Carrillo, D-Palmdale, prohibits state property, including parking lots, vacant land and garages, from being used to stage, process, detain or otherwise support federal immigration enforcement operations.

The measure also requires state agencies to identify properties that could be used for such operations, post signage, limit access and develop procedures to prevent unauthorized federal immigration enforcement activity on state property.

"California must continue fighting the Trump Administration to protect our immigrant communities and our constitutional rights," Gabriel said in a statement.

"I am proud that AB 1807 will prohibit federal immigration agents from using state property to carry out immigration enforcement, while AB 1806 will require an independent, transparent and thorough state investigation when an immigration officer shoots and kills an unarmed civilian. Together, these new laws will strengthen the rule of law and protect the people who call our state home."

Gabriel's office said the legislation was developed in response to federal immigration enforcement operations in Los Angeles and other parts of the country.

"As the author of the landmark legislation that created independent investigations of police shootings (AB 1506, 2020), I applaud Assemblymember Gabriel and Governor Newsom for extending this important accountability measure to include the actions of immigration agents through AB 1806," Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty said in a statement.

Carrillo said AB 1807 was intended to prevent federal agents from using state resources to carry out immigration enforcement operations.

"What we are seeing across our nation is the result of an administration that has normalized fear, intimidation and the use of force in our communities. That is why I am proud to stand with Assemblymember Gabriel to ensure that federal agents do not continue to terrorize immigrant communities and U.S. citizens in our state," Carrillo said.

AB 1806 and AB 1807 were sponsored by the California Immigrant Policy Center and supported by a coalition of labor, immigrant rights, legal aid, civil rights and faith-based organizations, according to Gabriel's office.

hl_en: California creates a seal to identify non-ultra-processed foods: how it will work
text_en:
California will launch a voluntary seal to identify non-ultra-processed foods, and supermarkets with gross sales above $10 million must make certified products visible. The law, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, will let manufacturers apply for state authorization to put the mark on their packaging. The program will be run by the California Department of Public Health. Producers must submit their products to accredited agents, who will assess whether they meet the state definition of a non-ultra-processed food. Certification does not require reformulating products or force companies to join, according to ABC News. Authorization lasts three years and must then be renewed.

Law AB 2244 was pushed by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who represents Encino. According to the state government's statement, the law sets a standard for which products may present themselves as non-ultra-processed. The aim is to bring to the front of the package information shoppers usually look for in ingredient lists, nutrition facts and additives. The state took the USDA organic seal as a reference.

For the state, an ultra-processed food or drink contains a "specified substance," such as colorings or stabilizers, and also has high levels of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar. A product will not qualify merely because the maker calls it natural, healthy or organic. "Like the USDA organic label, this new seal will give consumers clear and reliable information," Gabriel told KTLA. "Parents should not need a PhD in chemistry" to know what their children eat, he added. Newsom tied the measure to disease prevention.

hl_en: Who owns art stolen by the Nazis? Debate grows between museums and Holocaust survivors
text_en:
Who owns art stolen by the Nazis? Debate grows between museums and Holocaust survivors

Sept. 19, 2026, 9:18 PM EDT

Relatives of Jewish Holocaust survivors have recently filed two lawsuits in California arguing that they are the rightful owners of several pieces of art that were looted or stolen by the Nazis and are now in museums.

The lawsuits respond to a law passed in California in 2024 and a U.S. federal law passed in 2025. The state law makes it easier for survivors' descendants to file these claims. The federal law eliminated the deadline, originally set for December of this year, by which people who survived the Holocaust and later settled in the United States, or their relatives, could bring such civil claims for property taken from them between 1933 and 1945. Now the deadline, instead of a fixed date, is six years after they learn where the piece they link to their relatives is located.

The lawsuits were filed separately, though both in Los Angeles courts. One is against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, and the other is against the Auschwitz-Birkenau Museum. For their part, both museums argue that the works deserve to remain on public display.

Watercolor portraits

The dispute with the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial museum, built in remembrance on the site of the former concentration and extermination camp, concerns a series of watercolor portraits that Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt made of fellow captives. Her daughters are suing because they say their mother always wanted to recover the paintings, which she was forced to make by the Nazi Josef Mengele (nicknamed the Angel of Death for his sadistic experiments on Auschwitz prisoners).

[Caption: A watercolor portrait painted by Dina Gottliebova Babbitt, part of a lawsuit by her daughters against the Auschwitz-Birkenau Museum. Image of the work included as evidence, via the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.]

According to Gottliebova Babbitt's daughters, she painted them "on the condition that she and her mother be spared from the gas chambers," but "Mengele took the portraits from her" afterward, and she "never sold, assigned, transferred or voluntarily gave them up."

"The ownership the museum claims rests on postwar transactions and acts by people who had no legal right to the watercolors," the lawsuit alleges, according to The New York Times.

The Auschwitz Memorial says the watercolors are technically not Nazi-looted art, because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them while already a prisoner, so ownership is more open to question.

"We understand that the family has an emotional bond to these works, which Dina Gottliebova made on the orders of Josef Mengele in circumstances in which her life was at stake," said Paweł Sawicki, a museum spokesman.

He added that "the portraits of Roma victims are among the few remaining documents made by Mengele as part of his criminal experiments," and as such "must remain" at the museum because they are "documents related to the history of Auschwitz that preserve a memory of its victims."

A piece of 'restitution'

The other lawsuit targets the Norton Simon Museum, home to "Adam and Eve" by Lucas Cranach the Elder, a Renaissance artist known for biblical scenes and portraits of figures such as Martin Luther.

[Caption: A copy of "Adam and Eve," a diptych by Lucas Cranach the Elder, at its unveiling for a 2016 exhibition at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris. Jacques Demarthon / AFP via Getty Images]

The diptych was one of several pieces that Hitler's second-in-command, Hermann Göring, took from Dutch art dealer Jacques Goudstikker. Goudstikker's collection was later recovered by Allied forces, which gave the works to the postwar government of the Netherlands. The Adam and Eve diptych was later sold to the Norton Simon Museum in 1971.

The lawsuit argues that other parts of Goudstikker's collection have already been recovered by his heir, Marei von Saher, and that she should also be entitled to the diptych, which she has been asking the Norton Simon to return for years.

In 2018, von Saher had sued directly to obtain "Adam and Eve," but a court ruled in favor of the Norton Simon Museum.

This time the lawsuit was filed by the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, to which von Saher assigned the right to obtain the diptych on the condition that it later be sold and the proceeds used to "care for Holocaust survivors in the LA area who live in poverty."

Getting the work back would be "one piece of the puzzle in restoring my grandfather's legacy and his collection," Charlène von Saher, Marei's daughter, told the Los Angeles Times.

The Norton Simon Art Foundation said in a statement that the museum holds proper title to the work, and that a federal court established as much in 2018. The foundation added that "Adam and Eve" "have been on display at the museum for more than 50 years and will remain accessible to the public there for many years."

A complex history

The recent California and congressional laws on claims to possibly stolen art respond to a similar case.

That case centered on a masterpiece by Impressionist Camille Pissarro that shows an everyday scene in Paris and was painted in 1897.

[Caption: The painting "Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon, Effect of Rain" seen at the Thyssen-Bornemisza museum in 2019. Quim Llenas / Getty Images]

In 2022, a U.S. federal court ruled that the Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid held title to the work, which originally hung in the Cassirer family home in 1939. The Nazis told Lilly Cassirer Neubauer that the only way she could leave Germany was to hand over the painting, and in exchange they would let her obtain visas for herself and her husband.

An art appraiser submitted documents indicating the Cassirers allegedly received $360 for the painting. Today, "Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon, Effect of Rain" is estimated to be worth about $20 million.

Lilly Cassirer's grandson, Claude, lives in Los Angeles. The new California law has revived the case, and the U.S. Supreme Court ordered federal courts to review their earlier ruling. The hearing is scheduled for October.

The California law was championed by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who told The Associated Press that it is time for museums around the world to "engage in some soul-searching about whether they want to be on the right side of history."

With information from The Associated Press.

hl_en: New laws spark a legal battle in the US over Nazi-looted art
text_en:
New laws spark legal battle in the US over art looted by the Nazis

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California to press their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.

These are the first lawsuits filed since California and Congress recently passed laws that strengthen U.S.-based claims to artworks taken by force from Jewish families during World War II.

One of the lawsuits was filed Monday in Los Angeles Superior Court by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair, Daniel Gryczman, against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, seeking the return of "Adam and Eve." These are two masterful life-size oil paintings on wood created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.

The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held at Auschwitz. It demands the return of watercolors of other prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi doctor who earned the nickname "Angel of Death."

Spokespeople for both museums say the institutions hold legal title to the works and intend to keep displaying them to the public. The lawsuits do not specify the monetary value of the paintings.

Artworks pit Jewish families against museums

The subject of Nazi-looted art is an emotional issue, loaded with legal and ethical implications, that pits Jewish families who have suffered intergenerational trauma against museums that, in their view, are trying to preserve a painful but important chapter of history.

Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing more than 600,000 artworks across Europe belonging to Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces are in prominent museums around the world, which makes the push to recover them more complex than a simple property dispute.

Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, the sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has assigned her rights. The paintings were confiscated from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler's second-in-command, and passed through several hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Art Museum, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.

Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from recovered art to provide aid to the roughly 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area who urgently need it.

"These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces, stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and finance the machinery of war and death against the people," he said. "It is an honor for us to take on this role on behalf of the community and to use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live the last years of their lives with dignity, comfort and peace, something their relatives were denied during the Holocaust."

Marei von Saher said in a statement that she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family's cause. "This effort represents an important step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi-era atrocities," she said.

New legislation gives the lawsuits a second push

Jesse Gabriel, a Democratic Assemblymember from Woodland Hills, California, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that state law apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art confiscated during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution.

Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling that allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Impressionist masterpiece by Camille Pissarro.

That painting was taken from the Cassirer family by the Nazis in 1939. The case, which prompted the new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.

Gabriel said it is time for museums to "do some deep soul-searching about whether they want to be on the right side of history."

Museums want to preserve the paintings for posterity

The Norton Simon Museum released a statement noting that a federal court unanimously found in 2018 that the museum had valid title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up the case, leaving the lower court rulings in place.

The museum said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union at an illicit auction in Berlin, where they were acquired by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a descendant of the Stroganoff family. The museum then restored and preserved the pieces.

"For nearly 50 years, they have been on display at the Norton Simon Museum and will remain accessible to the public for many years to come," the statement said.

Pawel Sawicki, a spokesman for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced by Mengele to paint to document his horrific experiments and racial research "must remain at the Memorial" to document the man's crimes.

He said the paintings should not be mischaracterized as "Nazi-looted art," because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore did not own the watercolors.

While he understands the family's feelings, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele's criminal experiments and must be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.

"While fully respecting the rights of the people who created some of the documents we hold here, we believe that any loss to the Memorial's collections would constitute irreparable damage," he said. "... The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and a stain on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz."

Advocates hope the cases will now be judged on their merits

Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families trace and recover Nazi-looted art, said that in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed an update to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. That new law permanently removed the expiration date, allowing Holocaust survivors and their heirs to pursue recovery of these artworks indefinitely.

Greenberg explained that the new federal law gave families the right to claim their art for up to six years from the time they learn who holds it.

"These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer prevail in court," he said. "Every case will be heard on its merits."

He added that the new legislation also ensures these Jewish families are heard in court and have a fair process to determine ownership of stolen art.

"It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry are not lost or forgotten," he said. "Art can still be returned to its rightful owner."

text_en:
Last week, the California State Legislature approved AB 1626, key legislation that puts mental health and substance use disorder training in the hands of youth sports coaches. AB 1626, introduced by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel, Blanca Pacheco and Jacqui Irwin, passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and now heads to the desk of Governor Gavin Newsom.

For coaches across California, AB 1626 turns good intentions into real preparation. It requires K-12 sports coaches to complete training to recognize the warning signs of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance use disorders and suicidal ideation, and to know how to connect a struggling student athlete with resources. It also directs the California Department of Education to build a model training that recreational and club coaches across the state can use to do the same.

"For many young people, mental health intervention can be the difference between life and death," said Gabriel. "Coaches are in a unique position and are often the first to notice when young people are struggling and need help. This bill will empower youth sports coaches with the tools and training they need to help students in crisis." "I am grateful to all the coaches who have helped me build confidence and resilience, on and off the court," said Stephen Curry, NBA champion. "Every kid deserves that kind of coach, and we are proud to have invested to make sure coaches in Oakland have the tools to be great leaders. Policies like Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel's bill help create a solid foundation for coaching practices that can have a lasting impact on an athlete's life." A crisis unfolding on California's fields and courts: Studies show that teenagers across the state are facing mental health problems at an increasing rate. California's youth and children have experienced an alarming rise in suicide rates and feel more disconnected from school, work and relationships. Meanwhile, young athletes face their own elevated risks of depression, anxiety, body image struggles and eating disorders.

Coaches often see young athletes for many hours each week and may be the first to notice when something is wrong. Yet only one in five coaches reports feeling highly confident in their ability to support a student going through a mental health or substance use disorder, and four in five say they feel less than fully prepared. The goal is to ensure that the adults children already trust are ready to help when it matters most.

Backed by champions on and off the field: AB 1626 is sponsored by the California Alliance of Children and Family Services (CA Alliance), Mental Health America of California, the Play Equity Fund and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls. It is supported by State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond, the San Francisco Giants, the U.S. Soccer Foundation, the San Francisco 49ers, NAMI California, the American Academy of Pediatrics of California, the Association of California School Administrators, and dozens of education, youth and mental health organizations.

"This bill is about turning awareness into life-saving action," said Irwin. "The community I represent in Ventura County lost an extraordinary person when Sarah Shulze's life was tragically cut short by suicide in 2022. Sarah was a talented multi-discipline runner, and her loss underscores the urgent need to better equip the adults our students trust to recognize and respond to the warning signs of mental health crises."

"Everyone talks about prevention, but few invest in it. AB 1626 is prevention in practice," said Pete Weldy, CEO of CA Alliance. "Youth mental health has reached a crisis point, but early identification can change the trajectory of a young person's life. When a trusted adult, like a high school coach, is trained to recognize when a young athlete is struggling ... that coach can connect that young person with care and, in some cases, save their life."

What's next: Once AB 1626 reaches the governor's desk, he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

hl_en: California prepares a label for non-ultra-processed foods
text_en:
To respond to the lack of a unified federal standard, California has promoted a label for non-ultra-processed foods, based on an audited official seal with mandatory presence in large supermarkets, thereby seeking to offer consumers clear and direct guidance to help them in their daily shopping.

California is preparing a label for non-ultra-processed foods intended to make it easier for consumers to identify products that do not fall into the category of ultra-processed foods. Bill AB 2244, championed by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, proposes creating an official seal called "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified" and establishing an independent certification system supervised by the State's health authorities.

The bill has advanced rapidly in the California legislature, although it still must complete its passage before reaching Governor Gavin Newsom. The initiative is especially interesting for a reason that may go unnoticed: the fact that the United States still does not have a single, generally accepted federal definition of exactly what an ultra-processed food is. In fact, the FDA (Food and Drug Administration) itself and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) acknowledged this situation in 2025, when they launched a joint process to try to develop a uniform definition of so-called UPF (ultra-processed foods) for the whole country. A question arises almost inevitably: if Washington is still trying to decide what should legally be understood as an ultra-processed food, how can California meanwhile create an official label to identify the foods that are not?

Last October, Gavin Newsom signed AB 1264, a pioneering law that introduced a legal definition of ultra-processed food in California, also establishing measures to progressively remove products considered especially concerning from school cafeterias. Therefore, it is no longer correct to say that there is no legal definition of ultra-processed food anywhere in the United States; what does not exist is a uniform federal definition. California has its own legal definition for certain purposes, while the federal government is still working on its own.

How the "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified" certification system works

The bill does not intend to wait for Washington to finish its process. If it ultimately becomes law, California will create the "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified" seal, which may only be used by products certified by agents accredited by the California Department of Public Health. These agents will have to be registered, provide information about the certified products and submit to possible audits. In addition, the State will maintain a public list of the foods that hold the certification.

The system also provides that certification is not permanent: food products must be recertified every three years and, if they are reformulated, they will have to obtain certification again before they can continue using the accreditation seal. The goal is to prevent a product from keeping a label indefinitely even though its composition has changed.

But the proposal goes even beyond the package: large supermarkets that exceed 10 million dollars in annual sales and sell more than 25 certified products must make at least three of them clearly identifiable through physical separation, signs or other visual elements. The idea is that the information not be hidden in the fine print of the labeling, but can be used directly at the moment of purchase.

The challenge of identification for the consumer

Here one of the most interesting elements of this bill appears: the problem of ultra-processed foods is not only determining which products fall into the category, but also enabling consumers to recognize them in a simple way. Nutrition information and ingredient lists already exist, but interpreting certain ingredients, additives and technological functions can be complicated even for nutrition professionals.

hl: Registros revelan que fondos de $2.5 mil millones por los incendios forestales siguen sin utilizarse
author: Eric Leonard, Lorraine Roe and Lucia Walinchus Thayer
twhy: Gabriel's office is noted as co-author of the fire fund bill and declined an interview in an investigation of unspent funds.
hl_en: Records reveal $2.5 billion in wildfire funds remain unused
text_en:
NBC4 Investigates found that at least 60% has not been spent, relatively little money reached victims directly, and part of the funds was diverted to CHP deployments at immigration protests. Sixteen months after Governor Gavin Newsom announced a $2.5 billion relief package and other measures for victims of the January 2025 wildfires, state records show most of the fund remains unused, little money reached victims directly, and some was diverted to law enforcement for purposes unrelated to the fire response.

Of the $605 million spent to date, much went to state agencies that did fire-related work in the Eaton and Palisades fires, $37 million went to Los Angeles city and county fire departments to reimburse firefighting costs, and nearly $21 million was paid to the California Highway Patrol for road closures and security in fire zones. Records also showed about $14 million was used to pay CHP officers sent to protests against aggressive federal immigration enforcement in downtown Los Angeles, after state authorities authorized using fire relief funds for other purposes. That means 60%, about $895 million, of an initial $1.5 billion portion earmarked for fire relief has not been used despite great need.

"Two and a half billion dollars is a lot of money," said Nicole Vazquez, an Eaton fire victim and community advocate, who said she did not know the fund existed. Newsom's office declined interview requests earlier this year but said Thursday night there were limits on the money's use, writing that the $2.5 billion was designed as an advance for FEMA-reimbursable projects. The office of Encino Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, who co-authored the bill that created the fund, referred questions to the governor's office and declined to make Gabriel available for an interview.

hl_en: Editorial: For Zach Sokoloff as Los Angeles City Controller
text_en:
Of the two candidates, Sokoloff is best suited to face the difficult financial challenges of Los Angeles, and we recommend voting for him. In the June 2 primary for Los Angeles City Controller, Zach Sokoloff is the challenger facing incumbent Kenneth Mejia. The controller's role is to audit the city's finances. Though the controller does not manage the city budget, he has authority to investigate unjustified spending. His office has about 160 employees.

La Opinion considers that of the two, Sokoloff is best suited to confront the city's difficult financial challenges and recommends readers vote for him. In 2025, Los Angeles went through a severe budget crisis whose remnants persist. It had a deficit of almost a billion dollars from a combination of factors, including a drastic drop in sales, business and hotel tax revenue, and immense fire-related costs that caused 24 deaths and losses of up to $250 million. Also, $287 million in legal liability payments, 53% of them for LAPD conduct, including civil rights violations and excessive force. By year's end the worst consequences, the layoff of thousands of city employees, had been avoided through consolidation, reduced overhead and cancellation of about 1,700 vacant positions.

Mejia took office in 2022 promising transparency and accountability, riding a wave of criticism of the city establishment, especially the Police Department. Sokoloff plans to appoint a Chief Revenue Officer and audit core city services to see where the money goes. Sokoloff has the backing of Sen. Adam Schiff, Reps. Tony Cardenas and Ted Lieu, Attorney General Rob Bonta, Treasurer Fiona Ma, Speaker Robert Rivas and Assemblymembers Mark Gonzalez, Mike Gipson, Rick Chavez Zbur and Jesse Gabriel.

hl_en: Walmart will apply mandatory changes at checkouts and entrances: how it will affect customers
text_en:
Walmart customers in California could see changes in the labeling of certain products if bill AB 224 is approved. Recently, the largest U.S. retailer, Walmart, announced it is preparing to apply mandatory changes at checkouts and store entrances because of a new law that could change how customers place products in their carts. According to a statement from the retailer, because of the "labeling" law, Walmart customers in California will see a transformation in certain products, which under a new identification system will be classified as ultra-processed or not.

With the push of this bill, known as AB 224, consumers will easily be able to identify which foods are ultra-processed and which are not, as the latter will carry a "Certified by California" label indicating they contain more natural ingredients. If approved, this bill introduced by Democratic legislator Jesse Gabriel could be launched in 2028. The measure follows growing concern about obesity and other diseases related to high consumption of processed foods.

Gabriel recently said that "like the USDA organic label, this new seal will give consumers clear and reliable information and make it easier for them to find healthier foods free of harmful additives. Parents should not need a PhD in chemistry to understand what they are feeding their children." According to the CDC, daily consumption of processed foods among adults and children in the U.S. is 62%, and researchers link it not only to obesity but to type 2 diabetes, cancer and heart disease. Some manufacturers have said the changes could greatly harm the industry, while others are changing their products with more natural ingredients.

hl_en: California could show which foods are not 'ultra-processed' in supermarkets
text_en:
The Los Angeles Dodgers may have their sights set on a three-peat this year, but an L.A. lawmaker is aiming for his own four-peat.

In each of the last three years — from 2023 to 2025 — Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) has gotten laws enacted to regulate harmful ingredients in food products, including measures to keep them from being served in schools.

Now, he is leading a new effort to promote healthier eating.

Assembly Bill 2244 would introduce a first-in-the-nation seal on food packaging to identify non-ultra-processed products sold in supermarkets. The goal is to help consumers more easily identify healthier food options.

Gabriel, the father of three young children, noted that parents want to know whether what they feed their children is healthy, but find it difficult to determine whether a product is highly processed, since package labels list ingredients that are unfamiliar to the average consumer.

“Parents shouldn't need a PhD in chemistry to try to understand what they are feeding their kids,” Gabriel said during a recent press conference with reporters.

His proposed bill would allow companies to voluntarily participate in a certification program to verify that their products are not ultra-processed, based on scientific standards. Once that status is confirmed, the manufacturer would be authorized to place a “California Certified” seal on the front of its food packaging. The concept is modeled on the “USDA Organic” labeling system.

In addition, large supermarkets would be required to display these healthier foods more prominently, so that busy shoppers in a hurry can find them more easily.

“Healthy food shouldn't be hidden,” said Gabriel, who called his bill a “common-sense approach,” while still giving consumers the option of buying products without the distinctive seal.

Foods considered ultra-processed are high in saturated fat, added sugars or sodium, and contain additives such as flavorings, colorings, emulsifiers or thickeners. These products have been chemically modified and often contain harmful additives intended to enhance their flavor, texture, appearance or shelf life.

Experts have warned that ultra-processed foods — such as sodas — can be addictive.

Likewise, various studies have linked these foods to cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorders, obesity and other health problems.

According to the Environmental Working Group (EWG), a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that co-sponsors AB 2244, ultra-processed foods make up more than two-thirds of the average child's diet and more than half of the average adult's diet in the United States.

Bernadette Del Chiaro, EWG's senior vice president for California, said in an interview that the desire to eat healthy food is a nonpartisan issue, and she is confident AB 2244 will be approved by the state Legislature.

From supporters of U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s “Make America Healthy Again” initiative, to other advocates demanding the removal of toxic ingredients, to public health professionals, the desire to eat healthier food spans the entire political spectrum, Del Chiaro said.

[…] Both she and Gabriel are confident that other states will follow California's lead and pass similar legislation.

[…] Gabriel also noted that food manufacturers could be incentivized to change their ingredients in order to qualify for the California certification seal. That, in turn, could lead to a supply of healthier products that would fill store shelves not only in California but also in other states, even if those states do not adopt their own certification seal program.

[…] Like Del Chiaro, Gabriel was optimistic that his latest bill will have broad legislative support.

[…] In 2023, Gabriel pushed the California Food Safety Act, which was enacted to ban four harmful additives — brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben and Red 3 dye — in foods sold in the state, starting January 1, 2027.

[…] Last year, Gabriel authored the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, which gave the state a legal definition of “ultra-processed foods.” That law also requires schools to stop serving some of the most harmful ultra-processed foods by 2035. The legislation passed with the support of 119 of California's 120 state legislators.

[…] Gabriel said his latest bill simply expands on efforts already made in favor of healthier eating.

text_en:
CAFÉ COADO #212 | March 20–27

Hello! Café Coado is offered free of charge by the Fome Zero (Zero Hunger) and Comida do Amanhã (Food of Tomorrow) Institutes.

If this email was forwarded to you and you haven't yet subscribed to our news clipping, sign up to receive it weekly via either Institute's page.

HIGHLIGHT | COMIDA DO AMANHÃ INSTITUTE

This week's highlight from the Comida do Amanhã Institute is the third official launch of the Agroecological PNAE program, held March 26–27 in the municipalities taking part in the initiative in the state of Pará: Benevides, Barcarena, Abaetetuba and Marituba.

On Thursday the 26th, the event took place at the Benevides City Council, bringing together public officials, farmers, technical staff and representatives of partner organizations. On Friday the 27th, the program moved on to Barcarena with another formal presentation of the program, plus two technical visits: to the kitchen of the host school and to a community, to see first-hand the experience of a producer who benefits from the project.

One of the Agroecological PNAE's goals is to strengthen family farming and improve school meals through the National School Feeding Program (PNAE). It is run nationally by the Comida do Amanhã Institute in partnership with the Fome Zero Institute (IFZ), the World Food Programme's (WFP) Centre of Excellence against Hunger in Brazil, and the Rockefeller Foundation. In Pará, the initiative is supported by the Regenera Institute, Terra Preta and the municipal governments of Benevides, Barcarena, Abaetetuba and Marituba.

HIGHLIGHT | FOME ZERO INSTITUTE

Today's IFZ highlight is an article by Jorge Meza, FAO Representative in Brazil, published on our blog.

Each year the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) produces the global report on food security and nutrition, in which it publishes the prevalence of undernourishment. This figure indicates levels of hunger in the world, in countries and in regions. The 2025 report finds that 8.5% of the world's population is undernourished, that is, hungry. And there are important data linking hunger to income levels. FAO is present in more than 190 countries, and within the cooperation it offers, the question is: how to advance the organization's mandate in light of countries' practical experience? How to eradicate hunger?

hl_en: Debate that excluded candidates of color is canceled
text_en:
By Araceli Martinez Ortega. Under pressure and boycott warnings, the University of Southern California (USC) was forced to cancel the California governor's debate that excluded the four candidates of color. The event, which had invited only six of the contenders, all white, was scheduled for Tuesday, March 24, and was suspended less than 24 hours before it was to take place.

"Unfortunately, USC and KABC were unable to reach an agreement to expand the number of candidates participating in the debate. As a result, USC has made the difficult decision to cancel," USC said in a statement. Citing polls and fundraising, the debate would have left out former Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra, Superintendent Tony Thurmond and former state Controller Betty Yee. Invited were Democrats Eric Swalwell, Katie Porter, Tom Steyer and San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan, and Republicans Sheriff Chad Bianco and commentator Steve Hilton.

A day earlier, the leaders of the state Legislature's caucuses sent a strongly worded letter to USC President Beong-Soo Kim demanding all candidates be included. "The university's formula-based selection process, never before used for a debate of this magnitude, has produced a biased result. All prominent candidates who were excluded - Becerra, Yee, Thurmond and Villaraigosa - are people of color," they said. "If USC does not act properly, we call on California voters to boycott this debate." The letter was signed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, Senate leader Monique Limon, LGBTQ caucus leader Christopher Ward, Native American caucus leader James Ramos, women's caucus leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, Jewish caucus leader Jesse Gabriel, Latino caucus leader Lena Gonzalez, AAPI caucus leader Mike Fong and Black caucus leader Akilah Weber.

"We fought. We won!" said Becerra.

hl_en: Sacramento politics: If Rob Bonta runs for governor, who will take the Attorney General seat?
text_en:
SACRAMENTO – California Attorney General Rob Bonta has in recent months repeatedly been rumored to be considering a run for governor, immediately sparking talk of a "transfer of power" in political circles. Several key Democrats are reportedly maneuvering intensively, preparing to compete for this high-profile statewide "top legal seat" should Bonta formally step aside.

At least three Democratic figures – Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, State Senator Dave Cortese and San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu – have clearly expressed interest. If Bonta moves to run for governor, the 2026 Attorney General race is bound to become a focus of California politics.

Jesse Gabriel gets an early start, raising $1 million in campaign funds

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who represents the Encino area of Los Angeles, has moved fastest. He formally opened a campaign account last December and raised more than $1 million within a month. His donor list is star-studded, including former Facebook executive Sheryl Sandberg and Hollywood producer Marc Platt.

Gabriel chairs the Assembly Budget Committee and is close to Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas. He is regarded as a policy heavyweight of the Democratic Party's new generation. In seven years as a legislator he has advanced several high-profile bills, including one imposing a tax on firearms and ammunition to fund programs to prevent gun violence, and one to phase out synthetic dyes in food.

His spokesperson, Nathan Click, said: "If Bonta does not seek re-election, our campaign team is ready to go, and the support has been very strong."

Political observers say Gabriel's fundraising pace and social network resources put him ahead of the other potential candidates.

Dave Cortese is "ready to go," stressing transportation and justice reform

Another who has declared interest is State Senator Dave Cortese of San Jose. He currently chairs the Senate Transportation Committee. He previously served 12 years on the Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors and was elected to the state Senate in 2020.

In an interview, Cortese said plainly: "We are ready; we are just waiting for the moment Bonta makes his announcement."

He said that if he ran for Attorney General, he would focus on traffic safety, police reform and public trust. "I believe the Department of Justice should more actively promote transparency and accountability, rather than merely backing up law enforcement agencies."

People with knowledge of the matter said Cortese has already called a number of potential supporters and plans to begin fundraising in full once he formally launches his campaign. He stressed: "We will go live right away and will not miss any opportunity."

San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu prepares to return to the state stage

San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu is likewise seen as a strong contender. Sources say that if Bonta runs for governor, Chiu will "very likely" announce a run for Attorney General.

Chiu served in the state Assembly for nearly seven years and in 2021 was appointed by Bonta himself to take over as San Francisco City Attorney. He has a deep legal background and is known for his pragmatic image.

Political analysts believe that if Chiu runs, he could draw broad support from the Bay Area and the Asian American community, and that his clear positions on justice reform and community safety give him cross-ethnic appeal.

An insider familiar with the Chiu camp said: "Once he announces, he will immediately have strong local mobilization."

Bonta has still not made a public statement, but multiple sources indicate he is seriously considering a run for governor. Governor Gavin Newsom's term ends in early 2027. Although Bonta considered running last year, he had said that serving as Attorney General is "one of the most influential public offices in the country."

However, with President Donald Trump sworn in again early last year and the political climate changing sharply, and with the two people Bonta favored – former Vice President Kamala Harris and U.S. Senator Alex Padilla – both indicating they would not run for governor, he has been reassessing his own role.

Bonta reportedly has not settled on a timetable. California's candidate filing deadline is March 6, by which time he must decide whether to stay on or move to the governor's race.

Who is in, who is out? Rick Chavez Zbur clearly bows out

Among the many potential candidates, the only one to state clearly that he will not run is Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur of Los Angeles. In a statement to supporters on Monday, he said he will focus on his re-election campaign.

"I firmly believe we still have a great deal to accomplish in the Legislature – lowering the cost of living and raising wages for working families. These issues matter more than any individual office," Zbur wrote in the statement.

Analysts say Zbur's withdrawal means Southern California votes will be more concentrated on Gabriel alone, which could benefit his competitive position.

Prosecutors stir: Brooke Jenkins and Nathan Hochman draw attention

Beyond sitting legislators, there is also movement among local prosecutors. San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins and Los Angeles prosecutor Nathan Hochman are both seen as possible contenders.

People in political circles say Jenkins' camp is being "strongly encouraged" to run; if Bonta moves to the governor's race, she would very likely represent the prosecutorial establishment, campaigning on public safety and fairness.

Hochman challenged Bonta in 2022 and lost, but his tough rule-of-law image still commands a base of support. If he runs again, he would surely add heat to the race.

New Assemblymember Maggy Krell of Sacramento, although in office for only a year, is regarded by party leaders as a "dark horse." She served 15 years as a deputy attorney general in the California Department of Justice under five attorneys general, giving her deep experience.

Last year Krell introduced a bill to strengthen efforts against child sex trafficking. The Democratic caucus had originally planned to weaken its provisions, but under public pressure the bill ultimately passed in full, and she is seen as representative of a new generation of "tenacious" legislators.

Party insiders say that if she decides to run, she would attract considerable support from women and legal-profession voters. "Her story is real – from prosecutor to legislator, she represents a new force for justice reform."

If Bonta decides to run for governor, the Attorney General's seat is bound to set off a "civil war in the blue camp." From veteran lawmakers to new-generation legislators, and from prosecutors to policy experts, the potential candidates span regions and factions across the north and south of the state.

The contest is not only about a transfer of power but also symbolizes the future direction of California's Democratic Party: whether to continue Bonta-style progressive rule of law, or to turn toward a more pragmatic approach emphasizing safety and order.

So far, everyone is waiting for Bonta's decision. Only when he actually speaks will this statewide political contest formally begin.

hl_en: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass launches her re-election campaign
text_en:
Three people have formally announced campaigns against current Mayor Karen Bass. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass officially began her re-election campaign Saturday with a rally downtown, promising to make the city safer and more affordable while positioning herself as a candidate who will stand up to the Trump administration. Two days after the third anniversary of her inauguration, Bass launched her campaign surrounded by family, friends and allies at the Los Angeles Trade-Technical College Culinary Arts event space.

"This is simply exciting. I have to tell you my heart is full," she said. "This is very powerful and means a lot to me because it has been a very difficult year." Although she did not directly mention President Trump, her speech focused on her ability to confront his administration: "Who would have imagined we would have to defend ourselves from our own government?" Bass recounted the challenges Los Angeles still faces: recovery from January's Palisades fire, the affordable housing and homelessness crisis, and the federal immigration crackdown in the city. She praised her record on affordability through Executive Directive 1, a reduction in street homelessness through her Inside Safe program, and the recovery of downtown business activity.

Allies present included City Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson, council members Hugo Soto-Martinez, Curren Price, Heather Hutt and Adrin Nazarian, and Assembly members Sade Elhawary, Isaac Bryan, Jesse Gabriel of Encino and Mike Fong, state Sen. Lola Smallwood Cuevas, and former state Sen. Steven Bradford. Roxanne Hoge, chair of the Los Angeles County Republican Party, offered a different view of Bass's tenure.

text_en:
This decision would leave California migrants without free health care starting in 2026

[Caption: Gavin Newsom opted to stop enrolling low-income migrants and will begin charging a monthly premium starting in 2027. (REUTERS/Jose Luis Gonzalez/File Photo)]

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Wednesday that the state will stop enrolling new low-income migrants without legal status in the government-funded health care program starting in 2026. Beginning in 2027, those already enrolled will start paying a monthly premium.

The decision responds to higher-than-expected program costs and to economic uncertainty caused by federal tariff policies, The Associated Press (AP) reported.

The Medi-Cal program, which offers free health care to low-income adults regardless of immigration status, was implemented thanks to Newsom's push for universal health care in the nation's most populous state. However, the program's costs exceeded initial projections by $2.7 billion.

Which migrants will be affected by this new decision?

[Caption: Officials specified that children will not be affected. (AP Photo/Eric Gay, file)]

The freeze on new Medi-Cal enrollment will not affect minors, but starting in 2027, adults without legal status, or those who have it but are ineligible for federal Medicaid, will have to pay a $100 monthly premium. These measures are estimated to save California $5.4 billion for the 2028-2029 period.

"The state must take difficult but necessary steps to ensure fiscal stability and preserve the long-term viability of Medi-Cal for all Californians," the governor's office said in an announcement cited by AP.

The governor's administration stresses the need for these measures to maintain fiscal viability and ensure the sustainability of the Medi-Cal program for all Californians.

The governor's office emphasizes that the program's expansion, together with other factors such as rising pharmaceutical costs and the enrollment of older adults, generated a multibillion-dollar shortfall earlier this year, prompting the state to seek loans and authorize new funding.

AP reported that the state provides free health care to more than a third of its 39 million residents.

Fiscal pressure on California's budget has increased due to the combination of wildfires, tariff policies and the expansion of health care. Lawmakers anticipate a financial decline that could last for the next few years.

Newsom, who has blamed part of the deficit on President Donald Trump's tariff policies, estimates they have cost the state $16 billion in tax revenue.

The reasons behind this decision

[Caption: The decision seeks to cut the administration's spending. (AP Photo/Noah Berger)]

According to AP, the California governor will begin budget negotiations with lawmakers; however, it is not entirely clear where the Democrats who control the Legislature stand on the plan to halt enrollment of certain migrants in the free health care program.

Jesse Gabriel, chair of the budget committee, told the news agency before Newsom's proposal was announced that this would be "a very complex budget," saying they would have to make "difficult decisions."

In 2024, the governor and the Legislature reached an agreement to tap the state's rainy-day fund, cut spending and temporarily raise taxes on certain businesses. These plans sought to close a budget deficit of roughly $46.8 billion, according to AP.

Amid budget negotiations with the Democratic-majority Legislature, it remains to be seen how lawmakers will react to the governor's plan to freeze new enrollment in Medi-Cal. The outcome of these negotiations must be reflected in the final budget, which has to be approved before June.

hl_en: Popular lemonade recalled over a dye linked to possible cancer risks
text_en:
Oak Cliff Beverage Works (OCBW), a Texas company, recalled more than 16,000 units of its "Beverage Base Lemonade" in eight U.S. states because of undeclared Yellow 5, Daily Mail reported on February 26, 2025. The FDA classified the recall as Class II, indicating a low but possible probability of adverse health effects. Yellow 5, also known as tartrazine, is a synthetic petroleum-derived dye used in food, cosmetics and drugs. Although the FDA allows its use in regulated amounts, it requires that its presence be listed among the ingredients. In some people it can cause allergic reactions such as hives, eczema or asthma, Newsweek reported.

The recall affects 3-gallon containers expiring December 12, 2025 and 5-gallon containers expiring January 12, 2026, distributed in Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kentucky, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma and Texas. The FDA said 8,847 units of each size are included.

California passed a law banning the sale of products with six artificial dyes, including Yellow 5, taking effect December 31, 2027. The measure was promoted by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and backed by groups such as the Environmental Working Group and Consumer Reports. The regulation seeks to eliminate additives that have been debated in the scientific community and are banned in regions such as the European Union.
