hl_en: Initiative seeks to increase penalties for looting in disasters
text_en:
Officials and legislators announced AB 469 to harshly punish looters and fake emergency workers in disasters. Southern California officials and lawmakers announced Monday a bill that would toughen laws against looters and people who impersonate emergency workers during disasters and recovery. AB 469 seeks to keep would-be looters away from disaster zones, protect relief crews and protect the property of people forced out of their homes under mandatory evacuation orders. The proposal comes after January's terrible wildfires in the Los Angeles area, in which more than two dozen people were charged with looting in evacuation zones, some posing as firefighters.

"We had to make sure the remains of the communities stayed safe," said Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman. Under AB 469, looting would become a felony if committed under those conditions, which could raise the penalty from one to four years in prison. The bill would also make impersonating a firefighter or first responder during a disaster to evade law enforcement a felony.

"Our message today is clear: people who endanger our firefighters or prey on communities when they are most vulnerable must be held accountable," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino. In the Palisades fire area, a man and woman from Oregon were arrested for posing as firefighters with a vehicle they had allegedly bought at auction. Ventura County DA Erik Nasarenko said proper, fair charges must be filed for crimes in disaster zones. LA County Supervisor Kathryn Barger said this is not a victimless crime. AB 469 could take effect in January 2026, though lawmakers said they are working closely with Governor Newsom to pass it quickly.

hl_en: Legislation announced against looting and other crimes during disasters
text_en:
By Marvelia Alpizar. Bill AB 469 seeks to increase consequences for criminals who dare to commit crimes in neighborhoods affected by fires and other natural disasters. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman, Sheriff Robert Luna and several lawmakers announced Monday a bill to toughen laws against looting and impersonating emergency workers during disasters and recovery. AB 469 will give authorities better tools to end looting and impersonation of emergency personnel during wildfires and other emergencies.

The legislation is a joint effort of Democratic Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel (Encino), Jacqui Irwin (Thousand Oaks) and Blanca Pacheco (Downey). The bill will let prosecutors seek harsher penalties for looting and for those posing as emergency personnel during natural disasters. It would make looting a felony instead of a misdemeanor and raise possible prison sentences to four years instead of one. It also provides safeguards for damaged structures and vehicles in mandatory evacuation zones.

"We are not doing this to put people in jail; I want everyone to get the message that if you do this you will go not just to jail but to state prison for many years," Sheriff Luna said. The legislation was motivated by January's devastating wildfires, with more than two dozen arrests of people accused of looting in fire zones, some allegedly posing as firefighters. "For those who commit crimes, from looting to arson, impersonating firefighters, price gouging and financial scams, justice will be swift and meaningful," Hochman said last month.

hl_en: Los Angeles to push legislation to punish looters and impostors during disasters
text_en:
After the devastating Los Angeles fires that left thousands displaced, local leaders announced a new legislative initiative to strengthen laws against looting and impersonation of emergency officials during natural disasters. Assembly Bill 469, introduced Monday morning, aims to give authorities more effective tools against these crimes. At a news conference, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and District Attorney Nathan Hochman, joined by other local leaders, detailed the bill. It would increase penalties for those who pose as emergency personnel such as firefighters during disasters. Currently those arrested face up to a year in county jail; under AB 469 the crimes would become felonies with up to a year in state jail.

"This bill will close legal loopholes that make it hard to prosecute offenders, especially when looting affects mandatory evacuation zones," Gabriel said. Two people from Oregon were arrested for posing as Los Angeles County firefighters to enter an evacuated Malibu area during the Palisades fire, using fake firefighter gear. "This bill will extend protections beyond the active disaster, throughout the recovery and rebuilding process," Gabriel said.

Leaders also stressed acting quickly against those who exploit victims' desperation, such as price gougers and financial scammers. During the fires, local authorities reported an increase in looting in affected areas. Sheriff Robert Luna imposed a curfew in evacuation areas from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m., with National Guard support. More than a dozen people were arrested for looting and other crimes.

hl_en: California will invest $2.5 billion in recovery of areas affected by Los Angeles fires
text_en:
The state of California has approved a $2.5 billion aid package to support recovery of areas affected by the devastating fires in the Los Angeles region in recent weeks. According to AP, the measure was signed Thursday by Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom after bipartisan backing from the Legislature. The funds will go to response and recovery actions such as evacuations, shelter for survivors and removal of hazardous waste from affected homes. The package also includes $4 million for local governments to speed approvals for rebuilding homes and $1 million to help school districts rebuild facilities.

At a news conference in Pasadena, Newsom said the initiative aims to give hope to devastated communities. "This is about instilling a sense of hope," the governor said. The package also provides resources to strengthen response to future disasters, such as modernizing firefighting equipment and expanding early warning systems.

Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, chair of the special session's budget committee, shared his personal experience of being evacuated for six days because of the Pacific Palisades fire. Gabriel stressed that the approved funding is only the first step in a continuing effort to support survivors and protect communities from future fires. "No community is immune to these fires," he said, underscoring that the tragedy in Los Angeles has revealed the region's vulnerability.

California faces a persistent wildfire threat driven by strong Santa Ana winds as firefighters work to contain several fires that have devastated the region. At least 11 people have died and more than 35,000 hectares have burned in the south of the state, authorities said Friday. In Los Angeles and surroundings the fires have burned an area twice the size of Manhattan. The Los Angeles County medical examiner confirmed five deaths from the Palisades fire and six from the Eaton fire. Pope Francis expressed sadness for the victims. At least 11 people died and more than 150,000 remain under evacuation orders.

The Los Angeles Fire Department issued a new evacuation warning Friday due to the Palisades fire. According to Jesse Gabriel, member of the California State Assembly, the new warning affects parts of Encino, Tarzana and Woodland Hills. "We urge everyone, especially those living in hillside communities, to stay alert and be prepared to evacuate," Gabriel said in a social media post. The fire, which has forced hundreds of residents to evacuate, continues to pose a significant risk due to dry conditions and strong winds that hamper containment efforts.

text_en:
Gavin Newsom announces measures to shield California from Donald Trump: what his plan is

The Golden State's governor signaled that he will defend its residents against the president-elect's promises; the Democratic leader made his position clear on certain controversies

December 12, 2024 · LA NACION

[Caption: Gavin Newsom and Donald Trump hold different positions on immigration, border security, the economy and more.]

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he will do what is necessary to protect the state from possible policies of the incoming federal administration led by Donald Trump. In a special session convened in Sacramento, the governor and the state Legislature proposed creating a legal fund to safeguard fundamental rights, the environment, the state economy and programs that benefit millions of residents.

[Caption: The special session was held in the California Legislature.]

The summit, formally convened by Newsom, aimed to establish a litigation fund to strengthen the Golden State's legal resources against potential federal actions deemed harmful, the official statement said. Priority issues include protecting civil rights, reproductive freedom, access to clean water and clean air, and defending working families, including immigrant families.

The Democratic leader explained that the initiative seeks to ensure California's resilience against federal policies that could undermine the progress made in the state.

"California is a fundamental pillar of the country, from the economy to innovation to the protection of rights and freedoms. We are prepared to work with the incoming administration, but when there are excesses that threaten lives or rights, we will act," the governor said.

[Caption: Gov. Gavin Newsom seeks Joe Biden's support to secure key climate waivers before Donald Trump's return.]

Creation of a litigation fund for California

As the centerpiece of the strategy, Newsom and lawmakers proposed creating a fund of up to $25 million for the California Department of Justice and other state agencies. The money will be used to confront actions that may be considered unconstitutional, challenge illegal decisions in court and mitigate administrative harm.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta backed the proposal and said his office will be ready to act from day one of the new federal administration. "With billions of dollars at stake and our state's values at risk, we must be prepared," said Bonta, who said he will work closely with the governor and the Legislature.

Background from Trump's first term

Between 2017 and 2021, the first Trump administration tried several times to withdraw federal funds meant for California and to promote policies contrary to the state's values. During that period, the California Department of Justice filed 122 lawsuits against the federal government, amounting to roughly $42 million in litigation.

These legal actions not only protected key rights and programs but also generated tangible economic benefits for the state, Newsom's office noted.

[Caption: Donald Trump is known for his hardline policies against illegal immigration.]

For example, in one successful case, California recovered nearly $60 million in federal public safety grants. In another win, the defense of energy efficiency standards translated into estimated savings of more than $8 billion for consumers over the next three decades.

Working with the new Republican administration

Despite historical tensions, Newsom has stressed the importance of working with Trump where there is common ground. The governor recently traveled to Washington, D.C., to discuss with congressional and White House leaders key initiatives such as improving access to health care, mental health, fighting climate change and approving disaster funding.

"Where we can collaborate, we will. But where Californians' rights, safety and economic stability are in danger, we will be ready to respond," said state Senate President pro Tem Mike McGuire.

For his part, Assembly Budget Committee Chair Jesse Gabriel said that "we cannot afford to be caught unprepared."

hl_en: California prepares for the impact of Trump's second presidency
text_en:
The state Congress is holding a special session to guarantee funds to litigate immigration, civil rights, climate change and abortion cases. California is getting ready for the coming storm. The Democratic bastion is preparing a series of measures to resist the blows of Donald Trump's second presidency. The state legislature has been in special session since Monday, seeking to reinforce rights and guarantees for its 40 million residents, including some 11.4 million undocumented people.

"It is not about resisting, but about being pragmatic," said Governor Gavin Newsom, one of the president-elect's main opponents. "We have to be prepared. We would be fools not to get ready before January," he told the Los Angeles Times.

Newsom called the special session days after Trump's election victory. Democrats hold a supermajority in both chambers, ensuring a smooth legislative process. Legislator Jesse Gabriel on Monday morning introduced a measure to reserve $25 million of the state budget to face lawsuits that local authorities could face from the new federal government on climate change, immigration, abortion access and civil rights. California faced 120 lawsuits during Trump's first stay in the White House, which cost the state budget more than $40 million.

hl_en: California bans the use of 6 dyes in school food
text_en:
By Miyeilis Flores. Foods containing certain types of dyes will be taken off California school menus under the School Food Safety Act, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, which takes effect in 2028 but will be implemented gradually. These chemicals are added to a variety of foods offered in public schools and may have negative consequences for children's behavior and attention. The aim is to protect children from these additives and create a healthier school environment.

Three years ago reviews began on the effects of dyes on children's health, when a state report linked consumption of synthetic food dyes to hyperactivity and neurobehavioral problems in certain children. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment found a link in some children without ADHD diagnoses, according to Telemundo. And more recently, in March, Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel introduced the law.

Jesse Gabriel clarified to Telemundo that the law does not ban any food; it only requires manufacturers to replace artificial dyes in their recipes with natural alternatives. Using carrot or beet juice as natural colorants is not new in the food industry; it is common practice for consumers in the European Union, where synthetic dyes in foods and drinks are prohibited.

author: Robin Foster
twhy: HealthDay news on the dye ban; Gabriel 'thrilled', industry objection included.
hl_en: California bans 6 artificial dyes in foods served in public schools
text_en:
TUESDAY, Oct. 1, 2024 (HealthDay News) -- A new law just passed in California makes it the first state to tell public schools they can no longer serve foods containing six artificial dyes linked to health and behavior problems in children.

Gov. Gavin Newsom on Saturday signed the California School Food Safety Act. It bans Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2 and Green 3 in the meals, drinks and snacks served in school cafeterias across the state, though the law will not take effect until Dec. 31, 2027.

"Our health is inextricably linked to the food we eat, but fresh, healthy food is not always available or affordable for families," Newsom said in a news release after signing the bill. "Today, we refuse to accept the status quo and make it possible for everyone, including school-age children, to have access to nutritious and delicious food without harmful and often addictive additives. By giving every child a healthy start, we can put them on the path to a future with less risk of obesity and chronic disease."

The bill was first proposed in March by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, three years after a state report linked consumption of synthetic food dyes to hyperactivity and neurobehavioral problems in some children.

"Overall, our review of the human studies suggests that synthetic food dyes are associated with adverse neurobehavioral effects, such as inattention, hyperactivity and restlessness in sensitive children," the report's authors wrote. "The evidence supports a relationship between food dye exposure and adverse behavioral outcomes in children, both with and without pre-existing behavioral disorders [such as ADHD]."

Gabriel was thrilled with the signing of the new law.

"Once again, California is leading the nation when it comes to protecting our kids from dangerous chemicals that can harm their bodies and interfere with their ability to learn," he said in the governor's news release about the law. "This bipartisan law will empower schools to better protect student health and well-being and sends a strong message to manufacturers to stop using these harmful additives."

Importantly, the law only requires manufacturers to remove artificial dyes from their recipes and replace them with natural alternatives, such as carrot or beet juice. Many companies already do so for consumers in the European Union and other places that ban synthetic dyes in food and drinks, NBC News reported.

Consumer advocacy groups have long argued that the FDA's approval of artificial dyes rests on outdated research, and some studies show that children's bodies are more sensitive to chemical exposure.

"What made this kind of law necessary is that the FDA has been unable or unwilling to do anything about these issues for several decades," Brian Ronholm, director of food policy at Consumer Reports, told NBC News. "There is now much more data and information about the health effects than ever before."

Last week, the FDA held a public meeting to discuss the safety of food chemicals, including color additives, as part of a broader effort to address food safety in this country.

The International Food Additives Council said in a statement that state-specific legislation such as the California School Food Safety Act undermines the FDA.

"This legislation is not only misguided, but it also increases costs and complexity, ultimately affecting the population most in need of nutrition, while disrupting national food regulations and causing confusion for consumers," the group told NBC News. "This approach fosters unnecessary fear and distrust in the federal system."

But Gabriel said he hopes California's new law will spur more changes at the federal level.

"We think we are exerting the right kind of pressure on the federal government to step up and do the right thing and really bring the United States in line with so many other countries around the world," he told NBC News.

More information
The Center for Science in the Public Interest has more on the safety of food dyes.

SOURCE: California School Food Safety Act, Sept. 28, 2024; Gov. Gavin Newsom, statement, Sept. 28, 2024; NBC News

What This Means For You
California has become the first state to ban six food dyes in public school cafeterias because of their link to health and behavior problems in vulnerable children.

text_en:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed historic legislation banning six artificial dyes in food served in public schools. The measure, the first of its kind in the U.S., takes effect December 31, 2027, banning Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2 and Green 3 in the state's school cafeterias, according to NBC News.

The California School Food Safety Act was introduced by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel in March. It rests on a report by California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment that found a connection between consumption of these dyes and behavioral and health problems in children, according to NBC News. The banned dyes appear in cereals, ice cream, drinks, candy and more, and have been linked to hyperactivity and other neurobehavioral problems in children, per 2021 studies. The FDA has not established a definitive causal link in children without ADHD diagnoses.

Gabriel expressed satisfaction after the signing, saying he was "proud to be able to change the national debate on food safety." He added that the banned chemicals can harm children and interfere with their ability to learn. The law does not ban any particular food but requires manufacturers to remove artificial dyes from recipes and replace them with natural alternatives such as carrot or beet juice, a practice already common for European Union consumers.

The International Food Additives Council, a trade group, expressed displeasure with the legislation, arguing it could increase costs and complexity, hit the populations that most need nutrition, and affect national food regulation and consumer trust, according to USA Today. Experts such as Asa Bradman of UC Merced have said there are strong indications that food dyes can affect behavior, especially in children with ADHD.

hl_en: California breathes new life into the fight over the Thyssen's Nazi-looted 'Pissarro'
text_en:
A painting presided over the room that Claude Cassirer used as an office. It was a reproduction of Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon. Effect of Rain (1897), the work by Impressionist Camille Pissarro that has been at the center of a bitter legal dispute for almost two decades between the Cassirers, the Government of Spain and the Thyssen Museum in Madrid. "I had it made for my father. They framed it beautifully. Sometimes it causes confusion because when people see it they think the painting has already been returned to us...," says David Cassirer, son of Claude and grandson of Lilly Cassirer Neubauer, the original owner of the work, who died in 2010 and 1962, respectively.

The copy of the Pissarro painting, which was looted by the Nazis at the start of World War II, hangs today in the living room of David, who has just turned 70. "I look at it every day and in my mind I talk to it. I tell it 'come back to me, come back to us,'" says Cassirer from Denver, where he lives. The hope of that happening seemed to have been definitively extinguished last January, after the California Court of Appeals ruled against the Cassirers and held that Spain has the right to keep the painting, upholding several earlier judicial decisions in U.S. federal courts in 2015 and 2022. The three judges on the Court of Appeals panel unanimously found that Spanish law prevails over California law, which cemented the Pissarro's place in Madrid, although Judge Consuelo Callahan issued a separate opinion to stress that "Spain should have voluntarily relinquished the painting."

But recently the California government has given new life to the Cassirers' plea. Gavin Newsom, the state's governor, signed a law on September 16 to help "residents recover art and property stolen as a result of political persecution." Newsom enacted the measure at an event at the Holocaust Museum Los Angeles, surrounded by members of the Cassirer family. "It is a moral and legal imperative that these valuable pieces be returned to their rightful owners," the Democratic governor said. The governor is enacting around 900 new state laws these days. He signs only a handful in person. It was his decision to turn this ceremony into a symbolic act to demand justice.

The work was acquired in 1976 by Baron Hans Heinrich von Thyssen-Bornemisza after it had passed through several hands. In 1993 he sold his collection to Spain. Its complex history goes back half a century earlier. Lilly Neubauer, who was Jewish, was forced to sell it in early 1939 for 900 marks, about 360 dollars today (322 euros), to pay for a visa and leave Nazi Germany with her husband, a Munich doctor, bound for England. The money was deposited in an account Lilly never had access to. Her sister stayed in Germany to care for their mother and died in Auschwitz. Claude Cassirer, Lilly's grandson, discovered the painting, valued at tens of millions of dollars, and tried to recover it through diplomatic channels. When those did not work, in 2005 he began a legal battle to recover it, explains David Cassirer.

The new law, called Assembly Bill 2867 (AB 2867), began to take shape after the latest court setback. It was written by local lawmaker Jesse Gabriel, who before entering politics built a career as a lawyer litigating so that some families of Holocaust survivors could collect pensions for their work in Nazi concentration camps. This summer, the assemblymember visited Spain with a delegation to discuss energy and trade matters. During some downtime, he went to the Thyssen to see Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon. Effect of Rain.

"I thought the painting would be one of the star pieces, but it is not. It is in a wing with several other paintings. Returning it would have a minimal cost for the museum. The collection would still be impressive," Gabriel notes. "I found the kindness and excellent disposition of the government officials we met with incongruous with the resistance to returning a painting that was stolen," he adds. The law, supported by Democrats and Republicans, cites the Cassirer case in its text, but Gabriel stresses that the measure goes beyond this litigation and others stemming from the Holocaust. hl: Con una nueva ley, las escuelas de California prohibirán este tipo de alimentos en unos años
author: Ana André
hl_en: With a new law, California schools will ban this type of food in a few years
text_en:
By Ana André | DigitalRoom. Lawmakers of the Golden State approved a regulation so that schools in the state do not allow certain foods.

A new regulation in California could change the dynamics in the state's educational institutions, since assemblymembers approved a bill for schools to ban some foods. What is it about and when would it take effect?

A group of lawmakers of the Golden State sent a measure to Governor Gavin Newsom for his signature so that schools do not allow the circulation of some snacks, cereals, baked goods and others that contain "a series of synthetic food dyes." The measure, which would apply in the coming years, prohibits the distribution or sale of certain foods.

Which products will be banned in California schools? Starting in 2028, this new law would take effect, barring products that contain six common food dyes such as red 40, yellow 5, yellow 6, blue 1, blue 2 and green 3. These foods may still be sold in the rest of the state, since the restriction will apply only to California public schools and charter schools.

Why are these foods being banned in schools? Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat and the author of the bill, said that the synthetic ingredients "are dangerous and harm children," and also "interfere with their ability to learn." In fact, in his presentation he cited a study showing that synthetic food dyes are linked to "hyperactivity and neurobehavioral problems in children."

"I know that many of you were skeptical about this effort when we started, but you have taken the time to listen, learn and analyze the research, the science, the evidence and the data. The issue of food safety is and must be bipartisan," he said.

However, some industry groups representing candy manufacturers criticized the measure and argued that it "would exceed the authority of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)."

hl_en: No more Hot Cheetos: California bans them
text_en:
Seeking to improve students' health and well-being, California lawmakers approved a bill to ban the sale of foods containing dyes, among them the famous "Hot Cheetos." The measure, which would take effect starting in 2028, will prevent the distribution of those products in the state's public schools.

The California government's measure The state of California will begin taking these steps because of growing concerns about children's health in the state, where studies have linked certain dyes to developing behavioral problems such as hyperactivity and lack of attention.

Lawmakers and health advocates argue that these additives can interfere with children's ability to learn and that children deserve healthier food at their schools.

All foods containing dyes such as Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2 and Green 3 will be banned at school.

The only thing left is Governor Gavin Newsom's signature to complete the measure, which will affect snacks such as Cheetos Flamin' Hot along with other products such as:

The goal of the measure Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino and author of the bill, has emphasized that these synthetic ingredients are "dangerous" and "harm our children, interfering with their ability to learn." According to Gabriel, state studies have linked these dyes to hyperactivity and neurobehavioral problems in children. "The issue of food safety is and should be bipartisan," Gabriel said before the final vote, which passed the Assembly 55 to 0. Mixed reactions The bill has received bipartisan support and is backed by doctors, teachers and agricultural groups who see the measure as a necessary step to protect children's health. However, not everyone agrees. Industry groups representing candy manufacturers have firmly opposed it, arguing that the law exceeds the authority of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The Consumer Brands Association stated: "All of these additives have been thoroughly reviewed by federal and state systems and by many international scientific bodies and continue to be considered safe."

text_en:
A new law was approved in the state of California. The measure provides that, in California schools, some cereals, baked goods and other products containing synthetic food dyes have their days numbered.

California lawmakers have taken an important step by approving a bill that seeks to ban six artificial dyes in food served in the state's public schools.

The law that seeks to change food in California This bill, known as the California School Food Safety Act (AB 2316), now awaits Governor Gavin Newsom's signature to officially become law.

As NBC reported, the measure introduced by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel aims to eliminate synthetic dyes that have been linked to neurobehavioral problems in some children. If approved, the law would take effect in December 2027, making California the first state to ban these additives in school cafeterias.

Gabriel highlighted the importance of safeguarding students' health and well-being, emphasizing that the dyes in question are considered "nonessential ingredients" with natural alternatives available, such as turmeric or beet juice.

The ban focuses on the dyes Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2 and Green 3. It is not about banning specific foods or beverages, but about encouraging the replacement of synthetic dyes with safer options.

The main purpose is to reduce children's exposure to these additives, which, according to a study by the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment of the California Environmental Protection Agency, are linked to adverse neurobehavioral effects, such as inattention and hyperactivity, especially in sensitive children.

The law has generated controversy because of the involvement of various food-sector companies that will be affected. With the approval of the measure, they will have to change the ingredients in the products identified by the state of California.

What does the FDA say about the ban in this controversial California law? According to the findings in California, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has stated that there is no established causal link between synthetic dyes and behavioral problems in the general population of children. However, it acknowledges that some children may be sensitive to these additives, so it is reviewing the emerging science to ensure the safety of approved dyes.

AB 2316 adds to the California Food Safety Act, approved last year and also introduced by Gabriel. That legislation, which bans four food additives, such as brominated vegetable oil and Red 3, will take effect in January 2027.

It is important to note that ongoing review of the emerging science is essential to ensure food safety and protect the population's health, especially that of children sensitive to certain

additives.

hl_en: Bill could change what children eat in schools
text_en:
Assembly Bill 2316, known as the California School Food Safety Act, proposes banning the sale in California schools of foods containing six synthetic dyes: Red 40, Yellow 5, Blue 1, Green 3, Blue 2 and Yellow 6. These dyes, commonly found in baked goods, chips, soft drinks and candy, do not change the taste of food, but their impact on children's health has been a cause for concern.

Research indicates that these synthetic dyes can cause neurobehavioral disorders, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), in children. Gabriel, who proposed the law, noted that in Europe these dyes require a warning label.

The bill's author, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), said at a press conference that this legislation could have a significant nationwide impact. "We firmly believe that this bill, if it becomes law, will bring about changes in the marketing of foods aimed at children across the country," Gabriel said. "Given the way supply chains and food manufacturers work, it is unlikely that one version of the product would be made for California and another for Kansas."

Gabriel also stressed the senselessness of feeding students products that could counteract educational efforts. "It is illogical that while teachers work hard to help our students reach their goals, we give them foods at lunch or recess that undermine that effort," Gabriel said. He was joined at the press conference by State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond.

If passed, the law would take effect on December 31, 2027. The ban would not apply to foods sold during school fundraising events, as long as they take place on campus at least half an hour after the end of the school day or off campus.

This bill is one of many that must be approved by the Legislature before the August 31 deadline. Afterward, Governor Gavin Newsom will have about a month to sign or veto bills. "We are at a critical moment here in Sacramento," Gabriel concluded. "This bill has passed the California Assembly with a strong bipartisan vote and is about to reach Governor Newsom's desk."

hl_en: Bill would ban artificial dyes in California schools
text_en:
Bill would ban artificial food dyes in California schools

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (KABC) -- There could be some changes to the menus in California school cafeterias.

A bill proposed by state legislators would ban artificial dyes that they say are harmful to children and are often found in schools, including: Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3, Red 40, Yellow 5 and Yellow 6.

These are often found in popular snacks.

"The goal of this bill is to encourage manufacturers to make minor changes to their recipes," Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) told ABC7. "So that they can serve the same foods that we all love, that our kids love, but without these dangerous chemicals."

Lesley-Ann Brandt, an actress, activist and mother, said that allowing these chemicals undermines the resources that schools provide.

"When one child in the classroom is struggling, and I have seen it firsthand in my son's classroom, everyone is, and that affects their day and their ability to learn," Brandt said in an interview with ABC7.

California is the first state to guarantee universal meals.

"All students receive two free meals a day, regardless of their background or their neighborhood, and what they receive should be something healthy," said California State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond.

According to experts, research shows the harm these chemicals can cause.

"There has been some research linking some of these food dyes to neurobehavioral problems in children, including cognitive learning abilities, memory and problems with concentration at school," said Anna Iranosian of Providence St. Joseph Medical Center.

"These are dyes that are used to give foods and drinks really vibrant colors," Gabriel said. "So if you see something that is a really bright blue or, you know, a very vibrant green, it is often because these artificial dyes have been added to it. That includes things like chips, candy, soda and baked goods."

If approved, the bill would take effect on December 31, 2027.

Supporters of the bill hope it will clear the full Senate next week and be sent to the desk of Governor Gavin Newsom.

hl_en: California needs a million EV charging stations; something 'unlikely' and 'unrealistic'
text_en:
Public chargers must be built at an unprecedented pace to meet the goal in less than seven years, and then doubled to 2 million in 2035. The high cost ($120,000 or more for a fast charger) is just one obstacle.

California will have to build public charging stations at an unprecedented pace, and some experts say an unrealistic one, to meet the needs of the 7 million electric cars expected on its roads in less than seven years.

The scale of the build-out has alarmed many experts and lawmakers, who fear the state is not prepared as Californians buy more electric cars.

According to state projections, one million public chargers will be needed in California by the end of 2030, nearly 10 times the number available to drivers in December. To reach that goal, 129,000 new stations (more than seven times the current pace) must be built every year for the next seven years. Then the pace would have to accelerate again to reach the goal of 2.1 million chargers in 2035.

A robust network of public chargers, similar to the state's more than 8,000 gas stations, is essential to ensure that drivers have the confidence to buy electric vehicles over the coming years.

“It is very unlikely that we will reach our goals and, to be completely honest, the electric vehicle goals are a noble aspiration, but unrealistic,” said Stanford professor Bruce Cain, co-author of a policy report detailing California's EV charging problems. “This is a wake-up call for us to address more seriously the possible institutional and political obstacles before we commit blindly.”

Under California's landmark electric car mandate, a pillar of Governor Gavin Newsom's climate change agenda, 68% of all new model-year 2030 cars sold in the state must be zero-emission, rising to 100% by 2035, when 15 million electric cars are expected in California.

“We will look really foolish if we tell people they can only buy electric vehicles and we don't have the charging infrastructure to support that,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino who introduced a package of failed bills last year aimed at expanding access to car chargers.

“We are way behind where we need to be,” Gabriel told CalMatters.

There are major obstacles to accelerating the pace of new charging stations in public places. California will need billions of dollars in state, federal and private investment, streamlined permitting processes for cities and counties, major upgrades to the electric grid, and accelerated efforts by utilities to connect chargers to the grid.

State officials are also tasked with ensuring that charging stations are available throughout the state, in rural and less affluent areas where private companies are reluctant to invest, and that they are reliable and work every time drivers stop.

In Pacific Gas & Electric's vast service area, home to 40% of all Californians, electric car purchases are moving twice as fast as the construction of charging stations, said Lydia Krefta, the company's director of clean energy transportation. Californians now own more than 1.5 million battery-powered cars.

Patty Monahan, a member of the Energy Commission, the state agency responsible for funding and guiding the build-out, told CalMatters she is confident California can build the chargers its residents need in time.

hl_en: Proposal in California to bar schools from serving food containing chemical dyes
text_en:
By María José González. Food containing dyes is being linked to recent illnesses in children.

To help families who get their food directly from campuses, Assembly Bill 2316, by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), would prohibit California public school cafeterias from serving foods with several chemical dyes associated with possible health and behavior problems.

Among the foods that would no longer be served are those containing red dye 40, yellow dye 5, yellow dye 6, blue dye 1, blue dye 2 and green dye 3, as well as the food additive titanium dioxide.

New bill. Last April 23, the California Assembly Environmental Safety and Toxic Materials Committee voted to advance a bill to ban those six harmful food colorings and titanium dioxide, since the dyes have been found to cause neurobehavioral problems in some children, and titanium dioxide has been linked to DNA and immune-system damage.

For Assemblymember Gabriel, California has a responsibility to protect students from chemicals that harm children and may interfere with their ability to learn.

Gabriel said that, as a lawmaker, the father of a child with ADHD, and someone who struggled with the condition, he finds it unacceptable that schools are allowed to serve foods with additives linked to cancer, hyperactivity and neurobehavioral harm.

"This bill will allow schools to better protect the health and well-being of our children and will encourage manufacturers to stop using these dangerous additives," he said.

What products will be affected by this decision? Although this legislation will not ban any specific food or product, the aim is to encourage companies to make minor modifications to the products they sell in California and in schools.

The bill would affect certain cereals, condiments and baked goods, among other foods, and would make California the first state to ban the additives in schools.

hl_en: Food dyes are making children sick; proposal would bar schools from serving chemical-laden food
text_en:
Los Angeles — Every morning Margarita Pereira gets up early to make lunch for her nine-year-old daughter, Teresa. Without much money, she sometimes looks for fruit in the refrigerator, peels a carrot or some celery and adds an egg or ham sandwich to the lunchbox.

Pereira worries about the days when she has no money and knows her daughter has to eat at school. She knows that not all the food the schools offer is healthy, including cereals or foods that contain colorings.

“The truth is I don’t always make my daughter’s lunch because it’s very expensive for me, but I’d rather know what she’s going to eat than have her eat something with chemicals,” said Pereira, who did not want to give the name of her daughter’s school. Teresa Pereira and her daughter live in Los Angeles County.

Not far from Pereira, little Andrea, the daughter of Flor Jarrin, has to eat the lunch her school provides because her family is low-income and can’t afford to pack lunch every day.

“I understand that sometimes the food the schools give isn’t the best for the children, but it isn’t good for them to go without breakfast or lunch when they’re at school so many hours either,” Ms. Jarrin said.

“So people like me can only ask our kids to please eat the fruit or vegetables they’re offered first,” she said.

To help families that get their food directly from schools, Assembly Bill 2316 by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) would bar California public school cafeterias from serving foods with several chemical dyes associated with possible health and behavioral problems. Among them are Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2 and Green 3, as well as the food additive titanium dioxide.

On April 23, the California Assembly’s Environmental Safety and Toxic Materials Committee voted to advance a bill banning those six harmful food dyes and titanium dioxide, since the dyes have been found to cause neurobehavioral problems in some children and titanium dioxide has been linked to damage to DNA and the immune system.

According to Pereira, her daughter Teresa has Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders of childhood, characterized by inattention, frequent daydreaming, often forgetting or losing things, talking a lot, trouble resisting temptation, trouble taking turns and difficulty getting along with others.

Although Pereira does not claim that school food was or has been a factor in her daughter’s condition, she supports the bill.

“I think anything that is harmful to health should be removed from schools, especially because that is children’s second home,” Pereira said. “But you can’t tell your kids what to eat either; you can only hope they eat what you pack for lunch, and not every parent can provide lunch every day,” she said.

For Assemblymember Gabriel, California has a responsibility to protect students from chemicals that harm children and can interfere with their ability to learn.

Gabriel said that as a lawmaker, the parent of a child with ADHD and someone who struggled with the condition, he finds it unacceptable that schools are allowed to serve foods with additives linked to cancer, hyperactivity and neurobehavioral harm.

“This bill will empower schools to better protect the health and wellbeing of our kids and encourage manufacturers to stop using these dangerous additives,” he said.

Although this legislation would not ban any specific food or product, the goal is to encourage companies to make minor changes to the products they sell in California and in schools.

The bill would affect certain cereals, condiments and baked goods, among other foods, and would make California the first state to ban the additives in schools.

Last year, Gabriel successfully authored, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, the California Food Safety Act, which banned potassium bromate, propylparaben, brominated vegetable oil and Red 3 in foods manufactured, delivered and sold in the state.

In 2021, California’s Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment published a study finding that many food dyes and colorings, including the six dyes covered by AB 2316, make some children vulnerable to behavioral difficulties and reduced attention.

The bill comes as the number of ADHD diagnoses has risen nationally in recent years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Tasha Stoiber, Ph.D., senior scientist at the Environmental Working Group (EWG), said many children rely on school meals as a source of daily nutrition and calories.

EWG and Consumer Reports are sponsoring AB 2316. The bill will soon be heard and voted on by the Assembly Appropriations Committee at the end of May.

“Kids deserve healthy food that doesn’t negatively affect their ability to learn, and parents deserve confidence that the schools they send their children to aren’t serving them food that could harm them.”

In Ms. Jarrin’s view, there is no way the bill can be defeated.

“Thank God my daughter has no health problems, but it’s always important to avoid foods that could harm children in the future too. I hope many people support this bill, because imagine how many children could be spared an illness, and the money on doctors that hundreds of thousands of parents would save,” she said.

Titanium dioxide, for example, has been linked to damage to DNA and the immune system and has not been evaluated since 1966. In 2022, the European Union banned its use in food for sale, but it is still allowed in food sold in the United States.

The bill holds that a change in what is added to food is necessary, since many of these compounds have not been evaluated in years.

The well-known Red 40 has not been evaluated for health risks since 1971. Many studies show it may pose a risk to children’s brain development, hyperactivity and even cancer. Yellow 5 has been approved for use since 1931; the FDA affirmed its use under good manufacturing practices in 1969. Likewise, Yellow 6 was approved for use in 1931 and the FDA reaffirmed its use in 1986.

“Why are foods with these toxic dyes served in schools?” said Susan Little, EWG’s senior advocate for California government affairs.

“We know they are harmful, especially for some children. We need to protect this vulnerable group from exposure at school, a place where they eat and are expected to learn,” Little said.

Blue 1 has been approved for use since 1931; its use was confirmed in 1969. Blue 2 was last approved in 1983, and Green 3 has been allowed since 1931 and has not been reaffirmed since 1982.

If signed, AB 2316 would take effect in early 2025.

author: Rossana Marín

hl_en: All the details of the bill seeking to remove harmful additives from California school food
text_en:
The state of California wants to end children's consumption of potentially harmful food additives. To that end, it is seeking passage of A.B. 2316, backed by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who was previously the force behind the state's ban on Red Dye No. 3. This new legislation proposes a similar ban on Red Dye 40, as well as five other dyes and titanium dioxide, in foods distributed within the California school system.

The dyes in question, including Red Dye 40, Yellow No. 5, Yellow No. 6, Blue No. 1, Blue No. 2 and Green No. 3, have been questioned for their possible negative impact on children's health, especially those diagnosed with ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder).

The inspiration for A.B. 2316 comes from a collective call by parents nationwide who expressed concern about these additives, fueling Jesse Gabriel's initiative and the drafting of the California Food Safety Act that led to the ban on Red Dye No. 3.

Gabriel, who has shared his personal experience with ADHD, as well as that of his son, stresses the importance of this measure, especially for children affected by the disorder. “It's crazy that we have young people in our schools who are getting therapy for their challenges and then, at lunch, we serve them food with chemicals that undo all that good work,” Gabriel said.

The influence of these additives on children's diets is of notable importance to researchers and health professionals, who have pointed to the possible link between the consumption of certain artificial colorings and adverse effects on children's behavior and attention.

Food dyes, common in products aimed at children such as candy, breakfast cereals, bakery products, ice cream and sports drinks, as well as in less obvious products such as canned fruit and pickles, are under scrutiny because of food safety concerns.

Toxicology and food safety experts have highlighted the presence of these colorings in a wide range of processed foods, pointing to the potential risk they pose to health. “These dyes are in all kinds of foods,” said Jamie Alan, associate professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University, in comments reported by Yahoo Life.

“These dyes are often found in many foods marketed to children,” explained Gianfranco Cesareo, a law fellow specializing in food safety at the Environmental Working Group. “You'll generally find them in processed foods,” Alan added. Among the best-known products containing these colorings are Froot Loops, some varieties of Jell-O, Doritos, Crush Orange soda and Skittles.

A report by the California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment, published in 2021, showed the relationship between synthetic food dyes and behavioral problems in children. According to the study, which analyzed data from research conducted in humans and animals, there is a connection between these additives and adverse effects such as hyperactivity and other negative neurobehavioral outcomes in childhood.

That research highlights children's varying sensitivity to these compounds, with some tests, known as “challenge studies,” showing how certain children display disruptive behaviors after eating foods containing these dyes. Of the 25 studies examined, 16 showed a positive correlation between consumption of these additives and negative behavior, with this relationship being “statistically significant” in 52% of cases.

[…] This concern is heightened by the fact that the basis used by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to approve acceptable daily intake levels for synthetic food dyes rests on studies dating back as much as 70 years. “Seventy years ago, we had a very different understanding of science,” Gabriel notes.

hl_en: California considers law to ease recovery of stolen art after Thyssen's Pissarro ruling
text_en:
The ripples of the Pissarro case have reached California. The state Legislature is considering a bill meant to make it easier to recover artworks plundered through political persecution. The proposal was drafted by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who wrote it with special dedication to the Cassirer family, which has spent two decades suing Spain to recover Camille Pissarro's 1897 impressionist painting 'Rue Saint-Honore in the Afternoon, Effect of Rain,' which has hung in Madrid's Thyssen museum since 1993. In January an appeals court ruled the museum could keep the painting.

The law, Assembly Bill 2867, would allow any California resident to file suit for damages or to recover an artwork taken through persecution. It incorporates provisions of a 2016 federal law favoring recovery of art looted during the Holocaust. Civil suits could be filed against "museums, galleries, auction houses or art dealers" over works taken through fraud or threats, covering all kinds of art. It would not be enough for the other party to prove it legally acquired the work, and the losing party would pay the winner's legal costs.

David Cassirer, son of Claude, applauded the effort: "[My father] would be terribly disappointed by the recent US court ruling letting Spain keep the Pissarro stolen by the Nazis from his beloved grandmother. But he would be very glad that the California Legislature is taking the necessary actions to ensure the State's laws return plundered art to its rightful owners."

Gabriel's office did not respond to requests for comment from EL PAIS. The legislator says his initiative has support from politicians such as Attorney General Rob Bonta and Vice President Kamala Harris. Gabriel, representing the San Fernando Valley in the Assembly since 2022, is a constitutional lawyer with wide litigation experience who has defended Dreamers in court and co-chairs the Jewish caucus. The bill was to be presented to the full chamber Thursday, April 18, but did not reach a vote that morning; it needs 41 votes to go to the Senate and then Newsom.

hl_en: California governor unveils statewide plan to combat antisemitism
text_en:
California Governor Gavin Newsom this week presented the Golden State Plan to Counter Antisemitism, which has proliferated in recent years not only in California but globally. It is a comprehensive, whole-of-society roadmap for how to keep the Jewish community safe from discrimination and ensure inclusion in education. Jewish people make up 3% of California's population, but hate crimes motivated by religious bias made up 62.4% of all those reported in the state in 2022.

According to the Anti-Defamation League (ADL), which has audited antisemitic incidents such as assaults, harassment and vandalism in the United States since 1979, 3,697 cases of hate against Jews were recorded in 2022, the highest figure of all time.

Since the October 7 terrorist attacks in Israel, violence and threats have escalated. "This is unacceptable and demands action. This type of hate is not new. Targeting Jews for violence has a horrible and long history," Governor Newsom's plan states.

In May 2023, the Biden-Harris administration unveiled a National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism, something never seen before.

The California Legislative Jewish Caucus applauded Governor Newsom for publishing the Golden State Plan to Counter Antisemitism. "This plan is essential to combating the growing hate our community is experiencing," said Democratic Senator Scott Wiener of San Francisco, co-chair of the Latino caucus in Sacramento.

"In recent months we have seen a wave of hate against our community that many thought they would never see in their lifetimes. This has put our community on edge, and it is particularly affected by what we have seen in our schools from kindergarten through university," he said.

He added that the Governor's commitment to safe learning environments and guardrails against antisemitism in classrooms is essential.

"Jews have been a vital part of California since its founding, and we will continue to be; this plan recognizes that the state must protect vulnerable communities."

Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino said this is a moment that requires decisive action from all levels of government.

"We look forward to working closely with Governor Newsom's administration, our legislative colleagues, education leaders, law enforcement and community allies to ensure that we can counter hate and bigotry and protect our community."

He emphasized that the Jewish community, like people of all faiths and backgrounds, must be safe and welcome in the Golden State.

The Governor's plan addresses key issues affecting the Jewish community, including rising antisemitism on college campuses and in kindergarten through 12th grade courses, as well as continued funding for the California State Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP).

These initiatives are closely aligned with the Jewish Caucus's legislative and budget priorities. In particular, measure SB 1287 calls for strengthening codes of conduct, enforcement and reporting procedures at institutions of higher education.

Governor Newsom also committed to addressing hate in K-12 schools, a key concern of the Jewish community, since they consider it vital that all students, regardless of their background, can learn safely in California, free from prejudice, intolerance or discrimination. This includes strengthening Holocaust and genocide education, as well as initiatives to combat online hate.

hl_en: California proposed banning Flamin' Hot Cheetos in schools over artificial ingredients and additives
text_en:
In an effort to promote healthier eating habits among students, California is considering banning certain snacks and processed foods in schools, such as the popular Flamin' Hot Cheetos. According to CBS News, the legislative proposal was introduced by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and aims to remove from schools products containing artificial ingredients and additives such as Red 40, Blue 1 and titanium dioxide. The initiative responds to studies linking these dyes and additives to serious health problems, including DNA damage, cancer, hyperactivity and neurobehavioral problems. Gabriel has expressed concern, saying these chemicals are "linked to serious health concerns," and stresses the importance of protecting students from the risks of consuming them.

California law already requires that foods served in schools meet certain nutritional criteria, including that they be fruit, vegetable, dairy, protein or whole grain, and setting limits on calories, sugar and fat. Gabriel's proposal seeks to expand these rules to specifically ban the sale or distribution of foods containing the dyes Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3, Red 40, titanium dioxide, Yellow 5 and Yellow 6 in all public, charter and special schools in the state.

Studies by the National Institutes of Health have found that additives such as Red 3 can cause cancer in animals, and Red 40, Yellow 5 and Yellow 6 may be contaminated with carcinogens such as benzidine. Although an earlier bill included titanium dioxide, found in products such as Skittles, it was removed in the Senate amendment process. The FDA insists additional testing is needed to fully determine their toxicity, but emphasizes it does not approve food dyes shown to cause cancer in humans or animals. California was already a pioneer in 2023, the first state to ban four additives: Red No. 3, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil and propylparaben.

hl_en: California wants to ban Flamin' Hot Cheetos in schools: the reasons why
text_en:
A legislative proposal led by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel was recently introduced in California with the aim of promoting and encouraging better eating habits among students.

The initiative seeks to reduce the consumption of snacks containing high levels of additives and artificial colorings such as Red 40, Blue 1 and titanium dioxide, mostly found in snacks such as the popular Flamin' Hot Cheetos, among others.

The proposal states that these types of foods are harmful to health, causing hyperactivity, neurobehavioral problems, cancer and other diseases. For that reason, Gabriel emphasizes in the initiative the concern about the risk this may pose to the state's students, especially considering the high rate of childhood obesity.

Although in the United States the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approves the use of certain colorings in foods, it does require that tests be carried out regularly to determine the degree of toxicity. The lawmaker insists that the sale of these foods should be banned in all public schools. For its part, the National Institutes of Health has detailed in reports that some studies found, for example, that Red 3 dye can cause cancer in animals, that Blue 1, Red 40, Yellow 5 and Yellow 6 dyes can cause hypersensitivity, and that Yellow 5 specifically has genotoxic properties that in the long term can cause mutations in cancer cells.

The state of California is already a pioneer in certain bans on the consumption of additives in some foods, including brominated vegetable oil, propylparaben and potassium bromate, among others.

The flavor of Flamin' Hot Cheetos, Takis and Doritos could disappear from California schools. A bill proposes restricting the sale of these popular snacks because of their additives.

SAN FRANCISCO, CA.- A legislative proposal by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) could result in a ban on the sale of Flamin' Hot Cheetos, Doritos and Takis in California public schools.

The bill seeks to ban foods that contain certain additives, including six synthetic food dyes found in those products.

The intent is not to ban specific foods or products, but to encourage companies to make changes to the products they sell in California if they want them to be sold in the state's public schools.

The bill would also cover other products such as Jolly Ranchers, Sour Patch Kids and Mountain Dew.

The proposed legislation, known as Assembly Bill (AB) 2316, would also prohibit schools from serving foods containing titanium dioxide, a coloring agent often used in sunscreens, cosmetics, paints and plastics.

Gabriel's proposal follows the successful passage last year of AB 418, known as the California Food Safety Act, which banned the use of four dangerous chemicals in foods sold in California.

AB 2316 now goes to the Assembly Education Committee, where it is expected to be heard in the coming weeks.

text_en:
Other products that could be affected by this new proposal include Jolly Ranchers, Sour Patch Kids and Mountain Dew.

LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- Flamin' Hot Cheetos, Doritos and Takis could soon no longer be sold in California public schools.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) has proposed a new bill that would prohibit public schools from serving foods that contain certain additives, including six synthetic food dyes such as Red 40 and Yellow 6, which are found in Takis, Doritos and Flamin' Hot Cheetos.

"This legislation will not ban any specific food or product," Gabriel said. "The goal here is to encourage companies to make small modifications to the products sold in California if they want their products to be sold in California public schools, and let's be clear, that is a big market."

Public schools across the state serve nearly 3 million free lunches and 1.5 million free breakfasts every school day, according to Gabriel.

Last year, California became the first state to ban four chemicals used in well-known candies and other foods and beverages because of their link to certain health problems.

The law banned Red Dye No. 3, used as a food coloring in products such as Peeps, the marshmallow treat most associated with Easter. This chemical has been linked to cancer and has been banned in makeup for more than 30 years.

Other products that could be affected by Gabriel's new proposal include Jolly Ranchers, Sour Patch Kids and Mountain Dew.

hl_en: Push for public schools to serve children food without additives
text_en:
California could be the first state in the nation to prohibit its public schools from serving food containing additives linked to health problems in children such as cancer, damage to the immune system, neurobehavioral problems and hyperactivity.

This includes chips such as Flaming Hot Cheetos, Takis and Doritos, not to mention Froot Loops, Jolley Ranchers, M&Ms, Sour Patch Kids and Mountain Dew.

Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino introduced measure AB 2316, which prohibits schools from providing foods containing six synthetic dyes: Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2 and Green 3; as well as titanium dioxide, a coloring agent often used in sunscreens, cosmetics, paints and plastics.

The use of titanium dioxide in food has been banned in the European Union (EU) since 2022, while the United States requires products containing specific food dyes to carry a warning label about their potential harm to children.

"California has a responsibility to protect our students from chemicals that harm children and that can interfere with their ability to learn," said Assemblymember Gabriel.

"As a legislator, a parent and someone who struggled with ADHD (childhood neurodevelopmental disorders), I find it unacceptable that we allow schools to serve foods with additives linked to cancer, hyperactivity and neurobehavioral harm."

He added that this bill will allow schools to better protect the health and well-being of our children and will encourage manufacturers to stop using these dangerous additives.

It should be noted that the law does not seek to ban the sale of any product, including Cheetos, but rather their chemical ingredients.

In particular, a comprehensive research report published in 2021 by the California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA) concluded that "consumption of synthetic food dyes can result in hyperactivity and other neurobehavioral problems in some children."

The report also found that current FDA levels for safe intake of synthetic food dyes are based on studies conducted 35 to 70 years ago that were not designed to detect the types of behavioral effects that have been observed in children.

But it also reveals that "new studies indicate that current FDA guidelines may not adequately protect children."

"Particularly for Latino children, this is very good news because there are already many chronic illnesses in their families, in addition to there being a lot of consumption of junk food and snacks (sweets). It is important that this measure pays attention to what our children consume," said Evelyn Alemán, founder of the "Our Voice: Communities for Quality Education" Initiative, a platform that gives voice to Latino families on education issues. The study also noted the dramatic increase in recent years in the percentage of American children and adolescents diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

"Many children depend on school meals as a source of nutrition and daily caloric intake," said Tasha Stoiber, PhD, senior scientist at the Environmental Working Group.

"Children deserve healthy food that does not negatively affect their ability to learn; and parents deserve the confidence that the schools they send their children to are not serving them food that could harm them." The introduction of AB 2316 comes after last year's successful passage of AB 418, also by Gabriel, known as the California Food Safety Act, which banned the use of four dangerous chemicals in foods sold in California and helped spark a national conversation about the need for the United States to modernize its outdated food safety laws.

hl_en: More than 1,000 health workers avert a strike in LA
text_en:
By Jorge Luis Macías. At least 1,100 frontline health care workers at four facilities of Advanced Hospital Management Corporation (AHMC) in Southern California called off a planned five-day strike that was to begin Monday, March 11. Negotiators for SEIU-UHW and the executives of the for-profit hospitals reached tentative contract agreements in the final hours of talks early Thursday. The tentative agreement covers workers at Garfield Medical Center in Monterey Park and Monterey Park Hospital, whose contract expired December 31, 2023. Union workers also reached agreements last week at Doctors Hospital of Riverside and Greater El Monte Community Hospital.

The agreements address staffing shortages and patient care and include significant wage increases for caregivers. All contracts must still be ratified by workers. Victor Narro, a UCLA labor studies professor, sees the workers' possible win "positively": "In 2023 there were many strikes and we have seen unionism be reborn strongly."

The deal comes as the U.S. faces a decades-long health care staffing shortage that is especially serious in California. Projections show the state could be short 44,000 registered nurses by 2030. Hundreds of union providers went to the state Capitol to ask for better access to the profession. They are seeking a $500 million investment between 2025 and 2030 in California's 77 community college nursing schools and a package of three bills. AB 1695 would create a basic nursing course in high schools, AB 1577 would require hospitals to offer more clinical hours for nurses, and AB 1063 by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel would improve oversight of nurse-to-patient ratios.

Gabriel, a Democrat representing part of the San Fernando Valley, authored AB 1063 and says his support for nurses comes from watching his mother struggle in the profession. "Having talked with her about staffing ratios, about how many of our hospitals focus on profits over patients and profits over caregivers, there were times she felt that going to the bathroom during a 12-hour shift would put a patient at risk. That is unacceptable."

hl_en: Los Angeles Delegation Secures $300 Million in State Resources During Trip to Sacramento
text_en:
By Jose Herrera City News Service LOS ANGELES (CNS) – Mayor Karen Bass and other city officials announced Tuesday, Feb. 27, that the Los Angeles region will receive $300 million in emergency reimbursements, of which $60 million will directly benefit the city for COVID-19 expenses.

Bass and a delegation that included five City Council members were scheduled to wrap up two days of meetings at the statehouse in Sacramento on Tuesday and return to Los Angeles later in the day. According to Bass' office, during a meeting Monday with the state Office of Emergency Services, city officials were informed that Los Angeles would receive reimbursements for COVID-19 expenses from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Other funds will go toward homelessness and storm relief.

"We must keep doing everything possible to join forces at every level of government to save lives and bring Angelenos inside," Bass said in a statement. "I want to thank the governor for continuing his work to join us in delivering for the people of Los Angeles."

The delegation, which includes Bass, City Council President Paul Krekorian and Council members Bob Blumenfield, Hugo Soto-Martínez, Mónica Rodríguez and Eunisses Hernández, met with Gov. Gavin Newsom on Tuesday morning.

"When emergencies happen, the city of Los Angeles doesn't wait for outside help; we act immediately," Krekorian said. "The steps we took during COVID and our recent storms saved lives and bolstered the economy of the entire region, far beyond our city's borders. I want to thank Gov. Newsom for making sure the city of Los Angeles receives its share of federal funds to reimburse us for the enormous share of the burden we took on."

Newsom said that "state, local and federal partners are united to help our communities recover from disasters and emergencies. California is proud to support Mayor Bass and the city's efforts to help Angelenos rebuild from damaging storms, access housing and recover from the pandemic."

City representatives have met regularly with federal officials to raise the issue of outstanding FEMA payments, Bass' office said. In recent months, Bass met with Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, Acting Deputy Secretary Kristie Canegallo and FEMA Administrator Deanne Criswell.

The other entities in the Los Angeles region receiving reimbursements include the Los Angeles Unified School District, Kaiser Foundation Hospitals and Loma Linda University Medical Center. In addition to meeting with Newsom, the delegation met with several of his cabinet secretaries and other

officials, including Treasurer Fiona Ma, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, Senate President pro Tem Mike McGuire, Assembly Budget Committee Chair Jesse Gabriel, Senate Budget Committee Chair Scott Wiener and Nancy Ward, director of the Office of Emergency Services. On Monday, Bass' office used the visit to highlight the fact that 3,365 housing vouchers the city had already received have now been fully used, bringing homeless Angelenos indoors. In addition, Bass noted that the city won a $7.2 million Homekey Round 3 grant last week, the seventh such award the city has secured from the state.

Krekorian, a former Assembly member, told City News Service that it has been years since his last meetings at the Capitol.

"I don't remember a time when we've had a city delegation come here with a mayor and members of the City Council," he said Monday.

He said it is important, and impactful, for city leaders to visit state leaders. "When we're not here, if we're not heard, we'll be overlooked when it comes to budget decisions and policies," he said.

Rodríguez said the trip is an opportunity to connect with many lawmakers and elevate the issues that are "most pressing for the people of Los Angeles, particularly after COVID."

She agreed with Krekorian that it is important for city leaders to engage with state leaders and remind them that "we don't always have one-size-fits-all solutions for every challenge Californians face."

City officials lamented that the state is looking at a budget deficit in the next fiscal year. Los Angeles is also facing a possible $150 million deficit that could grow to $400 million as a result of spending and new labor contracts with several unions representing city employees.

Regarding interim housing funding, Bass stressed that "our priority always has to be saving lives, and when we work together, at every level of government, we can make real progress." "With more than 40,000 homeless Angelenos on our streets, it was unacceptable that voucher holders couldn't get inside," she said.

In January 2023, Bass said the city worked with the Housing Authority of the City of Los Angeles to increase its capacity, and the city is now at "full voucher utilization."

"We cannot sit idly by and allow homeless Angelenos to kill homeless Angelenos," Bass said in a statement.

Blumenfield noted that the city must take advantage of "all the state and federal resources on the table, and leave no stone unturned."
