hl_en: Anti-Israel Jewish protesters disrupt the start of California's legislative session
text_en:
Anti-Israel Jewish protesters disrupt the start of California's legislative session

[Caption: Assemblymembers Heath Flora, left, and Josh Lowenthal, right, leave the Assembly chamber as pro-Palestinian, anti-Israel protesters calling for a ceasefire in Gaza disrupt the first day of the California legislative session in Sacramento, California, Jan. 3, 2024. (Credit: Rich Pedroncelli/AP)]

SACRAMENTO, California – Hundreds of American protesters calling for a ceasefire in the war between Israel and Hamas disrupted the first California legislative session of the year on Wednesday, forcing the state Assembly to adjourn just moments after it opened.

As lawmakers had just heard the opening prayer and had barely recited the Pledge of Allegiance, pro-Palestinian, anti-Israel Jewish protesters all wearing the same black T-shirt rose from their seats and began chanting "Ceasefire now" and "Let Gaza live." Several people unfurled banners from the chamber gallery that read: "Jews say 'never again for anyone.'"

At first, Jim Wood, a Democratic Assemblymember from Healdsburg who was presiding over the session, tried to continue despite the chanting. But after a while, he called a recess and adjourned the session a few minutes later. Nearly all lawmakers left the chamber.

The protesters cheered when state officials turned off the chamber lights, switching on their phone flashlights while continuing to chant their slogans, including a long call-and-response from the gallery. "We are Jewish and Californian; we invite you, members of the Assembly, to join us in demanding an immediate ceasefire," they shouted.

[Caption: Protesters reveal T-shirts with messages calling for a ceasefire in Gaza on the first day of the California legislative session in Sacramento, California, Jan. 3, 2024. (Credit: Rich Pedroncelli/AP)]

The office of Democratic Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas declined to comment.

James Gallagher, Assembly Republican leader, said the protesters had obstructed their work.

"We are trying to open our session. It's true that we probably didn't have much to do today. But if their goal is to disrupt the business of government, I don't think that's a good way to get your message across," he said. "We can't let them disrupt our business. We have work to do. We have urgent issues to deal with this year."

Wednesday's protest was organized by far-left and radical anti-Israel groups, including Jewish Voice for Peace, IfNotNow and the International Jewish Anti-Zionist Network.

Binya Kóatz, a Jewish teacher and artist who lives in the San Francisco area, said that "as long as the United States gives Israel a blank check," Americans have "not only the right but also the responsibility to stop carrying on as if nothing were happening."

Kóatz explained that the groups chose to protest at the California State Capitol because, although these lawmakers do not control the federal funds sent to Israel, "we know that state legislatures get the attention of their national counterparts in California, and getting this body to call for a ceasefire now can put California at the forefront of the national movement."

This is not the first time protesters calling for a ceasefire have disrupted events in California's capital. In November, protesters forced their way into a Sacramento convention hall, forcing the California Democratic Party to cancel some events at its endorsing convention. Last month, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom canceled a Christmas tree lighting ceremony he was to attend in person after being warned that protesters planned to stage an action at the event.

The protesters did not disrupt the state Senate, which held its session as planned, during which lawmakers gave speeches in memory of former U.S. Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who died in September.

[Caption: After the lights were turned off, protesters calling for a ceasefire in Gaza use cellphone lights to demonstrate on the first day of the California legislative session in Sacramento, California, Jan. 3, 2024. (Credit: Rich Pedroncelli/AP)]

The war broke out on Oct. 7 when Hamas attacked Israel, invading the south of the country from the Gaza Strip with thousands of terrorists. The attack killed nearly 1,200 people, mostly civilians massacred by the terrorists who rampaged through communities in the south. More than 360 people were murdered at an outdoor rave, and more than 240 people were taken hostage and brought to Gaza. Israel responded by launching a military campaign aimed at destroying Hamas, removing it from power in Gaza and freeing the hostages.

In the United States, Wednesday was marked by disruptions at several state capitols. An emailed bomb threat sent to officials in several states led to the evacuation of offices or buildings in Connecticut, Georgia, Hawaii, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi and Montana. Other states, including Missouri, Maryland, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Oklahoma and Wyoming, received threats but did not evacuate.

The California legislative session, which began Wednesday and ends Aug. 31, is expected to focus on decisions about artificial intelligence (AI) and the huge budget deficit. But, as Wednesday's protest shows, the repercussions of the war between Israel and Hamas are bound to have an impact.

[Caption: Protesters calling for a ceasefire in Gaza gather in the Capitol rotunda on the first day of the California legislative session in Sacramento, California, Jan. 3, 2024. (Credit: Rich Pedroncelli/AP)]

The California Legislative Jewish Caucus sent a letter to state lawmakers on Wednesday asking for the creation of a committee to find policy solutions to protect the Jewish community.

"We have our own criticisms of Israel. We want the war to end," said Democratic state Sen. Scott Wiener, a member of the Jewish caucus. "We also know that the ceasefire resolutions we are seeing at the local level have sometimes veered into stoking anti-Jewish hatred, which is causing a great deal of fear in our community."

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Los Angeles, said his 3-year-old child now has to pass through metal detectors to enter preschool, which is located in a local synagogue.

"The level of fear, anxiety and tension is unlike anything I've seen in my entire life," Gabriel said.

hl: La lucha por el poder al interior de la Asamblea de California
author: Ben Christopher
twhy: Analysis of Rivas's committee shake-up names Gabriel a winner for landing the budget chair; brief mention, so milder rating.
hl_en: The power struggle inside the California Assembly
text_en:
Who's up and who's down? When news broke Tuesday night that new Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas had chosen new committee chairs and removed others, Sacramento's political sphere immediately filled with talk of winners and losers.

The winners include Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, the Davis Democrat who was named Assembly majority leader, and Encino Democrat Jesse Gabriel, who takes control of the budget committee, albeit at a time of budget deficit. He replaces Assemblymember Phil Ting of San Francisco, who said the eight state budgets he helped craft have boosted California's efforts on child care, climate change, and access to higher education and health care.

One apparent loser: Isaac Bryan of Culver City, pushed out of the majority leader post to be named chair of the Natural Resources Committee, who noted that the change left the new Speaker's inner leadership circle without any Black members.

But there is another big winner to emerge from Rivas's overnight reorganization.

Yes In My Backyard activists, YIMBYs, who promote legislation meant to make it easier to build housing of all kinds, even if that comes at the expense of local control over development decisions, have been on a winning streak this year.

The chorus of lawmakers willing to argue that the state does not face a housing shortage, or that the state need not get involved, has dwindled in recent years. At the end of the most recent legislative session, with Rivas leading the Assembly, the Legislature passed a series of bills that fast-track "any kind of affordable housing you might want to build."

This latest round of appointments puts an exclamation point on that trend heading into the 2024 session. By elevating aggressively pro-housing members and demoting those who are less so, Rivas appears to be laying the institutional groundwork for an aggressively pro-housing Legislature next year.

"Speaker Rivas has been consistent in his leadership on housing and also in his desire to make the Legislature a place that passes more transformative housing policies," California YIMBY spokesperson Matthew Lewis said today. "From our perspective, these committee assignments very much reflect that." Some of the appointments, he added, are "as good as it gets," Lewis added.

Topping the list of changes that pro-development activists are likely to be grateful for: San Diego Democrat Chris Ward is the new chair of the Assembly housing committee.

Ward will replace Oakland Democrat Buffy Wicks, who is as reliably pro-housing a lawmaker as you can find in the Legislature. But Wicks was a fervent backer of Rivas and an instrumental whip during his tumultuous run for the Speaker's post last year, and her rise to a higher post was assumed. But by swapping Wicks for Ward, Rivas keeps the committee on its predictable pro-density course.

The selection of Ward may send an additionally potent pro-housing signal. Last year, he introduced a surprisingly ambitious bill that would have prioritized dense urban development while also capping urban sprawl statewide. The idea went up in flames, torched in part by builders' lobbying. This appointment suggests Rivas is not inclined to punish Ward for his overreach.

Meanwhile, Wicks was given the top spot on the powerful appropriations committee.

In the Legislature, where virtually every bill with a price tag has to go before "appropriations" and where the chair has practically unlimited power to pass, gut or kill bills without any of the normal checks that hamstring lesser lawmakers, that in itself is still more good news for YIMBYs and their allies.

But Wicks's rise is also a notable change for the committee. The current chair, Chris Holden, a Pasadena Democrat, has been a reliable ally of labor unions and an advocate for tenants' rights, but has also been more likely than Wicks to safeguard local control over development decisions. Rivas is removing Holden from the committee entirely. Unlike the other committee appointments, which take effect immediately, this change takes effect Jan. 22.

On the transportation committee, the elevation of first-term Suisun Democrat Lori Wilson bodes well for advocates of dense development near transit hubs. Before joining the Legislature, Wilson was finance director for the national homebuilding company KB Homes. Even Bryan's apparent demotion from Assembly majority leader to mere chair of the Natural Resources Committee has significant implications for state housing policy. Earlier this year, that committee's chair, Arleta Democrat Luz Rivas, used her post to temper bills that increase density along the coast and to limit the scope of legislation that will let religious institutions build housing more easily.

Bryan, a member of the Assembly's renters caucus, is expected to be less antagonistic toward YIMBYs, especially when it comes to bills that boost affordable housing.

Bryan's successor as majority leader, Aguiar-Curry, was named by Rivas as vice chair in July. In a statement, she said she shares Rivas's "collaborative commitment" to all Assemblymembers, the Senate and the Newsom administration.

But Aguiar-Curry clashed with the Newsom administration after the governor vetoed her bill to require a human backup driver in large autonomous trucks. "Calling this proposal a ban is an erroneous and discouraging characterization of the intent and process described in the bill," she said in a statement.

CONFLICT OF INTEREST The leadership change among Assembly Democrats was expected after Rivas replaced Anthony Rendon on June 30, following a negotiated handover.

And some moves were telegraphed: Assembly Democrats were caught in the crossfire in July when the Public Safety Committee shelved a bill to increase penalties for child sex trafficking. Rivas stepped in, along with Gov. Gavin Newsom, and the committee reversed course. The bipartisan bill became law, marking a departure from Democrats' broader goal of reducing incarceration.

Now Assemblymember Reggie Jones-Sawyer, a Los Angeles Democrat who became the focus of the criticism, is losing his committee leadership.

The new Public Safety chair: Assemblymember Kevin McCarty, a Sacramento Democrat who has led education committees and who backed Rendon. He promised "balanced, common-sense" anti-crime policies.

In a statement, Rivas thanked Jones-Sawyer "for his work to achieve needed reforms in our justice system," but also said that "Californians have a right to be safe in their homes and on their streets." Last month, Rivas appointed a select committee to address the rise in high-profile retail crimes.

In another notable move, Assemblymember Mia Bonta of Oakland left her post as chair of the Budget subcommittee on public safety after questions arose about conflicts of interest because her husband is Attorney General Rob Bonta. She ultimately recused herself from decisions affecting his budget.

Her consolation prize: leadership of the Health Committee, where she will replace Assemblymember Jim Wood, who will be vice chair in his final session, as he has already announced he will not seek reelection next year.

While Rivas is elevating many of his supporters, he maintained that Assembly Democrats are not divided heading into an election year in which all 80 seats are on the ballot.

"The Assembly is united and ready to deliver," Rivas said in a statement. "That is what Californians expect from their Legislature and that is what this team will accomplish."

CalMatters.org is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that explains California public policy and political issues.

The article was originally published at https://calmatters.org/politics/capitol/2023/11/california-legislatureleadership-housing/ Read more at https://www.facebook.com/calmatters and www.calmatters.org.

hl: Presionan a funcionarios de California a exigir alto al fuego en Palestina
author: Sameea Kamal
twhy: CalMatters story on ceasefire pressure; Gabriel quoted once on duty to Muslim, Palestinian and Arab constituents.
hl_en: California officials pressed to demand a ceasefire in Palestine
text_en:
After Hamas' brutal Oct. 7 attack on Israel, in which 1,200 people died and more than 200 were taken hostage, California officials sprang into action.

Gov. Gavin Newsom booked a last-minute flight to Israel on his way to China because, his team said, California is home to the largest Arab American population and the second-largest Jewish community in the United States. In Israel, he met with government officials and the parents of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, a Californian being held hostage.

But the state's response has not been entirely evenhanded, even as Israel's mounting retaliation is killing thousands of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

Newsom did not venture into Gaza to meet with Palestinians on his trip. While the governor's office pledged last month to send humanitarian aid to both regions, aid was delivered only to Israel: 52 pallets of surplus medical and emergency supplies on Nov. 7.

The state blames the political situation for the aid not yet having reached Gaza, where, according to the United Nations' relief arm, residents lack access to food, clean water and fuel for electricity. Israel, along with Egypt, has long controlled the flow of goods and travel into the 140-square-mile region, which has been under Hamas rule since a military takeover in 2007.

Today, the Office of Emergency Services told CalMatters it anticipates aid could be delivered to Gaza as soon as this week, but that depends on whether the aid corridor stays open and for how long, which is more likely if an agreement is reached for at least a temporary pause in the fighting.

Israel today approved a provisional deal for the release of 50 women and children held hostage by Hamas, in exchange for 150 Palestinian prisoners. During a four-day ceasefire beginning Thursday, 300 to 400 aid trucks will be allowed into Gaza daily.

After symbolically ordering the state Capitol dome to display the blue and white colors of the Israeli flag on Oct. 9, Newsom met with Jewish community leaders via Zoom on Nov. 7 to discuss efforts to combat antisemitism.

Newsom has not held a similar session with Palestinian community leaders and has made no public statements on the growing calls for a ceasefire in Gaza from leaders of other countries and international bodies, and from Californians with relatives in Gaza.

After multiple inquiries from CalMatters, the governor's office said Monday that it hopes to "organize a formal meeting" with Arab, Middle Eastern, Muslim and South Asian leaders "in the coming days."

While the Legislature is out of session, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle issued statements in support of Israel. Assemblymember Evan Low, a Cupertino Democrat, said the Asian American and Pacific Islander caucus stands "in unwavering solidarity with Israel… It always has. It always will." On Nov. 7, all 18 members of the Legislative Jewish Caucus sent a sternly worded letter to University of California and California State University leaders urging them to "act to counter the wave of antisemitic incidents sweeping your campuses."

"We have been deeply comforted by the response of our elected officials across the

spectrum and from both parties," said David Bocarsly, executive director of the Jewish Public Affairs Committee of California.

He noted that his coalition of Jewish community groups had spent years building relationships with lawmakers and other communities since it formed in 1972. "We've seen really strong statements condemning terrorism and supporting Jews and Israelis... And it's really heartening to see so many elected officials show up for us," he told CalMatters.

While the state's support for the Jewish community after Oct. 7 is warranted, the Palestinian community also deserves attention, say leaders of advocacy groups and others. They say the state elected officials who have chosen to weigh in have done little to represent the needs of Palestinian and Arab constituents.

That imbalance has become even more glaring as casualties mount in Gaza. According to the Health Ministry, an estimated 13,000 civilians have died, including more than 7,500 women and children, at least 100 aid workers and 53 journalists. The humanitarian crisis in Gaza is also worsening: on Monday, the World Health Organization said most hospitals are no longer functioning.

Protesters have demonstrated at the state Capitol and around California for weeks, but the activism boiled over last weekend when they forced the state Democratic Party to shut down its Saturday night convention programs.

"With every breath, with every step, we have expressed our disappointment. We have expressed our disappointment for the last six weeks," said Omar Altamimi, policy and advocacy coordinator for the Sacramento Valley/Central California chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

"Today we gather… to say that we will not forget. We will not forget where you stand now, and that will affect our decisions a year from now," he said at a rally Friday at the Capitol. "Muslims across the country have pledged not to vote for any elected official who has not called for a ceasefire in the last month and a half. And we will hold them accountable."

Among the civilians killed are relatives of Californians, who say they have not received the same kind of public outreach from state leaders as the victims of the Oct. 7 attack.

Basim Elkarra, executive director of the same Council on American-Islamic Relations chapter, said he has lost at least 65 members of his family in the war, though that number may be higher since they lost contact with relatives a week ago, he said.

Rajaie Batniji, a physician at Stanford Medical Center and CEO of a health care company, said on social media that 37 members of his family have been killed.

And Luqman Elbakri, a senior at the University of California, Berkeley, who also has family in Oakland and Saratoga, said he found out on Oct. 23 that 22 members of his extended family had died in an airstrike, including six children under age 5. They all lived in the same high-rise building, common in Gaza because of the impossibility of building outward.

"My last name, 'Elbakri,' no longer exists in Gaza's civil registry," he said.

BOILING POINT State leaders have little direct influence over foreign policy, but they can exert some pressure on the federal government. While California Republicans almost uniformly support Israel, Democrats are more divided, and advocates have focused on them since they are in power.

That's why, on Nov. 7, 50 Democratic Party delegates sent a letter to Newsom asking him to publicly support the ceasefire resolution introduced by members of Congress and to "demand that the United States reaffirm its leadership role as a negotiator in the pursuit of lasting peace."

Newsom's office confirmed receipt of the letter but did not respond to the delegates, according to Fatima Iqbal-Zubair, chair of the Democratic Party's Progressive Caucus. But at the California Democratic Party convention last weekend, the demands of protesters and delegates were harder to ignore.

They loudly cheered Rep. Barbara Lee of Oakland, who has been the most outspoken in calling for a ceasefire among the leading U.S. Senate candidates. They interrupted other candidates' speeches. And they breached convention center security on Saturday, leading the party to cancel that night's formal events.

The canceled sessions included meetings of the Latino, Black and Native American caucuses, who said they planned to discuss resolutions calling for a ceasefire. But Norma Alcalá, chair of the Latino Caucus, said she understood why the protesters needed to make their point.

However, party chair Rusty Hicks called the protests "completely unacceptable," while the Legislative Jewish Caucus issued statements condemning what it called "anti-Israel protesters."

"We fully support the right to protest loudly and noisily. But breaching security and shutting down a democratic process, particularly with chants calling for the destruction of Israel and appearing to justify the Hamas attack, is completely unacceptable," the group said in a statement.

The protests included chants and signs with slogans, specifically "from the river to the sea," which many in the Jewish community consider antisemitic and a call for the annihilation of Israel, although a 2020 statement on antisemitism signed by hundreds of scholars questions that interpretation.

But Seth Morrison, a Bay Area resident and spokesperson for Jewish Voice for Peace, rejected the party's response.

"People are dying... and all of this is done with our tax dollars," he said. "To keep doing business as usual when our taxes are going to kill children, I'm old enough to have been involved in the Vietnam protests, and it's the same."

Mahmoud Zahriya, former chair of the California Democratic Party's Arab American Caucus, told CalMatters: "A ceasefire has now become synonymous, for some reason, with supporting a militia or a terrorist group, when a ceasefire is supposed to be the end of violence for all people in the region."

But it wasn't all protests or conflict at the convention.

The Progressive Caucus held a panel Friday night with Arab and Jewish speakers, discussing how, before British intervention at the end of World War I, Jewish and Arab communities lived together peacefully, and that the fight for Palestinian freedom does not mean harm to Jews.

"I think we have to hold multiple truths simultaneously. And we can let our hearts be broken by all of it. The war crimes committed by Hamas were an unbridled massacre. And the revenge Israel is inflicting on all of Gaza is a genocide," said one of the panelists, Penny Rosenwasser, an activist, author and founding board member of Jewish Voice for Peace. "And I want to keep working for a future in which every Palestinian and Israeli life is precious, and all people live in freedom and safety."

NUMBERS GAME The imbalance of power and representation can be explained in part by a few figures: while there are more than 1.2 million Jewish Californians, there are about 715,000 Arab Americans, according to recent estimates.

There are also differences in migration patterns and history.

Marc Dollinger, a professor of Jewish history at San Francisco State University, said that in the late 1840s, about 100,000 Central European Jews emigrated to the United States, fleeing nationalist movements in Europe and seeking economic opportunity. During the Gold Rush, thousands of them moved west. One of the first notable Jewish politicians: Adolph Sutro, mayor of San Francisco from 1895 to 1897.

Their early years were prosperous, according to Dollinger. But nationally, the Jewish community faced persecution in the anti-immigrant movement of the early 20th century and after World War II, which pushed them to fight to secure representation.

Historians trace considerable Arab American immigration to California to the 20th century.

But it has historically been hard to track the number of Arab Americans, since there is no "Arab" ethnicity option on the U.S. census. As of the last census, people could write it in under "white."

It is also hard to pin down an exact figure for the number of Palestinians, since many Palestinians were expelled from their homeland during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war and emigrated to Lebanon, Jordan or Syria before arriving in the United States. Many people identify simply as Arab, according to Rashad Al-Dabbagh, executive director of the Arab American Civic Council, which seeks to foster community engagement.

Al-Dabbagh also noted that Arab communities were subjected to "unreasonable surveillance" after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which has discouraged civic engagement, including not wanting to fill out the census.

Why that matters: In the 2022 election, despite the state's large Arab American population, the state of California was not required under federal data to publish election materials in Arabic. The state did require translations in San Diego County under its own additional calculation, which has a lower population threshold.

But while it has been hard for supporters of Palestine to gain ground in the past, the current activism for a ceasefire has grown beyond Muslim and Middle Eastern communities.

Individual California cities have issued resolutions, and support has come from members of the Vietnamese community in Orange County and Black Lives Matter chapters in Los Angeles and San Francisco.

There is also some support in the Jewish community. In the past month, the Sacramento and Bay Area chapters of Jewish Voice for Peace say they have seen a large increase in membership. The Sacramento chapter has tripled, according to David Mandel, a spokesperson for the group.

But by and large, Dollinger said, California's Jewish community is allied with Israel. In part, that is generational, he said.

"This was a generation that saw Hitler. And this is a generation that witnessed the Holocaust. So when the State of Israel was created in 1948, from that generation's perspective... this was an absolute necessity," he said. The next generation, he added, witnessed conflicts that threatened the country, including the Arab-Israeli wars of 1967 and 1973.

Tony Quinn, a longtime political consultant, said that while the war is dividing the Democratic Party nationally, Democrats have a wider majority in California and the support of most Jewish voters.

"It could have an effect on some of the congressional races," he said. "I think Democrats have high hopes... But if I were a Democrat in Michigan, I'd be really worried about how this will affect Democrats there."

MIDDLE GROUND As the Gaza war continues, there have been more calls from the international community for a ceasefire, including from leaders of the United Nations, Amnesty International, Oxfam America and Doctors Without Borders, and the governments of China, Brazil, Ireland, Belgium and Spain. They say Israel must do more to avoid civilian casualties and not impose "collective punishment" on Palestinians in trying to kill Hamas fighters.

In Washington, D.C., the number of House members who signed a ceasefire resolution grew from 13 to 43, including eight California lawmakers.

On Monday, Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui of Sacramento called for a "temporary negotiated ceasefire." "Lasting peace can only be achieved if Hamas' terrorist infrastructure is dismantled," she said in a statement. "At the same time, we must exhaust every option to prevent the deaths of innocent civilians."

Rep. Eric Swalwell, who represents the East Bay, has not called for a full ceasefire, but he did co-author a letter to Secretary of State Antony Blinken urging him to address Israeli settler violence in the Palestinian West Bank, which is not under Hamas control.

Others still seek a middle ground, supporting Israel's war against Hamas while showing compassion for Palestinian civilians. They also call for the release of some 240 hostages (mostly Israelis, but at least 10 Americans) held by Hamas and other militant groups.

In supporting more humanitarian aid to Gaza, Democratic Rep. Ami Bera of Elk Grove said that when he spoke with a Palestinian constituent, he heard the "pain, anguish, despair and anger" over a personal loss, and also the deep pain of Jewish constituents. Bera said in a video that while he believes in Israel's right to self-defense, "innocent Palestinians also have a right to life, peace and dignity."

Leaders of the Legislature's Jewish, Black, Latino, women's, Native American, Asian American and Pacific Islander, and LGBTQ caucuses signed an Oct. 26 letter to President Biden urging him to protect all civilians. And the governor announced $30 million to protect synagogues, mosques and other places of worship in California.

Sen. Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat and co-chair of the Jewish Caucus, said he has been calling for a "more surgical approach to Hamas rather than broader-based bombing." The other co-chair, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, said that while he feels a responsibility to the Jewish community, he also feels "a deep responsibility to serve my Muslim, Palestinian and Arab constituents."

Still, lawmakers' efforts to walk a tightrope are not paying off with activists and other members of the Palestinian community.

Outside the state Capitol on Friday, Hatem Bazian, a professor in the ethnic studies department at the University of California, Berkeley, and a well-known advocate for Palestinians, gave a speech before a prayer service, and his message was not only for the nearly 200 people seated on the lawn in front of him, but for politicians.

"Today we are in a different era in terms of political engagement and mobilization," he said. "If you don't vote for and support the issues that matter to us, we don't care if you speak Arabic and say 'Salam-u-alaikum' in a decrepit way, or if you say you like our food... What I want to see is how you voted. This is not a community that will be taken for granted from now on."

And if voters can't find a candidate who meets their demands, they should run for office themselves, Bazian said.

Ola Subeh, a 36-year-old Chino resident who has an aunt in Gaza, echoed the sentiment. He said he is looking into alternatives to Democrats for 2024, perhaps independent parties, though he knows they have no real chance.

"We'll have to find people who start running for public office, and voice their support for them and go out and do everything possible to get better people in office who represent our people, who care about humanity. We are not one-sided or biased, because we have always been treated like… like nothing, it's as if we don't even belong, don't exist."

Keane Chukwuneta, a Democratic delegate, said he sees the issue, fundamentally, as a question of whether or not representative government works.

"I hope the party machinery starts listening to these voices, because they clearly exist and they're not going anywhere," he said, adding that he would rather see organizers work within the Democratic Party to reflect the concerns he and others share.

"That's not happening," he said, "and I think that's why we're here."

hl: El Histórico Veterans Hall del Valle de San Fernando Conmemora el Día de los Veteranos
twhy: Community story on a Veterans Day event; Gabriel's office listed among officials recognizing honorees.
hl_en: Historic San Fernando Valley Veterans Hall Commemorates Veterans Day
text_en:
With a broad white mustache on his upper lip and a white jacket displaying military paraphernalia, Jerry Watts walked proudly across the stage on Sunday, Nov. 12, to be recognized for his military service at the special Veterans Day event at the Birmingham Hospital Veterans Hall (BHVH), which also celebrated the 248th anniversary of the U.S. Marine Corps.

The event, which was free and open to the community, was organized by a group of American veterans in the San Fernando Valley who work to support and draw attention to veterans' causes. Recently, the group spearheaded an effort championed by Los Angeles City Councilmember Bob Blumenfield to designate the Veterans Hall as a city landmark.

Attendees had the opportunity to see an indoor exhibit on the armed forces, learn about the special tradition of cutting the USMC birthday cake, view a tribute to the POW/MIA or Missing Man Table, and enjoy lunch, live entertainment and other family activities. During the event, Watts, a Purple Heart recipient and BHVH Commander, and former Commander Philip Nathan (posthumously) were recognized for their service by local elected officials, including Blumenfield, the Office of Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, the Office of Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and the Office of U.S. Congressman Brad Sherman.

Watts, who joined the U.S. Army in 1966 at age 21 and served as a gunner on UH-1 military helicopters called "Hueys" at the height of the Vietnam War, said the event was meaningful. "Being recognized was emotional for me," said Watts, one of the BHVH honorees. "Most of us who came back from the Vietnam War… felt in our minds that we were heroes, but we came home to find out we weren't; that people shunned us. That made it very hard and contributed to many veteran suicides and to not being able to be part of the community. Today is the first day in our lives that changes that, so that veterans can contribute and be heard," Watts added.

Watts and other veterans plan to reach out to local veterans to let them know there is a place in the Valley where they can find support.

Located at 6543 Corbin Ave. in Woodland Hills, the Birmingham Hospital Veterans Hall, also known as Disabled American Veterans Birmingham Hospital Chapter 73, and a five-acre parcel were purchased and donated in 1947 by disabled American veterans of World War II, their families and friends. Among the donors was 1930s child star and former U.S. Ambassador Shirley Temple Black, whose brother was wounded in the Battle of Iwo Jima. The property, which includes the 8,000-square-foot hall, additional buildings, a pool and a picnic area, was recently added to the City of Los Angeles' list of Historic-Cultural Monuments, an effort championed by Blumenfield. Today, chapter members lead veteran-to-veteran volunteer efforts that include donating 13,500 servings of soup to New Directions for Veterans and delivering canned goods, sandwiches, clothing and more to homeless veterans living on the streets. In recent months, BHVH helped house a veteran on the property. Additional efforts to support veterans include offering the facilities as a quiet, supportive and comfortable study area for young veterans in college, and as an open-mic space for veterans interested in comedy and entertainment. By hosting events at BHVH, the veterans hope to continue raising awareness and building community support for veterans' causes. "Our Veterans Hall is an important community asset, a historic landmark and a special gathering place for veterans," said Bob Akre, a local veteran and member of the BHVH executive board. "Thanks to the generous donation of this property by World War II veterans and their families, we can host events like this special ceremony recognizing those who have served in the U.S. military and live in our community, as well as their families. BHVH is part of our neighborhood, part of our lives, and it is where we come together to serve others," Akre added. For more information about the Birmingham Hospital Veterans Hall, visit the website at www.bhvh.us or call us at (818) 938-9118.

hl: California prohibió 4 aditivos alimentarios. Esto es lo que hay que saber
author: Dana G Smith
twhy: Notes Gabriel proposed the additive bill and said it would not remove foods from shelves.
hl_en: California Banned 4 Food Additives. Here's What to Know
text_en:
These substances are found in candy, tortillas and sodas and have been linked to serious health problems. California has banned four common food additives — Red Dye No. 3, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil and propylparaben — through the California Food Safety Act.

The law will take effect on January 1, 2027, which offers “considerable time for brands to update their recipes to avoid these harmful chemicals,” Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement to members of the California State Assembly on October 7, when he signed the bill. From then on, any person or entity that manufactures, sells or distributes food products containing these additives in California may be fined up to $5,000 for a first violation and up to $10,000 for each additional violation.

Here is what you need to know about the ingredients, why they were banned and what it means for you, whether you live in California or anywhere else.

What are the additives and which food products are they found in?

The four banned ingredients are most often found in ultra-processed foods. Red Dye No. 3 is used as a coloring in frostings or icings, drinks and red or pink candies, especially those flavored with cinnamon, mint, cherry or berries. This includes many holiday candies, such as Valentine's Day conversation hearts, Halloween candy corn and Christmas candy canes, as well as some brands of gummies. Brominated vegetable oil is found mostly in store-brand or generic citrus-flavored sodas, where it acts as a stabilizer for the flavoring oils. Potassium bromate acts as a leavening agent and propylparaben is a preservative; both are often used in packaged bakery products such as tortillas, breads and cakes.

Research conducted over recent decades, mainly in animals, has linked these four chemicals to cancer, reproductive problems and neurobehavioral disorders such as hyperactivity. Some of these problems may be due to the possible effects of some of these chemicals on the endocrine system, which controls hormonal function in the body.

One of the main goals of the California law is to protect children, who are often more likely to consume foods containing these chemicals. Experts say minors are also at greater risk of suffering the possible negative consequences of food additives because their developing organs are more vulnerable.

Because of these kinds of concerns, the use of these chemicals in food is already banned in the European Union, as well as in several other countries.

I don't live in California. Are other states also going to ban these ingredients?

New York state lawmakers proposed a similar statewide ban earlier this year; the bill is currently in the Senate Agriculture Committee.

In California, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who first proposed the bill in April, said in a statement that the goal of the bill was not to pull foods containing these additives from supermarkets. Instead, it will require food companies to “switch to the safer alternative ingredients they already use in Europe and in so many other places around the world.” If food manufacturers update their recipes for California, the removal of the chemicals may become widespread throughout the United States.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) periodically reevaluates authorized food additives at the request of interested parties or as relevant new research emerges. The FDA is currently reevaluating Red Dye No. 3 and brominated vegetable oil, which could lead to changes throughout the United States.

hl_en: California passes law to ban food additives in the United States
text_en:
The California Legislature approved the first bill in the United States to ban additives in food. As a result, four chemical substances could no longer be used in beverages and foods. First U.S. state to create this type of law This would be the first time a U.S. state has approved a bill like this, which seeks to ban four chemicals that are compromising Americans' health.

If Gavin Newsom, California's Democratic governor, approves Bill 418, the sale of foods and beverages containing Red Dye No. 3, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil and propylparaben will be banned starting in 2027.

This is the first time a state has banned food additives, despite their being approved by the Food and Drug Administration.

Although these four chemicals are illegal in the European Union and other countries around the world, in the U.S. they could still be found in products such as "orange sodas, frostings, hamburger buns, candy and processed foods," NBC News writes on its website.

Jesse Gabriel was the one who introduced the bill in the Assembly together with Buffy Wicks, and for them it is a victory for public health, since these four additives can be found in foods aimed at children. In addition, they are easily accessible to people with limited resources.

"This will make our food supply much safer," Gabriel told NBC News. "This will give parents more confidence that when they buy food at the grocery store, they don't have to worry that there is something in there that is dangerous for their kids."

hl_en: Governor Newsom Signs the Nation's First Bill to Regulate Voluntary Carbon Offsets
text_en:
Last weekend, Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation to establish the nation's first regulations for the voluntary carbon offset market, which has been plagued by accusations of corporate “greenwashing” and media reports suggesting that as much as 90 percent of the offsets marketed by certain companies fail to achieve any meaningful reduction in carbon emissions.

Assembly Bill (AB) 1305, written by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and co-authored by state Senators Lena González and Monique Limón, would require new transparency and disclosure requirements for buyers and sellers of carbon offsets, which would help ensure that companies engage in due diligence before making climate-related claims and encourage them to rely only on high-quality offsets that correspond to real emissions reductions or removals.

“AB 1305 is an important new tool to address the devastating impacts of climate change,” Gabriel said. “As we confront the climate crisis, we cannot afford to waste time on corporate greenwashing or bogus offsets that do nothing for our planet. This new law will ensure that companies keep their promises when it comes to climate action and that we are protecting our planet for future generations.”

AB 1305 will require buyers and sellers of voluntary offset credits to disclose the details of offset projects, the methodology for determining the number of credits issued, and the data and calculation methods needed to allow independent re-creation of emissions reduction estimates.

AB 1305 will also combat corporate greenwashing, the act of providing the public or investors with misleading or false information about the environmental impact of a company's products and operations, by requiring entities that make claims of significant emissions reductions or of being “carbon neutral” to disclose how those claims are accurate. This information will allow researchers and the public to better assess the legitimacy and effectiveness of the credits, as well as shine a light on misleading claims by polluting companies.

“Many carbon offsets in the voluntary carbon market do not represent real emissions reductions or represent far less than is claimed,” said Barbara Hays, director of UC Berkeley's Carbon Trading Project. “Offset credit quality varies widely, and the lack of transparency in project details and carbon calculations makes it difficult for credit buyers, raters and researchers to assess which credits are real and to evaluate the overall effectiveness of the program. The stakes are high. We are entrusting the effectiveness of our climate mitigation efforts today to a set of claims and calculations that we cannot review, under programs with known problems.”

hl_en: Governor Newsom Signs Landmark Legislation Banning Dangerous Food Additives
text_en:
Governor Gavin Newsom on October 7 signed first-of-its-kind legislation banning the use of four dangerous chemicals in processed foods and beverages sold in California.

Written by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland), Assembly Bill (AB) 418, the California Food Safety Act, would prohibit the manufacture, sale or distribution in California of any food product containing Red Dye No. 3, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil or propylparaben.

AB 418 was amended in the state Senate to remove titanium dioxide from the list of banned additives and to delay the bill's implementation until 2027 to give food companies time to negotiate new contracts and introduce new recipes.

"The governor's signature today [Saturday] represents a huge step forward in our effort to protect children and families in California from dangerous and toxic chemicals in our food supply," said Gabriel. "It is unacceptable that the United States is so far behind the rest of the world when it comes to food safety. This bill will not ban any foods or products; it will simply require food companies to make minor modifications to their recipes and switch to the safer alternative ingredients they already use in Europe and many other places around the world." Because of major flaws in the FDA approval process, which has allowed nearly 99 percent of food chemicals to escape meaningful, independent FDA review, the United States has become a global outlier on food safety. The use of these chemicals has already been banned in the 27 nations of the European Union (EU), as well as in many other countries, because of scientific research linking them to significant health harms, including cancer, reproductive problems, and behavioral and developmental problems in children. "AB 418 is the most important food safety bill in more than a decade, and its passage is a historic victory for protecting children and families from dangerous food chemicals," said Scott Faber, senior vice president of government affairs at the Environmental Working Group. "For decades, chemical companies have been able to exploit a legal loophole that allows food additives to escape proper FDA review and oversight. Because the FDA has failed to keep us safe, it has become the responsibility of states like California to step up and lead."

Many major brands and manufacturers, including Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Gatorade and Panera, have voluntarily stopped using the additives that would be banned under AB 418 because of concerns about their impact on human health. One of these chemicals, Red Dye No. 3, is already banned by the FDA for use in cosmetics.

hl_en: These are the four food additives California just banned
text_en:
The ban on four food additives is now law in California, United States. The rule, which takes effect in 2027, aims to stop the manufacture, sale or distribution of potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil, propylparaben and Red Dye No. 3. The law signed by Governor Gavin Newsom is a first in the country and will affect some 12,000 foods, including cereals, drinks and candy, according to USA Today. Although contained in thousands of products across the U.S., these additives have never been approved for human consumption by the FDA, so Newsom said the law is "a positive step forward" until the FDA reviews and sets national regulations for their use.

Jesse Gabriel, the Democratic legislator who pushed the law, clarified that the new rule "will not ban any food or product, it will simply require food companies to make small changes to their recipes and use safer alternative ingredients."

Opposing voices: the new law generated great controversy with associations representing producers of foods with these additives, who had opposed the measure for months. After the signing, the National Confectioners Association accused California lawmakers of "making decisions based on catchy phrases rather than scientific data," arguing the governor's signature would undermine consumer confidence and cause confusion.

Health effects: according to research, brominated vegetable oil can cause nervous system damage and chronic headaches; propylparaben caused fertility problems in mice; and potassium bromate is linked to thyroid and kidney cancer. Studies reported by the Daily Mail showed more than 10% of candies in the U.S. contain Red Dye 3, which caused cancer in lab animals at very high doses.

hl_en: California bans Red Dye No. 3 and other harmful chemicals in Skittles
text_en:
California has become the first U.S. state to ban the use of four potentially harmful additives, including Red Dye No. 3, in foods and beverages; the additives have been linked to a variety of illnesses, including cancer, and are already banned in dozens of countries.

Did California ban Skittles? What does Red Dye No. 3 or potassium bromate cause? California Food Safety Act What will change in California? Supporters of the law say it does not mean popular products will suddenly disappear from store shelves, but rather that companies will have to modify their recipes in order to offer the same foods and beverages with healthier ingredients. "Californians will still be able to access and enjoy their favorite food products, with greater confidence in the safety of those products," explained Governor Gavin Newsom, who signed the bill into law last Saturday. The proposal has been the subject of a false claim that California is trying to ban Skittles. In fact, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the Democrat who sponsored the bill, has said that Skittles are sold with alternative ingredients in the European Union, where the four additives are already banned. The Food and Drug Administration banned the use of Red Dye No. 3 in cosmetics in 1990 after evidence showed that it caused cancer in laboratory animals. But the government has not banned its use in food, and it is an ingredient in corn-based candies. Brominated vegetable oil and potassium bromate have also been associated with harmful effects on the respiratory and nervous systems, while propylparaben can negatively affect reproductive health. The California Food Safety Act prohibits the manufacture, distribution and sale of foods and beverages containing brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben and Red Dye No. 3, which can be found in candies, fruit juices, cookies and more. The law will not take effect until 2027, which according to Newsom will give companies enough time to "revise their recipes to avoid these harmful chemicals" in their products.

hl_en: California becomes first state to ban food dyes, generating controversy in the candy industry
text_en:
SAN FRANCISCO, CA - California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a modified law banning food dyes in the state, making California the first state to implement the measure. The law has generated controversy because of its impact on colorful candies such as Skittles.

Jesse Gabriel, author of the bill, received support from Arnold Schwarzenegger, the actor, bodybuilder and former governor of California. The National Confectioners Association has expressed concern, arguing the banned ingredients are safe according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

The approved bill removed titanium dioxide, which is used to color foods such as candy, from the ban. Its implementation was delayed to 2027 to give manufacturers a chance to adapt. California will thus become the first state to ban four food additives already banned in many other countries over possible health risks.

Also, Newsom vetoed a bill that sought to ban caste-based discrimination in California. The bill had divided the South Asian community, with some seeing it as necessary to fight discrimination and others arguing existing anti-discrimination laws were enough. Over the weekend the governor signed and vetoed several other bills on the environment, drug abuse and social media transparency. Other laws passed raise penalties for fentanyl possession, require naloxone at amusement parks and stadiums, and create a retirement benefit fund for mixed martial arts fighters. Newsom still has several bills to consider before Saturday's deadline.

hl_en: California Bans Chemical Additives Used in the Manufacture of Popular Candies
text_en:
California is the first state to ban four chemical additives used in the manufacture of some popular candies and in processed foods and beverages.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed bill AB 418 this weekend, which affects the manufacture of certain candies, such as Peeps, Hot Tamales and Dubbler Bubble Twist Gum, along with thousands of other processed food products.

The bill, introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of foods whose ingredients include Red Dye No. 3, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil and propylparaben. Officials praised the bill as "first-of-its-kind legislation" in the United States. According to the assemblymember's office, the bill does not cause products to stop being sold, but will require manufacturers to adjust their formulas.

"The use of the banned chemicals has already been regulated in the 27 countries of the European Union, as well as in many other countries, because of scientific research linking them to significant health harms, including cancer, reproductive problems, and behavioral and developmental problems in children," Gabriel explained. Major global brands and manufacturers, such as Coca Cola, Pepsi, Gatorade and Panera, have already voluntarily stopped using the additives banned under AB 418, which is known as the California Food Safety Act, due to concern about the impact on human health, the assemblymember's office said. In 1990, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) decided to ban Red Dye No. 3 in cosmetics, after it was linked to cases of cancer in animals.

The assemblymember said the agency reacted belatedly, and 33 years later the additive is still found in the food supply despite its link to cancer cases having been established.

The National Confectioners Association (NCA), which represents dozens of candy and chocolate manufacturers, criticized the bill signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, asserting that it replaces a uniform national food safety system with a patchwork of inconsistent state requirements created by legislative fiat that will cause an increase in the cost of food.

According to the NCA, the approved law enters territory that should be administered by the federal government and not by the states.

"They are making decisions based on sound bites rather than science. Governor Newsom's approval of this bill will undermine consumer confidence and create confusion around food safety," the NCA said.

Although the bill was signed this weekend, the ban does not take effect until 2027, so that candy and processed food manufacturers have enough time to negotiate new contracts and implement the necessary changes to their recipes.

Although there was full support for passing the bill as initially introduced, a fifth chemical additive, titanium dioxide, was set aside in an effort to obtain broader bipartisan support. Titanium dioxide is a coloring additive that makes products more visually appealing, in addition to helping keep the pigment from losing its brightness over time.

"Things like this are not partisan, they are common sense," declared former California governor and sports and fitness icon Arnold Schwarzenegger, who expressed his support for AB 418 in his daily Pump Club newsletter. "I am a small-government guy, but I have also seen that sometimes, in a world where every big industry has an army of lobbyists and our kids have no one fighting for them, the government has to step in," Schwarzenegger added.

hl_en: California Bans the Use of 4 Potentially Harmful Food Additives
text_en:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a bill that bans the sale, manufacture or distribution of food products with Red Dye No. 3 and other additives generally found in cereals, candy and soft drinks.

The measure is Assembly Bill 418, known as the California Food Safety Act, which bans the use of Red Dye No. 3, brominated vegetable oil, propylparaben and potassium bromate, CNN reports.

The law, promoted by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Buffy Wicks and backed by Governor Gavin Newsom, could [affect] 12,000 products that use those substances, according to the Environmental Working Group.

Newsom sent a letter to the California State Assembly on Saturday in which he states that “signing this bill is a positive step in relation to these four food additives until the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reviews and establishes updated national safety levels for these additives,” CNN quotes. The approval of AB 418 is a “huge step forward in our effort to protect children and families in California from dangerous and toxic chemicals in our food supply,” Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the author of the bill, told the Los Angeles Times.

Based on scientific research and their harmful health effects, including reproductive problems and cancer, these chemical additives are already banned in the European Union.

The announcement drew an immediate reaction from the National Confectioners Association, which criticized Newsom's measure, saying it will create confusion around food safety and undermine consumer confidence. The law “replaces a uniform national food safety system with a patchwork of inconsistent state requirements created by legislative fiat that will increase food costs,” they said in a statement. With fines of up to $10,000 for violations, the law would take effect on January 1, 2027. For Environmental Working Group president Ken Cook, the law “is a milestone in food safety, and California is once again leading the nation.”

hl_en: Death of Young Latino in San Pedro Reflects Rise in Gun Violence
text_en:
Joseph Isaiah Saldana had his whole life ahead of him when a bullet that went through the walls of the house where he was enjoying a birthday party killed him.

It was September 30 when police responded to a shooting at around 11:34 p.m. in the 1200 block of North Park Western Drive in San Pedro, in southern Los Angeles County.

Officers found four victims with gunshot wounds, among them 17-year-old Saldana, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

Joseph's unexpected death from a gunshot that went through the walls and reached him in the kitchen of the house where he was revived the issue of gun violence.

In addition to gun violence ending the life of a young man at a very early age, Joseph, a recent honors graduate of Dominguez Hills High School, seemed to have a bright future.

On the Joseph Isaiah Saldana GoFundMe page created to raise funds for the funeral, one can read that "Joe Joe had the sweetest demeanor and a smile that would light up a room."

The teenager is described as "an innocent kid who enjoyed spending his time listening to music, playing video games and spending time with his friends and family."

And they conclude by saying: "this tragedy has left everyone speechless… Joe Joe is survived by his father, his mother, his 3 siblings, his grandparents, his uncles, his niece and nephew, his aunts, his cousins and his friends."

All that police have revealed about the unfortunate tragedy is that the suspects fled in a gray sedan. Gun violence: According to an analysis of California Department of Justice statistics conducted by the Los Angeles Times newspaper, there is a worrying trend in the state, as more violent crimes are committed with guns even though the state is a leader in enacting laws aimed at greater gun control.

Data from the Criminal Justice Statistics Center suggest that violent crime has been on the rise since 2014, with a particular increase in the use of firearms in homicides and aggravated assaults. According to the Times analysis, in 2020 gun homicides rose 40.6%, and gun assaults grew by as much as 29% compared with 2019.

In California this year, we had a shooting in Monterey Park, another at a farm in Half Moon Bay, and one more at a bar in Trabuco Canyon.

Amid a series of shootings across the country that left at least 104 people dead in the last 72 hours, and following the decision of a U.S. District Court judge that blocked California's ban on high-capacity magazines, Governor Gavin Newsom enacted a package of new gun safety laws. One of the most important new laws is AB 28 by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino, which imposes an 11% excise tax on firearms and ammunition sold by gun manufacturers and dealers. AB 28 is estimated to generate $160 million annually to fund school safety and violence prevention programs, including initiatives to prevent school shootings, bolster firearm investigations and remove guns from domestic abusers.

It should be remembered that the federal government already applies a tax of between 10 and 11% depending on the type of weapon, which is used to fund wildlife conservation and hunter education programs.

In total, gun buyers will have to pay more than 20% in taxes each time they buy a new one. Other laws enacted by the governor are SB 2, which strengthens regulations on the public carrying of concealed weapons; SB 452, which requires microstamping on handgun cartridges to help trace guns used in crimes; AB 455, which keeps guns out of the reach of potentially dangerous people; AB 725, which updates the definition of a firearm to include ghost gun or homemade gun parts; and AB 732, which strengthens the process for removing firearms from people who are prohibited from possessing them.

hl_en: Governor Gavin Newsom Signs Firearms-Related Bills
text_en:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed several gun-related bills this Tuesday, September 26, among them a tax increase on sales and rules for people to obtain a permit to carry concealed weapons.

While the federal government already imposes taxes of 10% or 11% on the sale of guns and ammunition, depending on the type of weapon, California, with the signing of bill AB 28, will add a special 11% levy on the purchase of guns and ammunition.

With this decision, California will become the only state with a separate tax on guns and ammunition, according to the gun control advocacy group Brady.

With the revenue obtained from collecting the tax, California will pay for safety improvements in public schools and various gun violence prevention programs, some aimed at young people who belong to gangs.

The money from the federal tax, which has been in effect for more than 10 years, goes to wildlife conservation programs and hunter education.

There are exceptions to the tax, such as police agencies and businesses with extremely low sales. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the author of the bill, said the tax funds will go toward gun violence prevention and to reduce the costs associated with the health and criminal justice systems in treating patients who are victims of gun violence.

Another important bill signed this Tuesday was SB 2, by Senator Anthony Portantino, which will change the rules for carrying concealed weapons.

SB 2 requires permit holders to be 21 years old, in addition to banning concealed weapons in most public places, such as parks, schools, government buildings, hospitals and places where alcohol is sold, as well as at demonstrations and public gatherings.

According to the KTLA network, the California Rifle and Pistol Association filed a lawsuit against the law signed by Governor Newsom that bars people from carrying guns in most public places.

Senator Portantino said the desire to protect oneself with a concealed firearm is common sense, but said firearms may not be necessary on a golf course or in a restaurant.

Another bill signed by Newsom will require that all handguns sold in California starting in 2028 have microstamping technology, which leaves unique marks on bullets that will allow guns used in shootings to be traced.

The bill signings come a few days after the California Legislature approved a campaign led by Newsom to amend the United States Constitution.

The measure calls for a constitutional convention of the states to consider additional federal rules on the purchase and use of firearms, but two-thirds of the states need to approve similar measures for this process to move forward. California has one of the lowest firearm death rates in the country, ranking 43rd among 50 states, with 9 deaths per 100,000 residents, according to 2021 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

However, violent crime has recently increased, with the violent crime rate rising 6.1% in 2022, according to the California Department of Justice.

hl_en: Hope the Mission Executives Bike More Than 500 Miles to Advocate for Affordable Housing
text_en:
Hope the Mission executives arrived in Sacramento late last week after biking more than 500 miles to meet with state lawmakers and advocate for policy that supports affordable housing and the ability to build emergency and transitional housing.

Ken Craft, founder and CEO, and Rowan Vansleve, president, rode their bicycles from the organization's headquarters in the San Fernando Valley to the State Capitol. When they arrived, they were greeted by lawmakers Senator Caroline Menjivar (SD-20), Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo (AD-40) and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (AD-46).

Craft and Vansleve embarked on this trip to raise funds to open a new shelter and to advocate for housing policy, such as Senate Bill 4 (Wiener), which would provide a streamlined process for faith-based organizations and nonprofit colleges to develop affordable housing on their property, regardless of local zoning restrictions.

"We biked to Sacramento because we need a revolution in affordable housing and shelter to combat the housing and homelessness crisis in our state," Vansleve said. "We are also there to thank our lawmakers for developing good policies that encourage the development of affordable and supportive housing, and we want to encourage them to keep supporting similar policies. The problem can be addressed by working together through public-private partnerships, like Project HomeKey, which allowed us to open three family shelters in Los Angeles."

"To effectively address the homelessness crisis, we must build a strong coalition from our neighborhoods and local nonprofits to local governments and state offices," Menjivar said. "I am committed to working with city and county departments, community members and organizations, such as Hope the Mission, to ensure that our solutions are inclusive and successful. I thank Rowan Vansleve, Ken Craft and Hope the Mission for their dedicated service to California's most vulnerable."

At the arrival ceremony, Hope the Mission and the lawmakers reaffirmed their commitment to working together to address a problem that affects their districts and communities across California.

"Hope the Mission has done extraordinary work to help people experiencing homelessness in our community," Gabriel said. "But we must do much more to address our housing and homelessness crisis. We need more affordable housing and more tools and resources to help organizations like Hope the Mission permanently house more people."

"Addressing the homelessness crisis is one of the top priorities for our community members and our office, and Hope the Mission has long been a leader in getting our neighbors out of homelessness," Schiavo said. "I am grateful for their incredible feat (biking 500 miles) to raise awareness of the housing solutions needed. I am excited to work together to fight for the resources needed to ensure we have a home for everyone in need."

hl_en: X sues California to avoid revealing how it makes content decisions
text_en:
On Sept. 9, Elon Musk's X Corp filed a lawsuit to block California's content moderation law AB 578. In the filing, the company states that the law, enacted in September 2022, is unconstitutional because it violates the right to free expression. This argument stems from the "terms of service report" requirement that state authorities impose on social media platforms. X Corp argues this forces them to engage in speech against their will and interferes with the company's editorial judgments, which it says is unconstitutional.

The law enacted by the state of California aims to establish "transparency measures" under which certain companies must make their content moderation policies and statistics public. However, X Corp alleges that the state's true intent is to pressure platforms to remove content the state views as problematic. Musk's company thus describes the measure as also violating the AB587 law, the Dormant Commerce Clause. This law grants platforms immunity from liability, which applies to any action taken voluntarily to restrict access to material the provider considers obscene, lewd or violent.

In response to the lawsuit, the assemblymember who authored AB 587, Jesse Gabriel, issued a statement explaining that it does not stipulate any moderation policy; it only requires that information be made public about whether content is moderated and how this is done.

"If Twitter has nothing to hide, then it should have no objection to this bill," Gabriel posted on X Corp. Some tech groups have also spoken out against this law and in favor of X Corp's request to block the law, which provides for penalties of up to $15,000 for those who do not make public the information requested by the state. Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, told Ars Technica that publishing moderation work plans could have negative consequences for users, since it means each company could set its own editorial standards based on intrusive disclosures demanded by the government itself.

hl_en: California Approves New Tax on Sales of Guns and Ammunition
text_en:
California Approves a New Tax on the Sale of Firearms and Ammunition

The new tax would be 11%, comparable to the highest rate charged by the federal government on firearms in the United States; the money would be used to improve safety in public schools.

Published Sept. 8, 2023, 3:05 PM EDT. Updated Sept. 8, 2023, 3:22 PM EDT.

SACRAMENTO, California. – California lawmakers approved a new tax on the sale of firearms and ammunition, which could be 11%.

The state Senate gave the final approval needed for a new bill to impose the tax on the sale of firearms and ammunition in California.

According to the bill, the money collected from the tax will be used to improve safety in the state's public schools and to fund gun violence prevention programs.

According to the bill, the new tax would not be charged to people who buy firearms or ammunition, but would instead apply to the businesses that sell them in the Golden State.

However, before the tax on firearms and ammunition becomes a reality, the bill must go to Governor Gavin Newsom, who may sign it into law by October 14.

Firearm Taxes in California and in the United States

The bill passed by the California Senate proposes creating a firearms tax that would be the first of its kind in the United States.

The federal government already imposes a levy on firearm sales in the states and uses the money collected for wildlife conservation and hunter safety.

However, no state has taxes specific to firearms. In California, about $37 is already charged on firearm sales under different fee schedules, and that money is used to pay for background checks.

But the California governor's decision on a new tax on the sale of firearms and ammunition remains uncertain, even though he has been very critical of shootings around the country in which high-powered weapons are used.

"He has been an incredible national leader and champion on gun violence prevention issues, and he continues to be bold on this front," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Los Angeles and author of the bill.

"Let's not allow politics to get in the way of saving the lives of our children and providing mental health care in our school districts," added Democratic state Senator Anthony Portantino, according to an AP report.

If Governor Newsom signs the bill approved by the Legislature, the tax would take effect on July 1, 2024, and would generate about $159 million in the first year, according to an estimate by the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration.

But even if Newsom signs the bill, some gun rights advocates in the state say they are preparing to file lawsuits seeking to block it from taking effect.

Mass Shooting Between Gangs in Downtown

SACRAMENTO, California. – One of the criminal tragedies that marked this year was the mass shooting in downtown Sacramento in the early hours of Sunday, April 3, in which six people died and more than a dozen were wounded.

The incident occurred near K and 10th Streets, a few blocks from the State Capitol and the Golden 1 Center, at a time when Downtown streets were full of people leaving nightclubs and bars.

Three victims were identified as Johntaya Alexander, 21; Melinda Davis, 57, a woman experiencing homelessness; and Yamile Martínez-Andrade, 21, the only Hispanic victim of the shooting.

Also killed were Sergio Harris, 38; Joshua Hoye-Lucchesi, 32; and Devazia Turner, 29, who died at the scene and were later identified as members of two gangs that caused the shooting, according to police investigations. Several suspects were identified and arrested days later.

hl_en: Bill against dangerous substances in food advances
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — First-of-its-kind legislation to ban the use of five dangerous and toxic chemicals in processed foods and beverages sold in California was approved by its final policy committee, passing the Senate Environmental Quality Committee 5 to 1.

Introduced by Encino Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, Assembly Bill (AB) 418 would prohibit the manufacture, sale or distribution of any food product in California that contains Red Dye No. 3, titanium dioxide, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil or propylparaben.

The use of these chemicals has already been banned in the European Union (EU) and many other jurisdictions because of scientific research linking them to significant health harms, including cancer, reproductive problems and behavioral and developmental problems in children.

"Today's strong vote by our final policy committee marks a major step forward in our effort to protect children and families in California from dangerous and toxic chemicals in our food supply," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel.

"It is unacceptable that the United States is so far behind the rest of the world when it comes to banning these dangerous additives.

"We don't love our children any less than they do in Europe, and it is not too much to ask food and beverage manufacturers to switch to the safer alternative ingredients they already use in so many other nations around the world," he added.

Numerous scientific studies have linked these chemicals to significant health harms, including an increased risk of cancer, behavioral problems in children, harm to the reproductive system and harm to the immune system.

As a result, the EU and many other nations, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, China and Japan, have already banned their use in food.

In addition, many major brands and manufacturers, including Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Gatorade, Dunkin Donuts, Papa John's Pizza and Panera, have voluntarily stopped using these additives in their products.

AB 418 will not remove any products from the shelves, nor will it ban any product that California consumers currently enjoy. Products such as Skittles continue to be sold in stores across Europe using safe alternatives.

"For decades, the FDA has failed to keep us safe from toxic food chemicals," said Scott Faber, senior vice president for Government Affairs at the Environmental Working Group. "The chemical companies keep exploiting a loophole that allows food additives whose safety has not been adequately reviewed by the FDA. And the FDA consistently fails to reassess chemicals, even in light of new science. The food and confectionery industries know the review process at the FDA is broken," he added.

AB 418 is needed because chemical companies in the United States have been able to exploit a major loophole

and avoid meaningful independent review by the FDA of numerous food additives, which puts the United States far behind many other nations when it comes to food safety.

If it becomes law, AB 418 would require companies to make modifications to the recipes of products sold in California and could spur a nationwide transition toward safer alternatives.

AB 418 is expected to be considered by members of the Senate Appropriations Committee in August, after the Legislature's summer recess.
