hl_en: Governor signs protective order reform law
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — Last week, Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill (AB) 467, a bipartisan measure created by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, Democrat of Encino, that will strengthen judges' ability to grant and modify domestic violence protective orders. "At a time when violence against women and domestic abuse have risen to record levels around the world, it is critical that we ensure domestic violence restraining orders offer the most complete protection possible," said Assemblymember Gabriel.

"This legislation will clarify a judge's authority over these orders and extend the amount of time a court can modify the orders to ensure we provide broad protection to victims of domestic abuse," he added.

Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen, the bill's sponsor, praised the new law as crucial to ensuring that crime victims can ask the court to change the terms of restraining orders during the 10 years those orders are in effect.

In some cases, victims will need more protection from the court and in others less.

District Attorney Rosen said: "Giving judges the ability to modify their own court orders will help domestic violence victims manage the protections to keep them safe."

Ambiguity in current law has left some courts confused about when and for how long they have authority over domestic violence restraining orders and when they can modify provisions related to contact between the restrained person and the protected person, which may be a "peaceful contact" order (PCO) or a no-contact order (NCO).

Victims often seek to modify the order from PCO to NCO or vice versa.

Some courts have determined that if the defendant is no longer serving a sentence and is not on probation, they have no jurisdiction to modify the order, even if both the victim and the defendant request it. This confusion in current law is harmful to both victims and defendants.

AB 467 gives sentencing courts the authority to modify the terms of a peaceful contact order or a no-contact order and to make modifications to the order while the domestic violence protective order is in effect.

author: N+ Univision
twhy: Gabriel's related media literacy bill AB 787 is mentioned in one sentence.
hl_en: California seeks to combat fake news and cyberbullying with digital literacy in schools
text_en:
SAN FRANCISCO, California - Recognizing fake news, knowing the risks of social media and resisting cyberbullying could become required subjects in California's school curriculum under a bill moving through the Legislature. AB 873, introduced by Democratic Assemblymember Marc Berman of Menlo Park, would instruct the state's Instructional Quality Commission to incorporate digital literacy into K-12 curricula in English, math, science, history and social studies. Eventually all public school students would receive media literacy lessons every year in all subjects.

"We need to make sure the next generation has the critical thinking and analysis skills needed to discern what is presented to them online," Berman said. In 2018, California adopted optional media literacy guidelines covering online privacy and safety, doing online research and related topics. This bill goes further by specifically addressing misinformation and social media use, and would be mandatory in classrooms. The bill passed the Assembly unanimously and is now in the Senate Education Committee.

A related bill, AB 787 by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, Democrat of Woodland Hills, would require State Superintendent Tony Thurmond to survey schools on the current state of media literacy education and then devise a model program to implement statewide. But if AB 873 passes, media literacy would reach classrooms much sooner.

If one or both bills pass, California would join a growing number of states adopting media literacy curricula, in part due to concern about online misinformation and teens' growing social media use. In most states the guidelines are optional, but in some, such as New Jersey, Delaware and Texas, the lessons are mandatory. Berman said he was inspired to write the bill when he learned social media is the main source of news for many people, including teens. A 2019 Stanford study found two-thirds of students surveyed could not tell editorial content from advertising.

hl: 246 tiroteos y más de 17 mil víctimas en 147 días en Estados Unidos
author: Manuel Ocaño / Especial para La Opinión
twhy: Presents him as the legislator who won Assembly passage of a gun-industry tax to fund violence prevention, with favorable quotes.
hl_en: 246 Shootings and More Than 17,000 Victims in 147 Days in the United States
text_en:
This Saturday was the 147th day of this year, and 246 mass shootings and 23 mass killings had already been recorded in the country, leaving 17,130 dead, among them 107 children.

These may be cold figures from the archives of gun violence, but the business of selling guns does not stop, and it represents a human tragedy for the wounded, among them 252 children this year, and for the survivors. Even so, a national background check system of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) counted, through the end of April – the most recent month tallied this year – 1,369,296 new applications to purchase firearms, the equivalent of 11,410 new requests per day.

“It is shameful that gun manufacturers are making record profits at the same time that gun violence has become the leading cause of death for children in the United States,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. The lawmaker from north Los Angeles got the California Assembly to approve a bill to raise taxes on firearms businesses and use the money collected to fund gun violence prevention and school shooting safety programs.

The tax would be higher than the regular sales tax in California, and is considered an excise tax.

“This bill will fund critical school safety measures and proven violence prevention programs that will save lives and protect communities throughout California,” Gabriel said.

His proposal estimates that up to $160 million a year will be raised through a new excise tax on firearm manufacturers, dealers and sellers of guns and ammunition in the state of California. The money will help fund a whole package of programs to prevent the use of guns and mitigate their harm among Californians.

The funds could finance, for example, the state's Violence Prevention and Intervention program, as well as school mental health services and safety measures.

But Gabriel says the funds can also support firearm relinquishment programs for domestic abusers and other prohibited persons, services for victims of gun violence, and firearm safety education.

During the period when Assemblymember Gabriel's proposal was being debated in California's lower house, two of the largest shootings in California took place in just two days, both with assault rifles, in Monterey Park and Half Moon Bay.

Reina Webb, of Moms Demand Action in California, an organization that has supported Gabriel's proposal, said the bill would have made it at least a little harder for those guns to be sold in the state. The proposal “is a transformative approach to addressing gun violence and a crucial step toward improving the safety of all California families,” she said.

The measure has now moved to the California Senate, where it is expected to be approved without major opposition so that it can take effect on July 1, 2024.

The proposal, AB28, or the Gun Violence Prevention, Healing and Recovery Act, establishes an 11 percent tax on gross receipts from the retail sale of firearms, precursor parts and ammunition. “The bill would require that the money received in the fund, once appropriated, be used to fund various gun violence prevention, education, research, response and investigation programs,” the text says. It states that “gun violence is a public safety and public health crisis across the country. Firearms are now the leading cause of death for American children.”

Although the measure acknowledges that California's firearm death rates are lower than the national average, firearms are one of the leading causes of death, injury and trauma among young people, and especially among young people of color, in this state.

[…] Lawmaker Gabriel asserts that “gun violence also contributes to significant racial and socioeconomic inequality in safety.”

hl_en: Assembly passes bill against dangerous chemicals in food
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — This Monday, the California State Assembly approved first-of-its-kind legislation that would ban the use of certain dangerous and toxic chemicals in processed foods and beverages. Introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, Democrat of Woodland Hills, Assembly Bill (AB) 418 would prohibit the manufacture, sale or distribution of any food product in California containing Red Dye No. 3, titanium dioxide, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil or propylparaben.

These chemicals are already banned in the European Union (EU) and many other jurisdictions because of scientific research linking them to significant health harms, including cancer, reproductive problems, and behavioral and developmental problems in children.

"Today's strong vote is a big step forward in our effort to protect California's children and families from dangerous and toxic chemicals in our food supply," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel.

"It is unacceptable that the United States is so far behind the rest of the world when it comes to banning these dangerous additives.

"We don't love our children any less than they do in Europe, and it is not too much to ask food and beverage manufacturers to switch to the safer alternative ingredients they already use in Europe and many other nations around the world," he added.

Numerous scientific studies have shown the connection between the chemical additives named in AB 418 and alarming health outcomes, including an increased risk of cancer, behavioral problems in children, harm to the reproductive system and harm to the immune system.

The European Union and many other nations have already banned their use in food, and many major brands and manufacturers, including Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Gatorade, Dunkin' Donuts, Papa John's Pizza and Panera, have voluntarily stopped using these additives in their products.

Unfortunately, chemical companies in the United States have been able to exploit a major loophole in federal regulations to avoid meaningful independent review by the FDA of numerous food additives, which puts the United States far behind many other nations when it comes to food safety.

If it becomes law, AB 418 would require companies to make modifications to the recipes of products sold in California and would likely prompt a nationwide transition to safer alternatives.

"For decades, the FDA has failed to keep us safe from toxic food chemicals," said Scott Faber, EWG's senior vice president for Government Affairs.

"Chemical companies continue to exploit a loophole that allows food additives whose safety has not been adequately reviewed by the FDA. And the FDA consistently fails to reassess chemicals, even in light of new science.

"The food and confectionery industries know that the review process at the FDA doesn't work," he said. AB 418 now moves to the state Senate, where it is expected to be heard in committees in the coming weeks.

hl_en: This popular treat may contain cancer-causing ingredients; calls to change it
text_en:
SACRAMENTO, California - This Easter, Americans will eat more than a billion Peeps, the bright marshmallow chicks whose arrival on store shelves each year is a herald of spring.

What makes the treats so vibrant is erythrosine, a chemical that appears on ingredient labels as Red No. 3. It is one of several chemicals, along with titanium dioxide, used to color some of the nation's most popular candies, including Skittles and Hot Tamales. Both have been linked to cancer. More than 30 years ago U.S. regulators banned Red No. 3 in cosmetics, but the U.S. has still not banned it in food, to the dismay of some consumer advocacy groups.

Now a state lawmaker wants to ban erythrosine and titanium dioxide in California, plus three other chemicals used in products such as tortillas and some sodas. The bill, scheduled for its first public hearing next week, has generated headlines worldwide saying California wants to ban Skittles and other candy. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the Democratic author of the bill, said he wants to ban the chemicals, not the candy. He said many alternative ingredients are available, noting that the chemicals are already banned in Europe and companies still find ways to sell candy there.

"They still make Skittles in other parts of the world. What they do is take out these toxic ingredients and replace them with something else," Gabriel said. "What we really want is for these companies to make the same minor changes to their recipes that they made in Europe and elsewhere."

The National Confectioners Association says it is not so easy. Tastes vary across cultures, and changing ingredients would be a hardship for regional candy makers. "There is much more at stake here than a simple answer," said spokesman Christopher Gindlesperger.

The candy industry insists the chemicals "have been thoroughly reviewed by federal and state systems and many international scientific bodies and continue to be considered safe." Scott Faber of the Environmental Working Group said the only reason federal regulators still consider the chemical safe is a loophole exploited by chemical companies. "If the FDA doesn't fix this review system and keep us safe from dangerous chemicals in our food, it is up to states like California to keep us safe."

hl_en: 5 dangerous ingredients in our food that shouldn't be there
text_en:
By Scott Medintz (Consumer Reports). California is considering banning Red Dye No. 3 and other common additives, which could affect hundreds of foods, including in other states. Foods made with the ingredients California is considering banning include some grated cheeses (titanium dioxide), hamburger buns (potassium bromate), orange sodas (brominated vegetable oil), candies (Red No. 3) and corn tortillas (propylparaben).

A bill co-sponsored by Consumer Reports and the Environmental Working Group (EWG), now before the California Assembly, would ban the use of five chemicals as additives in food and drinks sold in the state, and could have far-reaching effects for consumers across the country. The substances have been linked to serious health problems, including increased cancer risk, nervous system damage, hyperactivity and other behavioral problems. All have been banned for food use by regulators in Europe.

A group of 10 trade organizations of food and beverage makers, distributors and retailers, including the American Chemistry Council, the International Association of Color Manufacturers and the American Bakers Association, oppose the bill, arguing the chemicals have already been reviewed by federal and state regulators and further evaluations should be allowed to continue. But Brian Ronholm, CR's director of food policy, says more must be done now: "Despite the well-documented risks these five food chemicals pose to our health, the FDA has not acted to protect the public. By banning these dangerous chemicals in food, California can protect public health in the state and encourage manufacturers to make their products safer for the rest of the country."

Why these five? Melanie Benesh of EWG says each is found in dozens or hundreds of products on shelves, each is clearly linked to health harm, and each has been banned in Europe. She says they are emblematic of a broader problem: "The FDA is not effective at reviewing the chemicals in the food we eat every day."

The FDA last reviewed the safety of brominated vegetable oil in 1977, potassium bromate in 1973, propylparaben in 1977, Red No. 3 in 1982 and titanium dioxide in 1966. Safer alternatives exist: sorbic acid instead of propylparaben, ester gum instead of brominated vegetable oil, and calcium carbonate instead of titanium dioxide.

hl_en: Lawmaker introduces bill to ban the sale of candy containing harmful chemicals
text_en:
A local California lawmaker has introduced a measure that would ban the sale and manufacture in the state of foods containing chemicals that are dangerous to health, most notably candy and soft drinks, seeking to bring the state in line with a similar measure approved in the European Union.

The bill by Democratic lawmaker Jesse Gabriel would make California the first state to ban Skittles or Hostess Ding Dongs, among other treats, unless they change their formulas to make them less harmful to health, since their chemicals can pose risks such as a weakened immune response, hyperactivity in children and an increased risk of cancer.

"I love Skittles. I love Wild Berry Skittles. I eat them all the time," lawmaker Gabriel told the Los Angeles Times. "I would vote against a bill to ban Skittles. What we're really trying to get them to do is change their recipes. These are all nonessential ingredients," he explained.

California lawmakers backing the bill pointed to a series of scientific studies that showed links between the chemicals, which include red dye, titanium dioxide, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil and propylparaben, and health problems.

One study cited by Gabriel's office found that titanium dioxide, used in Skittles as a colorant, was associated with reduced immune responses in rats.

A lawsuit filed last year in California against Mars, which makes Skittles as well as M&M's and Milky Way chocolates, claimed the colorful candies were "unfit for human consumption" because of titanium dioxide. The substance is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but the agency stipulates that it cannot make up more than 1% of the food's weight.

hl_en: Sale of Hot Tamales, Skittles and Others Could Be Banned Under California Bill
text_en:
The sale of Skittles, Hot Tamales candy, Dubble Bubble Twist Gum and other foods containing chemicals that, according to supporters of the legislation, are toxic and dangerous could be banned in California. A bill introduced by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Buffy Wicks, AB 418, proposes that the state stop the manufacture, sale or distribution of foods containing Red Dye No. 3, titanium dioxide, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil or propylparaben.

According to them, these chemicals can cause significant health problems, such as an increased risk of cancer, damage to the immune system and behavioral problems in children.

These chemicals can be found in very common commercial foods and drinks, and many consumers are likely not to recognize them by their scientific names.

For example, according to Label Insights, titanium dioxide can be found in cupcakes, trail mixes and ice cream. Propylparaben can be found in caramel chocolate.

“Californians should not have to worry that the food they buy at their neighborhood grocery store might be full of dangerous additives or toxic chemicals,” Gabriel said in a statement.

If approved, California would be the first state to have such a law.

Protecting children's food. He also explains that this bill “will correct a troubling lack of federal oversight and help protect our children, public health and the safety of our food supply.”

Many of the chemicals that would be banned have never been independently reviewed by the FDA or have not been reevaluated in decades, according to Gabriel.

“Instead, these chemicals entered the nation's food supply through a loophole in federal law, known as GRAS, or ‘generally recognized as safe,’ which was intended to apply to common household ingredients like vinegar,” he said.

They say that as a result of that gap, chemical companies have added new substances to the food supply with almost no meaningful federal oversight.

AB-318 has been double-referred, meaning it will be heard first in the Assembly Environmental Safety and Toxic Materials (ESTM) Committee. If approved, it will go to the Assembly Health Committee. The bill would have to be approved by both houses of the state Legislature and signed by Governor Gavin Newsom before it becomes law.

hl_en: Learn About the New Laws Taking Effect in 2023
text_en:
Starting in January, historic laws will take effect in California that will raise the minimum wage, allow immigrants to work as police officers, and let street vendors work with less likelihood of being harassed by health authorities and law enforcement officers.

"California leads, and we do so by following our moral compass and staying true to our values," said Governor Newsom.

"The Legislature is an invaluable partner and I thank them for their leadership and courage, and I look forward to continuing our work to improve the lives of Californians throughout the state."

Street vendors: One of the new laws is SB972 by Senator Lena González, which will make it easier for street vendors to obtain local health permits, formally enter the economy and better provide for their families. This will prevent them from being harassed by police and health departments.

Abortion information: Law AB 1242 prohibits police and law enforcement agencies from providing information to and cooperating with out-of-state entities regarding the legality of abortion in California. It also prohibits law enforcement from arresting a person for assisting in a legal abortion in California.

Law enforcement: A new law allows legal immigrants to be police officers, eliminating the provision that they must be citizens or permanent residents.

Anti-hate law: The new law AB 2282 by Democratic Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan of Orinda establishes that people who use any of three hate symbols, such as swastikas, nooses and cross burnings, will be subject to the strongest of criminal penalties.

Alert for Indigenous people: Law AB 1314 creates a system similar to the Amber Alert for Indigenous people who have gone missing under unexplained or suspicious circumstances.

Minimum wage: California's minimum wage will increase 50 cents to $15.50 per hour for all employers regardless of business size.

Pay equity: Law 1162 requires companies with 100 or more employees to include the median hourly rate by race, ethnicity and sex within each job category in the pay data reports they must submit to the state.

It also requires companies with 15 or more employees to post pay scales in job postings. New holidays: Several new laws establish April 24 as Genocide Remembrance Day; June 19 is the Juneteenth celebration; Lunar New Year Day is also created; and Native American Day will be the fourth Friday of September.

Jaywalking: A new law considers crossing a street outside a designated area an offense only when a reasonably careful person would realize there is an immediate danger of a collision.

More protections for cyclists: Previously, California law required vehicles to keep a distance of 3 feet when passing bicycles heading in the same direction, but a new law now requires them to move into another lane with due regard for safety and traffic conditions, "if practicable and not prohibited by law." Laws that benefit immigrants: AB 1232 by Democratic Assemblymember Kevin McCarty of Sacramento will allow newly arrived immigrants to access English as a second language courses at California community colleges by paying the same tuition as state residents.

AB 2004 by Democratic Assemblymember Cristina García of Bell Gardens strengthens the California dreamers loan program by requiring loan applicants to receive financial education, creates loan forgiveness provisions resembling federal loan programs, and increases the amount they can borrow for graduate programs.

[…] AB 2193 by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino provides low-income Californians, regardless of their immigration status, with legal assistance in civil matters affecting basic human needs. AB 2697 by Democratic Assemblymember Cecilia Aguiar-Curry of Winters gives access through Medi-Cal to community workers and promotores de salud (health promoters) who can facilitate and provide culturally appropriate care.

hl_en: California Legislative Session Ends With a Positive Balance for Immigrants
text_en:
The 2021-22 legislative cycle, which is about to end, has left a positive balance for immigrants in California, as Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law several measures that will offer greater opportunities to those who lack immigration status but who contribute every day to the state's economy through their work and by paying taxes. Under the new laws, immigrants will be able to obtain an official state identification card; street food vendors, health permits to work free of the threat of police; and low-income people will also have access to legal assistance in civil matters in the courts.

"California is expanding opportunity for everyone, regardless of immigration status," said Governor Newsom.

"We are a refuge state, a majority-minority state, where 27% of us are immigrants. That is why I am proud to announce the signing of today's bills to further support our immigrant community, which strengthens our state every day."

Below is the list of new pro-immigrant laws that will take effect in January 2023:

* AB 1232 by Democratic Assemblymember Kevin McCarty of Sacramento will allow newly arrived immigrants to access English as a second language courses at California community colleges by paying the same tuition as state residents.

* AB 1766 by Democratic Assemblymember Mark Stone of Scotts Valley authorizes the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) to issue identification cards to undocumented immigrants.

* AB 2004 by Democratic Assemblymember Cristina García of Bell Gardens strengthens the California dreamers loan program by requiring loan applicants to receive financial education, creates loan forgiveness provisions resembling federal loan programs, and increases the amount they can borrow for graduate programs.

* AB 2068 by Democratic Assemblymember Matt Haney of San Francisco requires that Cal/OSHA notices be translated into the language spoken by at least 5% of the workers at a workplace, which could be Spanish, Chinese or Tagalog. Normally these notices are posted only in English, and since this is usually information that can help save lives related to workplace safety conditions, under this new law they must be translated into the languages the workers speak.

* AB 2193 by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino provides low-income Californians, regardless of their immigration status, with legal assistance in civil matters affecting basic human needs.

* AB 2195 by Democratic Assemblymember Reginald Byron Jones-Sawyer of Los Angeles creates an alternative plea plan for those accused of drug crimes, which mitigates the harm in particular for Californians who are not citizens.

* AB 2697 by Democratic Assemblymember Cecilia Aguiar-Curry of Winters gives access through Medi-Cal to community workers and promotores de salud (health promoters) who can facilitate and provide culturally appropriate care.

* SB 972 by Democratic Senator Lena González of Long Beach modernizes the California health code so that street food vendors can obtain permits to sell without being harassed by police and health departments.

* SB 1141 by Democratic Senator Monique Limón of Santa Barbara eliminates the requirement that attendance at credit courses on a California Community Colleges campus count toward meeting the 3-year requirement and not exceed 2 years of full-time attendance.

Last month, Governor Newsom signed into law SB 836 by Democratic Senator Scott Wiener of San Francisco, which prohibits any party from disclosing a person's immigration status in open court in a criminal case, unless approved by the judge.

hl_en: California Has New Laws to Protect Against the Surge in Hate Crimes
text_en:
Amid a rise in hate-fueled violence across the country, Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law two measures to equalize and strengthen penalties for using hate symbols and to bolster security at religious and community nonprofit organizations, which are often targets of attacks.

The new law AB 2282 by Democratic Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan of Orinda establishes that people who use any of three hate symbols, such as swastikas, nooses and cross burnings, will be subject to the strongest of criminal penalties.

"At a time when hate permeates public discourse and violent extremism threatens our communities, it is critical that we take a clear and firm stand against bigotry in all its forms," said Governor Newsom.

"California will not tolerate violence that terrorizes any of our communities, and this measure updates state law to punish the use of universally recognized hate symbols. California will continue to lead the fight to eradicate hate and defend those who are targeted for who they are, how they identify or what they believe." In addition, AB 2282 equalizes the restrictions on where the symbols can legally be used and expands the restricted locations to include K-12 schools, universities, cemeteries, places of worship, private property, public spaces and workplaces, among other locations. "This legislation ensures that vulnerable communities are equally protected against the use of terrorizing symbols, such as burning crosses, Nazi symbols and nooses," said Assemblymember Bauer-Kahan.

Governor Newsom also signed AB 1664 by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Encino to strengthen the state nonprofit grant program that helps nonprofit organizations targeted by hate-motivated violence improve security at their facilities.

AB 1664 extends the program, which was set to expire in 2025, and allows grant recipients to fund additional uses, including security training.

A recent report by the California Attorney General shows that hate-motivated crimes have increased 89% over the last decade.

"In a world where hate crimes and antisemitism are on the rise, we need more than thoughts and prayers to keep us safe," said Assemblymember Gabriel.

"This new law will provide critical resources to protect vulnerable communities and will send a powerful message that California stands firm against hate."

California Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis said that as we continue to see a rise in hate crimes and antisemitic attacks in California and the United States, AB 1664 is a powerful counter-response to keep our most vulnerable communities safe.

Assemblymember Gabriel authored the legislation establishing the nonprofit security grant program in 2019 following the deadly shooting at Chabad of Poway, a synagogue in San Diego County.

Since then, the program has funded critical security upgrades at religious institutions, LGBTQ community centers, reproductive health facilities and other nonprofit organizations considered at risk of violent extremism.

This year's state budget included an allocation of $50 million for 209 community groups. California has provided a total of $110 million in funding for anti-hate programs.

Reactions: AB 1664 has the support of a coalition of marginalized communities at the center of hate-motivated violence.

Richard Konda, executive director of the Asian Law Alliance: "Since the start of the pandemic, Asian Americans, and especially women and the elderly, have been targeted by a staggering increase in hate, bias and violence.

[…] Samir Kalra, director of the Hindu American Foundation: "In the wake of the recent increase in hate crimes against Hindu Americans and Hindu temples, we are especially grateful to Assemblymember Gabriel for his continued leadership in ensuring that vulnerable institutions, organizations and communities in the state are better protected against hate.

hl_en: California will require social media companies to detail their content moderation policies
text_en:
Considered a frontier few were willing to cross, California has become this week one of the few states to take on big tech and increase regulation. The Democratic government enacted a law requiring social networks such as Twitter and Meta (Facebook) to reveal their policies on moderating comments and censorship, as a way to combat disinformation, hate speech and extremism.

The law was born as a direct reaction to the January 2021 storming of the Capitol by Donald Trump supporters. Starting in 2024, companies must give California's attorney general detailed reports explaining how they moderate online debate, including whether it is left to artificial intelligence and how offenses and removed comments are ranked. Companies that do not comply will be fined.

"California will not stand by while social media is weaponized to spread hate and disinformation that threaten our communities and our core values as a country," Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement Tuesday.

The industry objected. "Forcing social networks to share their moderation policies and strategies in detail is like handing a blueprint of your house to burglars," said Adam Kovacevich of the Chamber of Progress, a center-left coalition that includes Meta and Google. The group has not ruled out challenging the law in court on First Amendment grounds.

The bill, known as AB 587, was written by local Democratic legislator Jesse Gabriel and had Republican support. Florida and Texas have introduced similar initiatives, but theirs aim to restore right-wing voices they say have been censored. Gabriel told The Washington Post his law is different: "We are only asking for more transparency. Unless they have something to hide, why would companies fear sharing such basic information about their consumers and users?"

Newsom also has until the end of the month to sign the California Age-Appropriate Design Code, meant to make the internet friendlier to minors.

hl_en: Bills to regulate social media content are approved
text_en:
California lawmakers on Tuesday sent Governor Gavin Newsom two groundbreaking bills aimed at limiting the downsides of social media, blaming Congress for failing to act on the problem.

A first-of-its-kind measure would require social media companies to make public their policies for removing disturbing content and provide details on how and when they remove it. The second bill would require companies offering online services attractive to children to follow age-appropriate design code principles meant to keep children safe, including not profiling a child or using a child's personal information in ways that could harm the child's physical or mental health or well-being.

"The online world has created enormous opportunities, but also real and imminent threats to children, vulnerable communities and American democracy as we know it," said Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, author of the first bill.

"We believe California has a special obligation and a special opportunity to lead on these issues," Gabriel added at a Tuesday news conference. "We are proud of our tech economy and know that many of the companies these bills would regulate are local California companies. But with the dysfunction in Washington, D.C., we believe California must step up and lead."

Gabriel's measure would require companies to say how they regulate their own content under their terms of service. It stalled last year over free speech concerns before passing the Senate 33-3 and the Assembly 48-0. It states that it is the Legislature's intent that the attorney general or city attorneys bring civil actions against violators.

Although the measure had bipartisan support, Republican Senator Melissa Melendez worried it could be used to punish legitimate but unpopular content, particularly because Attorney General Rob Bonta is a progressive Democrat. Democratic Senator Thomas Umberg, who carried the bill, said the measure "basically does not censor content. If you don't have a policy, you have nothing to report."

Senator Scott Wiener said the bill sought by the Anti-Defamation League is particularly important to the Jewish Caucus given rampant antisemitism on social media. Opponents include the California Chamber of Commerce, the Computer and Communications Industry Association, the Consumer Technology Association, the Internet Coalition, NetChoice and TechNet.

hl_en: 'Fatal' Bill in Sacramento
text_en:
A substantial increase in the number of deaths and injuries is the forecast of numerous community leaders who hope Governor Gavin Newsom will reject bill SB 930, which would extend until 4:00 a.m. the hours for selling all types of alcoholic beverages in bars, taverns, restaurants and nightclubs.

The measure was approved Friday 9-2 in the state Assembly appropriations committee, including the votes of two doctors: Joaquín Arámbula (D-Fresno) and Akilah Weber (D-San Diego), as well as Isaac Bryan (D-Los Angeles), Mike Fong, Eduardo Garcia (D-Coachella), Chris Holden (D-Pasadena), McCarty, Bill Quirk (D-Hayward) and Robert Rivas (D-Hollister). Opposing the bill were Frank Bigelow (R-Madera) and Marc Levine (D-Marin County), and those who abstained from voting, which is similar to a "no," were: Lisa Calderón (D-City of Industry), Megan Dahle (R-Redding), Laurie Davies (R-San Juan Capistrano), Mike Fong (D-Monterey Park), Jesse Gabriel (D-Woodland Hills).

"Lives at risk and certain deaths is what this bill would cause," Mayra García, advocacy manager of the organization Alcohol Justice "The Industry Watchdog" in California, told La Opinión. "Innocent children and families are the ones who are going to suffer the consequences of this absurd law."

The bill will be heard Monday on the Assembly floor. If approved, it will go immediately to Newsom's desk for him to sign into law or veto before September 30. A similar measure by the same Senator Wiener was vetoed by former Governor Jerry Brown.

"[Jerry] Brown rejected it because he was focused on public safety, and [Gavin] Newsom is not like Brown; he is more liberal and is very likely to sign it, because he is also a pro-business [governor] and has a background of owning wine and liquor businesses."

The pilot program would apply to the cities of Cathedral City, Coachella, Fresno, Oakland, Palm Springs and West Hollywood, and the city and county of San Francisco.

Currently, the Alcoholic Beverage Control Act provides that any licensee, agent or employee of the licensee who sells, gives or delivers to any person any alcoholic beverage between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m. of the same day, and any person who knowingly purchases any alcoholic beverage between those hours, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

That law provides that money collected as fees be deposited in the Alcohol Beverage Control Fund, and that money is generally allocated to the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, as appropriated by the Legislature. However, Senator Scott Wiener's bill SB 930 would require that, beginning January 1, 2025, and before January 2, 2030, the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control carry out a pilot program that would authorize that office to issue an additional-hours license to a licensee located in a qualified area, which would authorize the city to permit, with or without conditions, the sale, delivery or purchase of alcoholic beverages on licensed premises between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m.

"This bill is bulls**t," summed up Richard Zaldívar, executive director of The Wall Las Memorias, an organization that provides mental health, alcoholism, depression and drug abuse services to members of the LGBTQ community. "We are currently seeing an increase in drug and methamphetamine abuse, depression problems and suicides, and in the middle of the coronavirus and monkeypox pandemic, the last thing we need is for people to abuse alcohol," he added.

"Besides, the police already have so much work, and devoting security resources to looking after drunks makes no sense. This law [SB930] is a bad decision and there is nothing rational about it."

In defense of his bill, Senator Wiener argues that many bars and venues still face debts, even though "to-go" alcoholic drinks were allowed, even at the height of the pandemic. "Although we are now in a very different phase of the pandemic and the bars that survived are open at full capacity, many of these small businesses are still struggling. We need to give them every possible tool to help them survive, which includes allowing them to stay open until 4 a.m. Nightlife is a fundamental part of who we are as a state, and our world-class bars and nightclubs deserve a fighting chance."

hl_en: Parents will not be able to sue social media companies over addiction, according to a California bill
text_en:
A one-of-a-kind proposal in the California Legislature, meant to hold social media companies accountable for harming children who become addicted to their products, would no longer let parents sue platforms such as Instagram and TikTok.

The revised proposal would still make social media companies liable for damages of up to $250,000 per violation for using features they know can addict children. But only prosecutors, not parents, could file the lawsuits. The bill was amended last month, CalMatters reported Thursday.

The bill's author, Republican Assemblymember Jordan Cunningham, said he made the change to ensure the bill had enough votes to pass the state Senate, where he said several lawmakers were "nervous about creating new types of lawsuits." "They are afraid it will open the floodgates to frivolous claims," Cunningham said.

TechNet, a group of tech CEOs and senior executives, says it is nearly impossible to separate social media content from the features used to deliver it. Its California executive director, Dylan Hoffman, said the bill violates First Amendment rights. Cunningham rejected the argument, saying the bill would give companies an incentive to police themselves.

The bill is one of several proposals this year aimed at social media companies. One, by Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, would require social media companies to publicly disclose their policies for removing problematic content and explain in detail how and when they remove it. Another, by Senator Tom Umberg, would let Californians targeted by a violent social media post seek a court order to remove it. A third, by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, would require companies to meet certain standards when marketing to children online.

hl_en: What to Do About the Continued Rise in Hate Crimes in California?
text_en:
“And now what's next? What is going to be done?”… those are the questions several leaders and experts are asking after learning of the latest and troubling report from the California Attorney General's Office on hate crimes in California in 2021. On average, hate crimes in California rose nearly 33% last year, the highest level reported since 2001, and the most affected groups are African Americans and Asians, but there was also a rise in crimes involving bias based on sexual identity.

“The report shows beyond any doubt that the epidemic of hate we saw unleashed during the pandemic remains a clear and present threat,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta.

“In fact, reported hate crimes have reached a level we have not seen in California since the aftermath of the September 11 terrorist attacks.”

He said that while there is no single solution, it is up to all of us to answer the call, because when our communities feel empowered, they step up.

“Now, more than ever, it is critical that we stand together: there is no place for hate in California.” Among the most important findings of the report on hate crimes in California in 2021: * Crimes against African Americans were the most frequent, increasing 12.5% from 456 in 2020 to 513 in 2021. * Hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation increased 47.8% from 205 in 2020 to 303 in 2021. * Crimes against Asians increased 177.5% from 89 in 2020 to 247 in 2021.

* Crimes against Latinos increased 29.6% from 152 in 2020 to 197 in 2021.

* Among hate crimes involving religious bias, the most frequent were against Jews, and they increased 32.2% from 115 in 2020 to 152 in 2021.

* From 2020 to 2021, the number of cases filed for prosecution with hate crime charges increased by 30.1%.

Alarming trend. Brian Levin, director of the Center for the Study of Hate and Extremism at California State University, San Bernardino, who is a week away from releasing his own numbers on hate, said the top five groups targeted for attacks last year in Los Angeles are African Americans, gay men, Latinos, Jews and Asians. “In California, 29% of the attacks have been against African Americans, 11.2% against Latinos, 14% against Asians and 12% against gay men.”

He said that nationally, every state in the nation except Ohio recorded an increase in hate attacks.

“This upward trend we have seen over the last four years in the country is alarming, and even more so that it has extended into the first part of this year, 2022.”

Crimes based on sexual orientation. Oscar de la O, vice president of the organization Bienestar, said what they have noticed most is that society in general feels more empowered to express its hatred toward other people, not only because of sexual identity but also against those they see as foreigners, and they dare to shout at them to go back to their countries of origin because, according to the haters, they do not belong in the United States.

“More and more, incidents are being reported to us on public streets and on buses, and transgender women are the ones who receive the most harassment.”

He pointed out that the biggest concern is that this hateful behavior they are seeing every day is becoming normalized, and they fear the community will accept it as part of their lives.

“It's not only the harm they do to people, but it also affects their self-esteem. That's why it's important that they report it and not stay silent.”

De la O acknowledged the importance of Attorney General Bonta's report, but asked what they are going to do now. “Where are the campaigns to change policies, what else is coming to make this stop? We are very concerned because we have seen over the last 5 years that the numbers keep rising.”

[…] To confront attacks in the online world, they have pushed measure AB 8587 by San Fernando Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, which seeks to bring accountability and transparency to social media.

hl_en: Lawmaker seeks to combat street racing
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — The California State Assembly approved Assembly Bill (AB) 2000, which will prohibit street racing and sideshows in parking lots across the state. The measure, introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, Democrat of Woodland Hills, aims to crack down on dangerous driving, including street racing, "sideshows" and street takeovers, which continue to cause injuries and deaths across California. "All too often, illegal street racing and sideshows devastate families, harm innocent bystanders and cut young lives short," Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel said in a statement.

"Communities in the San Fernando Valley and across California are sick and tired of this reckless behavior. This bipartisan legislation will crack down on dangerous activities and help save lives," he added.

Statewide, the pandemic has led to a sharp increase in illegal street racing activity, as drivers took advantage of roads emptied by stay-at-home orders.

In 2020, the California Highway Patrol responded to more than 25,000 calls related to illegal street racing activity statewide, an alarming increase of more than 3,500 calls over the previous year.

In Southern California, street racing and sideshows have become extremely popular.

In August and October 2021, respectively, a Calabasas teenager was among three people killed by apparent street racers in a three-vehicle collision in Burbank caused by street racing, and a Woodland Hills woman was killed and seven others were injured after a driver lost control during a race.

Last week, police arrested three dozen people at several illegal street takeovers in and around Los Angeles and the San Fernando Valley.

Law enforcement groups across the state have identified driver's license suspensions as an effective tool to deter illegal street racing activity.

AB 2000 allows courts to issue a driver's license suspension for an exhibition of motor vehicle speed during a sideshow held in a parking lot, an area not currently covered by law, and thereby helps further deter people from taking part in these dangerous activities.

"AB 2000 will help us save lives and prevent more crashes and drivers going to prison for manslaughter," said Lili Trujillo, founder and executive director of Street Racing Kills, a nonprofit created in 2014 after Trujillo's 16-year-old daughter, Valentina, was killed in a street racing incident.

"An exhibition of speed in a parking lot is all too common now and people are getting hurt and killed; AB 2000 is definitely a great tool to help us save lives," she said. "There are countless stories every week across California about illegal street racing and dangerous sideshows that shut down streets, cause crashes, damage neighborhoods and put lives in danger," said Assemblymember Vince Fong, Republican of Kern County.

"They are unpredictable, destructive and can lead to senseless deaths that devastate families. AB 2000 is an important and necessary step to crack down on illegal sideshows to make our communities safer and save lives," Fong said.

AB 2000 now moves to the Senate, where it is expected to be heard in the policy committee in the coming weeks.

hl_en: Assemblymember García seeks $1 billion for parks
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — As the Legislature considers the upcoming state budget surplus, Assemblymember Eduardo García (D-Coachella) is leading a $1 billion budget request to support the State Parks Program and the Outdoor Equity Grants Program.

On Tuesday, May 17, Assemblymember García joined Democratic Sen. Monique Limón (Santa Barbara) and Democratic Assemblymembers Robert Rivas (Salinas), Wendy Carrillo (Los Angeles), Jesse Gabriel (Woodland Hills) and Cristina García (Bell Gardens) to promote this parks capital funding request at the California State Parks Foundation's Rise Up for Parks rally.

"Access to local parks and outdoor recreation improves community health and transforms lives. A historic budget surplus gives us the opportunity to bring major investments directly to Californians, and this $1 billion request for community parks and outdoor equity programs should be a priority," García said.

"Our ability to replenish funding for grant programs, such as state parks, that have already proven effective is vital as we strive to fulfill California's promise of parks for all," he added.

Funds for the State Parks Program are currently exhausted.

This program has proven successful in awarding grants to California's most underserved communities.

It has allowed California to award $803 million in grants since the passage of Proposition 68 in 2018.

García and other lawmakers want to allocate $800 million of the $1 billion requested to replenish those funds and help more communities build new parks and improve existing ones.

The lawmakers note that the pandemic has put a sharper focus on the inequities that continue to exist in the availability of local parks and green spaces and in access to outdoor programs across the state, making this $1 billion funding request all the more urgent. Senators María Elena Durazo and Monique Limón and Assemblymembers Robert Rivas, Wendy Carrillo, Cristina García and Ash Kalra signed Assemblymember García's $1 billion funding request for the California Department of Parks and Recreation.

hl_en: Democratic lawmakers propose $400 rebate to ease gas costs
text_en:
Following the surprise rise in gas prices across the country, a group of Democratic lawmakers will push for a possible rebate of at least $400 to all taxpayers, to minimize the effects of this cost on California families' wallets.

Why did lawmakers propose a $400 rebate as the gas tax went up? This measure will help soften the blow of the recent increase in gas prices, after thousands of Californians protested the sudden rise in this fuel, which is essential for moving families and supplies for businesses.

The lawmakers fighting for the rebate are Cottie Petrie-Norris of Laguna Beach, Cecilia Aguiar-Curry of Winters, Rebecca Bauer-Kahan of Orinda, Jesse Gabriel of Encino, Adam Gray of Merced, Jacqui Irwin of Thousand Oaks, Evan Low of Campbell, Blanca Rubio of Baldwin Park, Sharon Quirk-Silva of Fullerton and Carlos Villapudua of Stockton.

The gas increase is not the only one; there were also price increases in food, rent and other essential daily items, changes that negatively affect the finances of millions of families in California.

Meanwhile, some lawmakers continue to push to avoid the 51-cent gas tax that was applied, but not everyone agrees, and that initiative was halted in recent days.

"This proposed $400 rebate would cover the current gas tax of 51 cents per gallon for a full year, 52 trips to the station for most vehicles," the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Governor Gavin Newsom published by the LA Times.

The $400 rebate would apply to all residents regardless of immigration status This letter is signed by Assembly Speaker Anthony Rendon and Senate President pro Tem Toni Atkins, who are calling for this stimulus to avoid a larger crisis among the state's population. "In particular, we believe a rebate is a better approach than suspending the gas tax, which would severely affect funding for important transportation projects and offers no guarantee that oil companies would pass the savings on to consumers," they said.

Newsom and other politicians continue working quickly to minimize this negative impact on residents' wallets, and he promised a few days ago that he will return all the money paid in gas tax to all California residents.

In addition, the $400 rebate would apply to all California residents, regardless of their immigration status and whether their tax filings are up to date.

If this gas tax is suspended, there will be a considerable reduction in the fund used to build, repair and maintain roads in California.

hl_en: Californians could receive a $400 rebate because of high gas prices
text_en:
California lawmakers are proposing a $400 gasoline rebate for every state taxpayer, including those who do not drive, amid record gas prices.

According to a press release, Democratic Assemblymember Cottie Petrie-Norris of Irvine and other lawmakers will propose using $9 billion of the state's budget surplus to give each California taxpayer a $400 rebate. They said the rebate would more than cover the current 51.1-cent-per-gallon gas tax over a full year of weekly fill-ups for a car with a 15-gallon tank.

Other lawmakers in the proposal include Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, Jesse Gabriel, Adam Gray, Jacqui Irwin, Evan Low, Chad Mayes, Blanca Rubio, Sharon Quirk-Silva and Carlos Villapudua.

"Many Californians are in serious financial trouble at the pump and are looking to California's leaders for help," Petrie-Norris said. "We believe a rebate is the best approach to put money directly in people's pockets."

The rebate is only a proposal for now and would have to pass several committees and votes. Meanwhile, Republicans say a bill to suspend the gas tax for at least six months failed. Matt Shupe, chair of the Contra Costa County Republican Party, called it a missed opportunity for bipartisanship.

hl_en: Governor Newsom Urged to Give $400 Per Taxpayer to Counter Excessive Gas Prices
text_en:
A group of 10 Democratic lawmakers in Sacramento proposed to Governor Gavin Newsom that a portion of the budget surplus be used to give a $400 rebate to every taxpayer in California, to help cover part of the high cost of gasoline and the across-the-board increase in the prices of goods and services. "We ask that this proposal be included in the state budget and considered as soon as possible," they told him in a letter sent to Newsom and to the Democratic leaders of the state Legislature.

The lawmakers said they were deeply concerned about the rise in the price of gas and how it has affected Californians.

"We are committed to providing quick relief."

They explained that the proposed $400 rebate would cover the current gas tax of 51 cents per gallon for a full year, and 52 trips to the gas station for most vehicles.

"We believe a rebate is a better approach than suspending the gas tax, because that would severely affect funding for important transportation projects and offers no guarantee that oil companies would pass the savings on to consumers."

They point out in the letter that their proposal is intended for every taxpayer to receive this rebate, including those who do not own or drive a car.

"They too have seen an increase in their living expenses due to the rising cost of gasoline." They argue that California has been a world leader in the fight against climate change and, to remain consistent with its values, people should not be discouraged from using public transportation and clean-energy vehicles. "By offering this rebate broadly, we ensure that we help all Californians during this difficult time."

They state in the letter that many Californians are feeling the financial pain when they go to fill their gas tanks, and are waiting for help from their leaders in California.

"It is vital that we respond quickly and decisively."

The letter was also sent to Assembly Speaker Anthony Rendón, Senate President Toni Atkins, Nancy Skinner, chair of the Senate budget committee, and Phil Thing, chair of the Assembly budget committee.

It contains the proposal of Assemblymembers Cottie Petrie-Norris of Laguna Beach, Cecilia Aguiar-Curry of Winters, Rebecca Bauer Kahan of Orinda, Jesse Gabriel of Encino, Adam Gray of Merced, Jacki Irwin of Thousand Oaks, Evan Low of Campbell, Blanca Rubio of Baldwin Park, Sharon Quirk Silva of Fullerton, Carlos Villapudua of Stockton, and independent Assemblymember Chad Mayes of Yucca Valley.

The Republican leader in the Assembly, James Gallagher of Yuba City, said in a statement about the rebate proposed by the Democrats that it was about time they did something.

"Californians are suffering and it is taking Democrats weeks to act."

He said the measure should be fast-tracked to the governor's desk and directed to working Californians who truly feel the pain of high gas prices.

"Though this is a start, as Republicans we will work to also suspend the gas tax and stop the coming increases. With inflation at its highest point in 40 years and gas prices breaking records, $400 will go pretty fast."

At the end of February, Governor Newsom proposed in his $286 billion budget for fiscal year 2022-23 suspending the 5.6% gas tax increase that takes effect in July, in order to save drivers money. Suspending that gas tax increase would mean losing more than $520 million in revenue. The governor also proposes delaying the increases scheduled for 2023 and 2024. "Because California is so strong and we are the fastest-growing economy of all Western democracies over the last five years or more, our economic output is solid," Newsom said when presenting his plan.

hl_en: All California Taxpayers Would Receive $400 Rebates…
text_en:
All California taxpayers would receive $400 rebates to cover gasoline costs under new proposal

A group of Democratic state lawmakers on Wednesday called for sending a $400 rebate to all California taxpayers to help soften the blow of the recent increase in gasoline prices. The proposal comes as pressure mounts to help Californians struggling with fuel prices, as well as with increases in the costs of food, rent and other everyday essentials. Republican lawmakers have been pushing to temporarily suspend the state gas tax of 51 cents per gallon, but face opposition from the Democratic legislative leadership.

“This proposed $400 rebate would cover the current gas tax of 51 cents per gallon for an entire year, 52 trips to the station for most vehicles,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Governor Gavin Newsom, signed by Assembly Speaker Anthony Rendon and Senate President pro Tem Toni Atkins.

“In particular, we believe a rebate is a better approach than suspending the gas tax, which would severely affect funding for important transportation projects and offers no guarantee that oil companies would pass the savings on to consumers,” they noted in the letter, obtained by the Los Angeles Times on Wednesday.

Newsom pledged to address California's high gasoline costs and has been working with the Legislature to craft a tax relief package after promising in his State of the State address last week that he would “put money back in the pockets” of Californians who have been financially affected by the sharp rise in gasoline prices.

Newsom administration officials have said several ideas are being considered, although suspending or reducing the state gas tax does not appear likely.

Rendon and Atkins issued a joint statement last week ruling out the idea, saying it would not provide substantial assistance and could reduce funding for crucial road and bridge repairs throughout the state.

Instead, they favored broad tax relief to help Californians struggling with rising costs, not only for gasoline but also for food, rent and other essentials of life. The proposal announced Wednesday came from a group of 10 Democrats: Assemblymembers Cottie Petrie-Norris of Laguna Beach, Cecilia Aguiar-Curry of Winters, Rebecca Bauer-Kahan of Orinda, Jesse Gabriel of Encino, Adam Gray of Merced, Jacqui Irwin of Thousand Oaks, Evan Low of Campbell, Blanca Rubio of Baldwin Park, Sharon Quirk-Silva of Fullerton and Carlos Villapudua of Stockton, and one independent Assemblymember, Chad Mayes of Yucca Valley. Several of the lawmakers are generally seen as business-aligned moderates in the Assembly Democratic caucus. They have scheduled a press conference for Thursday to provide more details.

Republican leaders quickly gave their support to the measure, although they still vowed to push to suspend the gas tax.

“This bill should be fast-tracked to the governor's desk and targeted to California workers who are really feeling the pain of costs at the pump,” Assembly Republican Leader James Gallagher of Yuba City said in a statement Wednesday night.

The proposal, the lawmakers said in their letter to Newsom, should be considered as part of state budget negotiations that will begin in late spring. Early estimates of the size of California's budget surplus have varied and will not become clearer until taxpayers file their returns next month. Even so, most estimates have been much larger than the projected $9 billion cost of the Democratic effort.

hl_en: California Democrats Want to Provide a $400 Rebate to Cope With High Costs…
text_en:
After the high cost of gasoline has gained ground throughout California, Democrats are seeking to have the expense citizens are incurring offset with a $400 rebate to all taxpayers in the state.

This effort is led by the Democratic caucus in the state legislature. According to the legislative proposal, the money would go to all taxpayers in the state, not just motorists.

"This proposed $400 rebate would cover the current gas tax of 51 cents per gallon for a full year, 52 fill-ups for most vehicles," the lawmakers said in a letter addressed to Governor Gavin Newsom.

"In particular, we believe a rebate is a better approach than suspending the gas tax, which would severely affect funding for important transportation projects and offers no guarantee that oil companies would pass the savings on to consumers."

Unlike other states in the country, where gasoline has not yet reached $5 per gallon, in California the picture is severely complicated for motorists, who, according to data from the American Automobile Association (AAA), are paying an average of $5.78 per gallon.

According to the organization's reports, in some parts of the state prices are even higher: such is the case of Mono County, which recorded an average price of $6.50 per gallon.

At a press conference Thursday, Assembly members argued that the rebate is a better option than temporarily suspending the 51-cent-per-gallon gas tax because it gives recipients more freedom in how they use the money.

The bill, if approved, would take effect this spring, but a specific date has not yet been disclosed.

The proposal was presented by 10 Democrats: Assemblymembers Cottie Petrie-Norris, Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, Rebecca BauerKahan, Jesse Gabriel, Adam Gray, Jacqui Irwin, Evan Low, Blanca Rubio, Sharon Quirk-Silva and Carlos Villapudua, and one independent, Assemblymember Chad Mayes.

hl_en: Report: Hate and Antisemitism in Los Angeles
text_en:
Since the start of the pandemic, an increase in racial hate incidents has been recorded in Los Angeles. The increase included attacks against members of the Asian American community, Native Americans, African Americans, and members of the LGBTQ community, but in a more worrying proportion, against Jews in Los Angeles.

To share information on the subject and debate the ways in which governments and residents can combat this increase in the circle of racial, ethnic and religious hate, the publication The Forward recently organized a digital event presented by the city Controller, Ron Galperin.

Also participating were Rob Eshman, editor of The Forward; Serena Oberstein, of Jewish Wold Watch; Gamal Palmer of Conscious Builders; and Jeffrey Abrams, director of the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) in Los Angeles. The incidents include crimes such as assault, vandalism and harassment.

Last year was the third highest since this data began to be compiled in 1979, according to the ADL. The triggers of antisemitic expressions of hate vary. For example, the conflict between Israel and the Hamas organization in Gaza led to a 100% increase in attacks, including when a group of people asked diners at a restaurant frequented by Jews who was Jewish, in order to assault them.

The parameters are similar among the different organizations that compile the information, such as the ADL, the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

The details are not complete. For example, there are no statistics on what proportion of those Jews wear the kippah or yarmulke (skullcap) characteristic of the religious, which makes them recognizable. Likewise, it is not known how many LGBT people remain in the closet, or how many promotions and raises African Americans did not receive. There are not even statistics on the looks Muslim women receive on the street. "As the son of a Holocaust survivor, as a Jew and as a gay man, I am very concerned about the increase in acts of hate," said Ron Galperin. "The COVID-19 pandemic contributed to that, as did social media. So did national and international leaders inciting hate instead of contributing to reconciliation." "Our obligation," said Galperin, "is to work together, the members of various communities, because an attack against one is an attack against all. We have an obligation to take care of one another."

"The concern within the Jewish community," said Gamal Palmer, "is how to simultaneously oppose antisemitism and remain allies of the Black, Asian and Muslim communities. Because differences and division exist, even within the Jewish community, regarding the observance of religious precepts, or internal politics between Democrats and Republicans, or the issue of Israel."

"This division does not allow us to approach the problem of antisemitism from the outside. It does not let us work with our natural allies."

Ron Galperin: "I see it on the left, the right and everything in between. Antisemitism is not new. We have lived through two thousand years of expulsions, pogroms, refugee life, mass murders, forced conversions. Now," said Galperin, "there are new manifestations of antisemitism, which are rebranded as if they were only hatred of the state of Israel. Let us be clear that criticism of Israel is not in itself antisemitism, and I myself do not agree with everything its government does. But I would not be here if it were not for the state of Israel. The hatred of Zionism is such that they compare it to Nazism, which is repugnant. But over the years it has become something that is politically correct."

[…] "That is why Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel's bill AB 8587 in California will require social media companies to be truly transparent, open. They will have to inform the state's attorney general what their policies are and how they put them into effect to limit hate. They will have to provide the information: how many times did they delete hateful content, here and around the world?" Rob: Is there anything more that can be done at the municipal level? What can cities do, Ron Galperin? Galperin: We have a civil rights department that also analyzes the hate expressed on social media and how it affects the tone of civic dialogue. I believe we must use this information to unify people. We have to use technology to do good, just as they use it to foster hate.

[…] (*) Gabriel Lerner is Editor Emeritus of La Opinión.

hl_en: Assemblymember Recognizes Valley Honorees for Their Contributions and Positive Service
text_en:
State Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Woodland Hills) hosted a special awards ceremony on Nov. 14 recognizing the achievements and contributions of 12 individuals and organizations that have positively impacted the San Fernando Valley over the past year.

The honorees included educators, activists, firefighters, frontline health workers, small business owners and notable civic and community leaders.

The celebration, held at the neighborhood restaurant Soy y Luna in Tarzana, recognized the 2021 nonprofit of the year, small business of the year, educators of the year, environmentalist of the year, businessperson of the year, activist of the year, community heroes of the year and youth leader of the year. "It is an immense privilege to be able to honor such a remarkable group of individuals and organizations from the San Fernando Valley," Gabriel said. "In the midst of another challenging year, it was inspiring to see these people step up to serve our community and help those in need. I am so grateful to represent such a diverse, vibrant and caring community in the San Fernando Valley."

The honorees were recognized for a variety of contributions and achievements over the past year, including delivering meals to frontline health care workers during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, empowering women restaurateurs through small business grants and mentoring, collecting nearly 50,000 pounds of trash, providing food delivery and vaccination services for homebound seniors, launching a task force to confront racism, and promoting early literacy and parent involvement in child development and education. They were presented with special resolutions from the California Legislature recognizing their service to the San Fernando Valley.

Photo (top row, left to right: Jenna Hauss, president and CEO of ONEGeneration, 2021 nonprofit of the year; Battalion Chief Andrew Wordin, Los Angeles Fire Department, 2021 community heroes of the year; Daniel Steiner, principal of Taft Charter High School, 2021 educator of the year; Tim Gaspar, principal of Gaspar Insurance Services, 2021 businessperson of the year; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel; Frank Torres, chief of staff of SEIU Local 121 RN, community heroes of the year; former Los Angeles City Controller Wendy Greuel, 2020 Woman of the Year; Deputy Chief Trevor Richmond, Los Angeles Fire Department, 2021 community heroes of the year; Astine Suleimanyan, legislative coordinator of SEIU Local 121 RN, 2021 community heroes of the year)

(bottom row, left to right: Maxwell Suwaki, founder of OVERDUE, 2021 environmentalist of the year; Kiyomi Kowalski, board member of Valley Outreach Synagogue, 2021 activist of the year; Rachael Rosenberg, founder of Bundles of Kindness, 2021 activist/youth leader of the year; Gayle Batiste, president of SEIU Local 121 RN, community heroes of the year; Jamie Olivas, program supervisor at the Child Development Institute, 2021 educator of the year)

(Not pictured: Debbie Decker, executive director of West Valley Food Pantry, 2020 nonprofit of the year; Sandra Cordero, chef and owner of Gasolina Cafe, 2021 small business of the year)

The post Assemblymember Recognizes Valley Honorees for Their Contributions and Positive Service appeared first on The San Fernando Valley Sun.

hl_en: Calls to Refrain From Participating in Illegal Street Races During Halloween
text_en:
Lawmakers and families who have suffered the loss of loved ones due to illegal car racing called on those who like to carry out these dangerous stunts to refrain from doing so during Halloween weekend, since there will be many families on the streets and they could put their lives at risk.

"There are going to be a lot of people out in the streets taking their children trick-or-treating. We ask that they have respect and not do it. They should never take part in car races or drag races, but even less at this time of year when there will be many children out," said Lili Trujillo Puckett, who in 2014 founded the nonprofit organization Street Racing Kills, after her 16-year-old daughter Valentina died in an illegal street race.

She died when a young man who offered to drive her home after a youth party came across another driver on the road and started racing him. The contest ended in tragedy.

"We have to raise awareness of the dangers of illegal car racing," said Trujillo Puckett. This week, a woman died when a car being chased by police crashed right into a Halloween store in the Van Nuys neighborhood of the San Fernando Valley, where she was.

The vehicle was being driven at high speed and without lights by a minor under 18, whom police were chasing for doing donuts, or spins, on a street that had been illegally closed off.

Dangerous driving activities, including street racing, dangerous car stunt exhibitions and street takeovers, have soared during the pandemic, said Doug Shupe, spokesperson for the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety.

And he noted that, tragically, the results have been deadly. "Participants are not only putting themselves at risk but are endangering spectators, other drivers, passengers, cyclists and pedestrians." That is why, he said, as we approach Halloween weekend, when there will be children of all ages on our streets trick-or-treating, we must remind the public of the dangers of street racing and hopefully prevent another tragedy from happening.

In Northridge, spokespeople for the Automobile Club of Southern California, leaders of the group Street Racing Kills, police officers and Assemblymembers gathered: Kern County Republican Vince Fong; Jesse Gabriel, Democrat of Woodland Hills; Laura Friedman, Democrat of Glendale; and Adrin Nazarian, Democrat of Van Nuys.

This year, Governor Gavin Newsom signed law AB 3, which increases penalties for participants in illegal races who take over parking lots or intersections to carry out their risky driving maneuvers. "Valley residents are fed up with dangerous street racing and reckless sideshows," said Assemblymember Gabriel.

"This new law is an important first step and sends a clear message that cracks down on those who selfishly put themselves and others at risk."

Police agencies explain that a risky car exhibition, known in English as a sideshow, occurs when 2 people block or impede traffic on the highway for the purpose of performing stunts with their cars, races and high-speed exhibitions for spectators.

These activities often lead to street racing after the show.

Under the new law, participants in this type of illicit activity can be fined up to $500 and be subject to suspension or restriction of their license.

"Illegal car stunt exhibitions in vacant lots or public intersections continue to devastate families in our communities and create unnecessary risks for our youth," said Assemblymember Fong. He added that law enforcement is essential to stopping these dangerous exhibitions before they start.

author: Betty Marquez Rosales
twhy: Briefly describes his AB 309 within a bill-signing roundup.
hl_en: Governor Gavin Newsom signs $123.9 billion package to support K-12 education
text_en:
Governor Gavin Newsom on October 8 signed a $123.9 billion package to increase broadband infrastructure, develop mental and behavioral health programs and require all high school students to take an ethnic studies course before graduating. The 22 bills included in the package amount to the highest per-pupil funding in the state's history, according to a press release from the governor's office. A pair of bills signed last Friday will extend a state program that seeks to provide broadband access to Californians through grants. Some parts of California have struggled to attract internet service providers and have lacked the broadband infrastructure to do so, particularly in less populated areas. The pandemic has worsened the problem, especially in the early months when students depended on distance learning.

Assembly Bill 14, introduced by Assemblymember Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, a Democrat from Winters, and Senate Bill 4, introduced by Senator Lena González, a Democrat from Long Beach, expand the California Advanced Services Fund program through 2032. They also extend the tax on phone bills that is used to fund the program. The amount of the tax will remain the same.

In addition, SB 4 extends the California Advanced Services Fund from 2026 to 2032 and increases its annual funding cap. The fund provides grants for various broadband access projects, which will now include one for broadband access at unserved non-residential locations, such as fairgrounds, which are used for local and state emergency response.

“This is great news that will make a significant positive difference in the lives of Californians,” González said in a press release.

“The enactment of SB 4 and AB 14 means that kids will no longer have to do their homework outside fast-food restaurants.”

The mental and behavioral health bills will receive about $4.3 billion.

That includes AB 309, introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino, which calls for the California Department of Education to consult with the state Department of Health Care Services to develop protocols for schools to use voluntarily when referring students for mental health support. The package also includes SB 14, written by Senator Anthony Portantino, a Democrat from La Cañada Flintridge, which adds to the reasons a student may receive an excused absence for illness. The new option is “for the benefit of the pupil's behavioral health.” Portantino also introduced SB 224, which requires that mental health instruction be included in existing health education courses in middle and high schools.

One of the most anticipated bills was AB 191, which requires all public and charter high schools to offer a one-semester course, at a minimum, in ethnic studies. The bill will take effect during the 2025-26 school year. Beginning with the graduating class of 2029-30, high school students will have to complete a one-semester course in ethnic studies to receive their high school diploma.

hl: El gobernador Newsom firma un paquete de leyes que respaldan a los restaurantes y bares
