hl_en: Governor Newsom Signs Package of Laws Supporting Restaurants and Bars
text_en:
California Governor Gavin Newsom approved a COVID-19 recovery package that supports small hospitality establishments throughout the state, including restaurants and bars.

Signed at a restaurant in Oakland on October 8, the legislative package includes Assembly Bill (AB) 61, Senate Bill (SB) 314 and SB 389, bills that, among other provisions, extend special COVID-19 permits such as outdoor dining and to-go alcoholic beverage licenses.

Funds for the package will come from the governor's California Comeback Plan, which allocates $10.2 billion in support for small businesses. So far, the state has spent $4 billion on an emergency grant program and $6.2 billion on tax relief for small businesses.

"These innovative strategies have been a lifeline for the restaurants hardest hit during the pandemic, and today, we are keeping the entrepreneurial spirit going so businesses can continue creating exciting new opportunities and supporting vibrant neighborhoods throughout the state," Newsom said.

The state support comes at a time when many Black-owned small businesses in California, including restaurants, are struggling to recover after being hit hard by the COVID-19 pandemic. According to research by UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS), 13% of Black-owned businesses have had to close due to the pandemic, compared with 8% of white-owned ones. For Latino-owned businesses, that number is even higher, at 18%.

Because of the pandemic, Black businesses have experienced greater loss of income, more employee layoffs and less success in obtaining government-funded aid, such as assistance from the federal Paycheck Protection Program.

"We have all seen the consequences of the pandemic and the recession, and the effect on BIPOC people and BIPOC small business owners has been devastating," said Tara Lynn Gray, director of the California Office of the Small Business Advocate. She spoke at an IGS event last week titled "Diversity and Entrepreneurship in California: An Undergraduate Research Symposium."

"These are problems that need to be addressed. Access to capital remains a challenge," Gray continued. "We see bankers such as Wells Fargo, Citi and JP Morgan Chase making significant investments in BIPOC (Black, Indigenous and people of color) small businesses, communities and individuals. That is a trend I would like to keep seeing."

Gray noted that there are a number of state programs, such as the COVID-19 relief funds for small businesses, that prioritize providing relief funds to underserved businesses in the state.

Written by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and Senator Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco) respectively, AB 61 and SB 314 establish a one-year regulatory grace period for businesses operating under temporary COVID-19 licenses to obtain permanent expanded licenses, such as authorization for outdoor dining. The one-year grace period will begin once the pandemic emergency declaration has expired.

"Outdoor dining has been a critical lifeline that has helped these establishments keep their doors open during these difficult times," Gabriel said.

"AB 61 provides important flexibility so that restaurants can safely expand outdoor dining and continue serving the communities they call home. I applaud Governor Newsom for his thoughtful leadership in protecting both public health and small businesses as we continue to emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic," Gabriel continued.

hl_en: Period for selling food and alcohol at outdoor restaurants extended
text_en:
Governor Gavin Newsom gave restaurant owners good news by signing several laws that allow them to continue serving alcohol with meals at tables placed outdoors as well as to sell food with alcoholic beverages to go.

The measures will remain in effect for up to one year after the governor lifts the COVID-19 pandemic state of emergency.

"Many states of emergency remain as law for years, so we expect several years of relief due to these policies," said Patrick George, spokesperson for the California Restaurant Association (CRA). "This is going to benefit businesses, especially now that we have to ask for proof of vaccination," said Marco Uriarte, owner of the restaurant Emporio Sushi & Mariscos, with two locations in Orange and Downey.

Uriarte says that for them, selling alcohol with meals is essential because people like seafood with a beer, a drink or a glass of wine.

"Also with the food they come to pick up at the restaurant, they order micheladas, chamochelas and other mixed drinks." AB 61 provides flexibility so that restaurants can continue selling food with alcohol service outdoors. This includes a more efficient process for restaurants to obtain permits without going through financial and bureaucratic hurdles.

SB 314 increases the amount of time that a catering permit for events can be used at the same location within a one-year period.

SB 389 extends for 5 years the ability of restaurants to sell beer, wine and cocktails with meals that customers pick up.

"Together, these measures will help restaurants get back on their feet and will provide more options for consumers, whose lives have changed dramatically since the beginning of the pandemic," said Jot Condie, president of the California Restaurant Association.

He said that as restaurants recover from the Delta variant downturn, this legislation will generate opportunities and confidence.

"These key provisions will allow restaurants to serve the public and chart the course on the long road to economic recovery."

Condie recalled that beginning in the spring of 2020, many people started ordering takeout food and have continued doing so.

"The ability to order a drink with a takeout meal, in an expanded space outside a restaurant, or to expand the use of banquet catering permits, will allow restaurants to stabilize and increase their options for serving food to the public."

The CRA expects expanded outdoor dining to remain essential for many community restaurants, as Californians return to local restaurants in greater numbers.

For businesses that temporarily expanded their premises, the legislation paves the way for these changes to outlast the pandemic.

"Neighborhood restaurants are the backbone of communities throughout California, but too many are hanging by a thread," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, author of the AB 61 measure.

"Outdoor dining has been a critical lifeline that has helped these establishments keep their doors open during these challenging times," he added.

AB 61 provides restaurants the regulatory flexibility to increase their capacity to serve outdoors and sell alcohol with meals.

The COVID-19 pandemic has challenged small businesses throughout the state, particularly the restaurant industry.

While the National Restaurant Association reports modest job growth in the last 2 months, with California leading the nation in job gains, employment remains below pre-pandemic levels and nearly 4 out of 5 restaurants are short-staffed.

hl_en: Law AB57 will allow law enforcement to better prevent and respond to hate crimes
text_en:
Law AB57 will allow law enforcement to better prevent and respond to hate crimes: Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel

Law AB57, signed last week by Governor Gavin Newsom, will allow law enforcement to better prevent, respond to and document hate crimes, said Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of Woodland Hills. Chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, Gabriel is the author of the bill, which will put into practice specific recommendations from the state auditor to improve the performance of the authorities.

The measure was approved with bipartisan support in both the State Assembly and the California Senate. “The recent violence against the Asian American and Jewish communities is unacceptable and demands a strong response from all levels of government,” said Assemblymember Gabriel.

“At this moment, when so many in our state feel vulnerable, we must do more to protect those who are targeted by hate. Our legislation will significantly strengthen law enforcement training and coordination to ensure that California is better prepared to confront hate crimes and protect vulnerable communities,” he added.

Hate crimes against vulnerable communities on the rise. Law AB57 comes after a year that saw a dramatic increase in hate-motivated violence in the United States, leaving fear and concern among vulnerable communities.

Crimes against Asian Americans in the largest U.S. cities increased by 164% over the past year.

The Anti-Defamation League reported an increase in incidents against Jews in recent months, including violent attacks in the city of Los Angeles.

AB57 is part of a legislative package. Law AB57 is part of a package of legislative bills that seeks to address the rise in hate crimes and violent extremism throughout the United States.

The laws are based on specific recommendations from the California State Auditor, which found in a 2018 audit that law enforcement agencies in the state routinely failed to properly identify, report or respond to hate crimes.

The audit's conclusion indicated that inadequate policies and a lack of oversight by the California Department of Justice contributed to systemic underreporting of hate crimes throughout the state.

hl_en: Outdoor dining expands in California to help small businesses
text_en:
Los Angeles — Although food businesses can now welcome customers indoors, many establishments, especially small ones, still have not recovered financially from the closures during the pandemic.

Now these businesses have the flexibility to keep operating outdoors to serve more customers, including those who are not yet comfortable going indoors.

AB 61, signed this weekend, takes effect immediately to allow more outdoor food preparation and service, make more use of the surrounding space, and ease the service of alcoholic beverages.

The COVID-19 pandemic has challenged small businesses across the state, particularly in the restaurant industry. While the National Restaurant Association reports modest job growth over the last two months, with California leading the nation in job gains, employment remains below pre-pandemic levels and nearly four in five restaurants are short-staffed.

In August 2021, California also had 234,800 fewer eating and drinking establishments than in August 2019.

“Neighborhood restaurants are the backbone of communities throughout California, but many are hanging by a thread,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the bill’s author.

“Outdoor dining has been a critical lifeline that has helped these establishments keep their doors open during these difficult times,” he said.

Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti said the measure is crucial for the region, which has many visitors.

Madelyn Alfano, immediate past chair of the California Restaurant Association’s board of directors and owner of Maria’s Italian Kitchen in the San Fernando Valley, said the restaurant industry has been hit hard by the pandemic.

“With indoor dining still closed in most places, outdoor dining has become an important lifeline for restaurants,” she said.

“Nothing is more important to me than the safety of our customers and the ability to keep serving delicious meals to my community,” she said.

hl_en: California governor signs laws supporting small businesses
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation building on the state's successful pandemic adaptations and unprecedented support for affected small businesses, including measures that let restaurants continue to benefit from alcoholic beverage sales and expanded opportunities for outdoor dining.

"These innovative strategies have been a lifeline for the restaurants hit hardest during the pandemic, and today we are keeping that entrepreneurial spirit alive so businesses can continue creating exciting new opportunities and supporting vibrant neighborhoods across the state," said Governor Newsom. "California will continue to put the lessons learned during the pandemic into practice to support our ongoing recovery and strengthen our ability to meet future challenges head-on," he added. The Administration took steps during the pandemic to allow restaurants and bars to expand their operations outdoors into areas such as sidewalks and parking lots.

AB 61 by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (Encino) and SB 314 by Senator Scott Wiener (San Francisco) give businesses that temporarily expanded their premises under this regulatory relief a one-year grace period after the end of the emergency to apply for a permanent expansion.

When announcing the extended regulatory relief in June, Governor Newsom urged local governments to facilitate outdoor dining through local zoning and programs that support and promote expanded outdoor, takeout and delivery options.

"Neighborhood restaurants are the backbone of communities across California, but many are barely hanging on by a thread," said Assemblymember Gabriel.

"Outdoor dining has been a critical lifeline that has helped these establishments keep their doors open during these difficult times.

"AB 61 provides important flexibility so restaurants can safely expand outdoor dining and continue serving the communities they call home," he said.

"Outdoor dining is a popular and successful pandemic-era change that small businesses across the state, and their customers, passionately want to keep," said Senator Wiener.

"SB 314 ensures that the public can continue enjoying outdoor dining with alcohol and that our neighborhood small businesses can keep benefiting from this change.

"The hospitality industry has been hit hard by the pandemic, and it is important that we make changes to modernize our entertainment and hospitality laws to give them more flexibility and more ways to serve customers safely," he said.

SB 389 by Senator Bill Dodd (Napa) allows restaurants, bars, breweries and wineries that sell food to offer alcoholic beverages to go with food orders until Dec. 31, 2026. The legislation builds on the regulatory relief announced by the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control in

June that extended to-go alcoholic beverage sales with food delivery through the end of the year. "This is an important step to help our restaurants, which have been hit very hard by the pandemic," said Senator Dodd.

For California Restaurant Association president and CEO Jot Condie, the road to recovery for restaurants will be very long, and the importance of these measures taken together will remain a fundamental part of helping restaurants recover, rehire large numbers of Californians and continue serving the public safely.

To strengthen the state's pandemic preparedness, the governor signed additional measures expanding the services various health professionals can provide to patients, including laws allowing optometrists, dentists and podiatrists to administer COVID-19 vaccines and tests and legislation authorizing pharmacists to administer a wider range of vaccines and tests.

The legislation builds on emergency actions taken by the state to expand the health care workforce supporting the state's pandemic response.

hl: Presentan en California ley de responsabilidad en redes sociales

hl_en: California social media accountability bill introduced
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Woodland Hills who chairs the Assembly Committee on Privacy and Consumer Protection, announced that the legislative body has approved a bipartisan bill seeking to regulate social media companies in the State of California.

The measure, called the Social Media Transparency and Accountability Act of 2021 (or Assembly Bill AB 587), would require social media platforms to publicly disclose their corporate policies regarding hate, disinformation, extremism, harassment and foreign interference, as well as key metrics and data regarding the enforcement of those policies.

"Californians are increasingly alarmed by the role of social media in promoting hate, disinformation, conspiracy theories and extreme political polarization," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel.

"It is time for these companies to provide real transparency in their content moderation practices. The public and policymakers deserve to know when and how social media companies are amplifying certain voices and silencing others," he added.

According to the lawmaker, this is an important first step in a broader effort to protect democracy and better regulate social media platforms.

In recent years, the lawmaker said, Twitter, along with other social media platforms, has been implicated as a place where hate groups develop.

Recently, investigations have shown that the violent riots at the Capitol in early January of this year were instigated and encouraged by posts made on social media.

Despite widespread concerns, social media companies' efforts to police themselves have been widely criticized as extremely inadequate.

According to Gabriel, AB 587 would address the lack of transparency by requiring platforms to submit semiannual reports disclosing their corporate policies on hate speech, disinformation, extremism, harassment and foreign political interference.

They would also be required to disclose their efforts to enforce those policies and any changes to their policies or enforcement practices.

AB 587 would also require quarterly reports disclosing key metrics and data regarding such content, including the number of pieces of content, groups and users flagged for violations; the method of flagging (for example, human reviewers, artificial intelligence, etc.); the number of actions taken; and the type and content of the action flagged.

"This legislation would bring us closer to holding social media companies accountable for the hate and harassment they allow on their platforms, especially when that hate and harassment lead to violence," said Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive officer of the Anti-Defamation League.

"The reporting requirements described in the bill will put Big Tech's conduct under a bright light, and we hope that social media companies will respond by improving their corporate policies and the enforcement of those policies, or that the reporting requirements will provide enough evidence to take legal action against them if real progress is not made," Greenblatt said.

AB 587 is expected to be reviewed by Senate committees in the coming weeks.

hl_en: Lawmakers approve tenant protection program
text_en:
SACRAMENTO — The California State Assembly approved legislation to establish a statewide eviction defense program to protect California's most vulnerable tenants.

Introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Woodland Hills Democrat, and backed by a broad coalition of more than 50 leading community and nonprofit organizations, Assembly Bill (AB) 1487 would create the "Homelessness Prevention Fund" to fund training, outreach and legal services aimed at preventing displacement and homelessness among particularly vulnerable California tenants.

"Preventing evictions is key to addressing our homelessness crisis, particularly given the devastating impacts of COVID-19 on our most vulnerable tenants," said Assemblymember Gabriel. "This effort will leverage existing programs to address one of the root causes of the current crisis and help prevent homelessness before it starts.

"It builds on an approach that has been shown to protect vulnerable communities, reduce homelessness, save taxpayer resources and improve the equity and efficiency of our court system," he added. The State Assembly's approval of AB 1487 follows growing statewide and local momentum for eviction defense programs across the country.

Last month, Washington state passed a bill requiring the state to provide eviction attorneys for low-income individuals and families.

Maryland lawmakers also recently passed an eviction defense bill, as did Connecticut.

In California, the cities of Los Angeles and San Francisco have also enacted their own versions of eviction defense legal aid programs.

"A person's ability to adequately address fundamental issues such as their ability to stay housed should not depend on whether they can afford a lawyer," said Diego Cartagena, president and CEO of Bet Tzedek Legal Services.

"Unfortunately, in California, we face a serious justice gap, such that there is one lawyer for more than 10,000 eligible low-income clients," he said.

According to the attorney, the bill helps address the most urgent access-to-justice problem we currently face, building on existing programs to increase the number of legal aid attorneys available to help individuals and families facing housing insecurity and homelessness.

"Providing this support is the only way we can protect people's lives and prevent a worsening of the homelessness crisis in California," Tzedek said.

The COVID-19 pandemic has already exacerbated eviction and homelessness rates, with an estimated 13.2 million

adults, nearly 1 in 5 renters, behind on rent because of the pandemic. Data have shown that evictions are not only caused by economic hardship but are themselves a root cause of poverty and homelessness, as nearly 50 percent of homeless adults cite evictions or rent-related problems as factors contributing to their homelessness.

In addition, there is a marked disparity and power imbalance in eviction-related legal proceedings, with approximately 3 percent of tenants having legal representation, while more than 81 percent of landlords are represented.

When tenants are unrepresented, they face case outcomes that can result in disruptive displacement 78 percent of the time or more. However, when they are represented, legal aid providers can help tenants avoid disruptive displacement 95 percent of the time.

Data have shown that evictions have a disproportionate impact on communities of color. A 2020 study found that Black and Latinx tenants, particularly women, were overrepresented among eviction defendants, and these individuals were more likely to experience costly serial eviction filings compared with their white counterparts.

Gov. Gavin Newsom's recent May revision of the California budget included $60 million over three years to provide legal aid services to tenants and landlords to prevent evictions and foreclosures.

These additional funds will provide free legal services for landlord-tenant issues, including legal assistance for counseling, tenant education programs and eviction prevention. Lorin Kline, Director Attorney of the Legal Aid Association of California, expressed confidence that budget negotiations in the Legislature will show how vital it is that we fund legal aid for vulnerable tenants, most of whom are currently unrepresented and without help. "Our $200 million request is an investment that will not only save thousands of tenants from illegal and devastating displacement, but will also save the state money in the long run," Kline said. Providing legal representation to particularly vulnerable low-income tenants has proven to be an effective and cost-efficient strategy for addressing homelessness.

A 2019 report on the Los Angeles Eviction Defense Program estimated that for every dollar spent on an eviction defense program, Los Angeles would receive approximately $4.50 in value in avoided costs for emergency shelters, local rehousing programs, and health and mental health services.

Similarly, reports found that investment in legal aid in Baltimore could result in $17.5 million in avoided costs annually, while for New York City the figure is $320 million annually.

AB 1487 capitalizes on growing momentum, both in California and across the country, to help tenants affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The measure is expected to be heard in Senate policy committees in the coming weeks.

twhy: Mentions him once recalling the Northridge earthquake as a child.
hl_en: 25 years since the Northridge earthquake, the appetizer of the 'Big One' in Los Angeles
text_en: At 4:30 a.m. on January 17, 1994, the ground shook in the north of Los Angeles. The magnitude 6.7 earthquake occurred on a fault under the Northridge neighborhood, which gave it its name. Fifty-seven people died, most of them trapped while sleeping in apartments not built to withstand the tremor. The photo shows Highway 14, north of Los Angeles, destroyed by the quake, with the body of a police officer who plunged off on his motorcycle. The Northridge quake was the latest warning that Los Angeles, one of the most seismically active areas in the world, must prepare for a catastrophic scenario at some point in the next 100 years: the so-called 'Big One'. Damage was estimated at over 20 billion dollars at the time (about 35 billion today, according to the California Earthquake Authority). Most buildings had no earthquake insurance. A stretch of Highway 118 collapsed, and overpasses on this and other freeways were destroyed, paralyzing the city and damaging electrical infrastructure. Seismologist Lucy Jones said at the 25th anniversary that Northridge 'was not a big earthquake' for an expert; half a million people felt it, while in the 'Big One' scenario, a magnitude 7.8 on the San Andreas fault, 10 million would feel it. Jones often says it is not a question of if but when. Los Angeles has never experienced a major earthquake in the era of telecommunications. In a Northridge apartment block, 16 people died. On the 25th anniversary, the California Assemblymember who represents the area, Jesse Gabriel, recalled that he was 12 years old that morning: 'I remember waking up in the middle of the night. The window above my bed was shaking. My father came into the room and took my eight-year-old brother and me out. We slept in our minivan for a couple of days because we were afraid to go back to our house.' Since then the city has launched programs to encourage retrofitting of known fragile buildings, but thousands of structures still need reinforcement. This January, 25 years after Northridge, Los Angeles launched its first mobile app (ShakeAlertLA) that will send notifications seconds before earthquakes.

hl: Defensores, Políticos Quieren que se “Redirijan” los Fondos del Acuerdo de Aliso Canyon
twhy: Report on the Aliso Canyon settlement notes Gabriel joined Sherman and Stern in seeking to redirect funds to residents; critics target SoCalGas.
hl_en: Advocates, Politicians Want Aliso Canyon Settlement Funds "Redirected"
text_en:
Congressman Brad Sherman, state Sen. Henry Stern and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel have jointly announced efforts to redirect the Aliso Canyon settlement funds to community projects that reduce dependence on natural gas.

The city of Los Angeles, the county, state officials and the Southern California Gas Company recently reached a tentative $119.5 million settlement over the 2015 Aliso Canyon leak. The settlement must still be approved by the court and is subject to a comment period until September 12.

Stern and Gabriel said they plan to unveil new legislation before the comment period closes to ensure that the settlement funds "are allocated to projects that directly benefit the Los Angeles-area residents and ratepayers" most impacted by the leak.

Of the tentative $119.5 million settlement, more than three-quarters of the funds are proposed to go to projects that do not directly benefit the community affected by the 2015 disaster, which forced more than 10,000 residents from their homes and continues to affect the northern San Fernando Valley with health problems, according to a statement from Stern's office.

An estimated $26.5 million is slated for loans to Central Valley projects meant to reduce an amount of methane pollution equivalent to what Aliso Canyon spewed during the historic blowout. And up to $34 million goes to projects that keep California dependent on the methane stored at Aliso Canyon.

A class-action lawsuit involving about 9,000 plaintiffs has again been filed against SoCalGas. The plaintiffs have publicly stated their dissatisfaction with the settlement, since they believe it would end a lengthy state investigation into the leak, which they say has not stopped despite efforts to eliminate it.

Matt Pakucko of the advocacy group Save Porter Ranch argues that the settlement in this form could weaken the lawsuit.

"The problem is that it does not address the current dangers of the facility. It is a tacit approval for the facility to keep operating," Pakucko said.

"So if elected officials don't come out and say there is [still] danger, that it's safe then, yes, it affects the lawsuit."

Pakucko added that state Attorney General Xavier Becerra "should be investigating the gas company for the negligence and mismanagement that allowed the blowout to happen in the first place." SoCalGas advocates the use of dairy gas in Los Angeles' plan to transition to 100 percent renewable energy and has urged transportation officials to buy hundreds of gas buses, according to the community organization Food & Water Watch.

Local residents and Food & Water Watch representatives have also long criticized the use of cleanup funds to import gas from dairies in the Central Valley, which they say SoCalGas would use

to refill the dangerous Aliso Canyon facility.

"We are going to fight to make sure this money goes back to the residents most affected by the SoCalGas blowout, not to benefit the gas company," said spokeswoman Alexandra Nagy. "It makes no sense to reward the company responsible for the largest gas disaster in U.S. history with a deal that enriches it.

"This settlement shows Governor Brown's decision to protect SoCalGas instead of the health of families in the San Fernando Valley. Instead, he should shut down Aliso Canyon for good, now." The advocacy group is urging that $34 million be used for mitigation efforts that benefit the communities most affected by the Aliso Canyon gas leak. Such efforts could include investments in electrification, energy efficiency and renewable energy technology.

The leak was discovered in October 2015 and continued sending methane into the atmosphere until February 11, 2016, when it was announced that it had been plugged. By then, an estimated 109,000 tons of methane had entered the air.

At its peak, the gas leak forced an estimated 15,000 residents of the Porter Ranch area to relocate temporarily.

Limited operations resumed at the facility in late July 2017 with the blessing of state regulators. Efforts by Los Angeles County officials to block the resumption of operations failed in court.

SoCalGas has settled other litigation arising from the leak, including an $8.5 million settlement with the South Coast Air Quality Management District, which included $1 million in funding for an SCAQMD-sponsored health study on the leak's impact, although County health officials said $35 million to $40 million would be needed for a proper study.

hl_en: Runoffs to be held in two of Tuesday's special elections: District 39 and District 45
text_en:
Runoffs to be held in two of Tuesday's special elections: Assembly Districts 39 and 45 will see contests between a Democratic candidate and a Republican

Two state Assembly districts in the San Fernando Valley will go to a runoff on June 5 and will have a Democratic candidate versus a Republican, after no one obtained more than the 50% of the votes needed to secure a victory.

The only winner of the trio of special elections was Sydney Kamlanger, who received 69% of the votes and will fill the seat left vacant by Sebastián Ridley Thomas in District 54, which includes areas such as Baldwin Hills, Culver City, Inglewood and Leimert Park.

District 45 – which includes areas such as Northridge, Winnetka and Woodland Hills and other parts of the southwest San Fernando Valley – will also see a runoff between Democrats and Republicans after Jesse Gabriel received 32% of the votes, followed by Justin Clark with 27%.

This contest also came about following the resignation of Assemblymember Matt Dababneh early in the year, after a woman accused him of holding her in a hotel bathroom in Las Vegas and asking her to touch him, which she refused, although he masturbated in front of the woman anyway.

It should be remembered that June is not the end of these contests.

Voters in these three districts will return to the polls on June 5 not only to decide the winner of the contests still in dispute, but also to decide who will represent them for the next two years in the Assembly. Several of these candidates (both winners and losers) will be on the ballot again. If no one obtains more than 50% of the votes, the top two vote-getters will go to a runoff in November.

hl_en: Angelenos go to the polls today to replace Assemblymembers who resigned over sexual harassment allegations - They will choose representatives for Districts 39 and 45 in the San Fernando Valley and District 54 in Los Angeles in the State Assembly
text_en:
Voters in three areas of Los Angeles will go to the polls today to choose three new Assemblymembers who will fill the seats left vacant by Raúl Bocanegra of Pacoima and Matt Dababneh of Encino, who were forced out amid accusations of sexual harassment.

In addition, other voters will choose the Assemblymember who will replace Sebastián Ridley Thomas in District 54, who left office because of persistent health problems, having undergone surgery five times last year. The candidate who receives more than 50% of the votes in this Tuesday, April 3 election will be declared the winner. If no one obtains a majority, the two candidates with the most votes will advance to the June 5 primary election, where the winner will be decided.

Because there are many candidates in each contest, no winner is expected to take a majority.

District 39 Bocanegra, who represented District 39 in the northern San Fernando Valley, resigned from office on November 27.

The 39th is a mostly Latino and Democratic district that includes areas such as Arleta, Lake View Terrace, Mission Hills, North Hollywood, Pacoima, Sun Valley, Sunland-Tujunga, Sylmar and San Fernando.

Five Democrats are competing for the vacant seat: Patty López, the former Assemblywoman seeking to return to the seat Bocanegra won from her; Yoli Anguiano; Patrea Patrick, Luz Rivas and Antonio Sánchez. And Republican Ricardo Antonio Benítez.

Anguiano has a long career of community service; she was an Assembly employee, a former Los Angeles city commissioner, a former member of the Mission Hills Neighborhood Council, and currently works at Homeboy Industries.

Luz Rivas is an engineer who was a public works commissioner for the city of Los Angeles. She received the endorsement of Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti to go to Sacramento, as well as that of the Democratic Party. Antonio Sánchez worked for former Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa and currently works in job training for veterans and students; he has the support of several unions.

Patrea Patrick is a political and environmental activist who ran and lost in a bid for Congress in District 30 in 2016.

Benítez, the only Republican on the ballot, is a contractor of Salvadoran origin who is once again seeking to win a seat in the state Legislature. He has tried twice before but has not gotten enough votes. He has the support of some Republican lawmakers.

The two candidates who have managed to raise the most campaign funds are Rivas and Sánchez.

District 45 The District 45 seat became vacant when Matt Dababneh resigned on January 1 after being accused of sexual harassment.

It is a district located in the suburbs of Los Angeles, predominantly white. 30.38% of the population in this district is Latino.

District 45 covers Calabasas, Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Encino, Reseda, Northridge, West Hills, Winnetka, Woodland Hills, Tarzana and Bell Canyon, the latter in Ventura County.

Eight candidates are seeking to fill the place left by Dababneh: six Democrats, one Republican and one independent. The Democrats are: Serna Sharp, Jeff Bornstein, Ankur Patel, Ray J. Bishop, Tricia Robbins Kasson, Jesse Gabriel, John Popoch and Daniel Brin. There is also Republican student Justin Clark, while Dennis P. Zine and Scott Silverstein have no party preference.

Independent Dennis Zine withdrew from the race in February, but his name will appear on the primary election ballot.

District 54 On December 27, Sebastián Ridley Thomas resigned his District 54 seat because of health problems that made it difficult to carry out his legislative duties.

District 54 is very urban and ethnically very diverse. 30.50% of the population is Latino, but there are no Latinos among the contenders for the vacant seat.

Four candidates, three Democrats and one Republican, are seeking to take his place in the Assembly. They are Democrats Sidney Kamlager, Grayson Pangilinan and Tepring Michelle Piquado, and Republican Glen Ratcliff. District 54 includes Culver City, Baldwin Hills, Century City, Crenshaw, Leimert Park, Mar Vista, Mid-City, West Los Angeles, Westwood, Inglewood, Ladera Heights and View Park-Windsor Hills.

By law, the winners serve a two-year term, but they can be re-elected every two years until completing 12 years, when by law they can no longer continue in office.

However, these elections are only to complete the terms that the resigning Assemblymembers did not finish, so voters in these districts will go to the polls once more in November to choose who will represent them for the following two years, said Brenda Durán, spokeswoman for the Los Angeles County Registrar's Office.

According to Los Angeles County, each of these special elections costs $1.6 million. She attributed the high cost to hiring poll workers, printing ballots and voter guides, and transporting election equipment.

hl_en: Ryan: Congress wants to protect 'dreamers'; the Republican leader says it is what the majority wants
text_en:
A bipartisan majority in Congress wants to protect some 800,000 young immigrants who arrived as children years ago but lack residency permits, Republican Rep. Paul Ryan said. The Speaker of the House said in a recent interview that "there's a good part in this (.) a majority in Congress" wants to protect the young immigrants while also increasing border security.

President Donald Trump said this week he was "fairly close" to a deal with Democratic lawmakers to guarantee protection for immigrants covered by the DACA program, the English acronym for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, created by former President Barack Obama. DACA suspends deportation proceedings and grants work permits to its beneficiaries, some 800,000 young immigrants who came to the country illegally as children or stayed after their visas expired. Trump announced a few weeks ago that he will dismantle the program in six months and has asked Congress to work on the issue.

Ryan said any legislation to protect the 'dreamers' must come hand in hand with greater border security.

"We won't be comfortable fixing a symptom of the problem without dealing with the root cause," the congressman told Milwaukee radio station WISN-AM.

Lawsuit Six immigrants brought to the United States as children who are now teachers, university students and a lawyer sued the Trump administration over its decision to eliminate a program that protects them from deportation.

The lawsuit filed Monday in San Francisco says the move violates the constitutional rights of immigrants who lack legal status and provided information about themselves to the federal government in order to participate in the program.

"The consequences are potentially catastrophic," said Jesse Gabriel, an attorney for the plaintiffs. "These people can communicate very clearly and powerfully the extent to which they have organized their lives around this program."

The lawsuit adds to others filed over Trump's decision to end DACA.

More than a dozen states, from Maine to California, have sued the federal government over its decision to eliminate the program, arguing similar constitutional violations. Another plaintiff is the University of California system.

Gabriel said the impact of Trump's decision weighed directly on his clients' lives and the decisions they made to advance their careers in the United States.

He gave the example of Dulce García, a 34-year-old lawyer in San Diego who came to the United States from Mexico when she was four. García recently signed a lease for an office and hired employees, thinking she could stay and work in the United States under the program, Gabriel said.

"Now the government has cut the ground out from under her," he said.

The other plaintiffs are teachers, a medical student and a law student. They come from Mexico and Thailand.

Justice Department spokesman Devin O'Malley blamed the Obama administration for starting the program and said the department will defend Trump's decision.

"What brought us to this point was the previous administration's arbitrary decision to circumvent the authority of Congress," he said. "The Justice Department is going to defend this administration's position and restore the rule of law."

hl: ?El caso de Daniel destapa prejuicios con mexicanos?
author: Agencia El Universal
twhy: Pre-legislature story on a DACA recipient's legal team lists Gabriel among Gibson Dunn attorneys; no further mention.
hl_en: Does Daniel's case expose prejudice against Mexicans?
text_en:
Érika Flores MEXICO CITY, Feb. 24 (EL UNIVERSAL).- Daniel Ramírez, the 23-year-old Mexican "dreamer" detained on Feb. 10 by U.S. immigration authorities, has a team of 16 lawyers from major law firms who will defend him against the Department of Homeland Security. Among them are Luis Cortés Romero, also a "dreamer," and Elizabeth Hawkins, who spoke about how Ramírez's legal team came together and the importance of this case, which could have significant legal repercussions for immigration in the U.S.

"When Daniel's brother called us, I told him not to worry because he was protected by DACA and should be released that same afternoon. When he wasn't released, we met to discuss the case because this detention seemed very strange to us, with no criminal history of any kind; that's why we took the case, to investigate the injustices," Cortés explained.

He said that among the irregularities in the case is that they accused Daniel of being a gang member because he has a tattoo, and that in his statement he wrote "the officers accuse me of being a gang member," a sentence that was erased from the document. Cortés understands the environment of the immigrant community and the "dreamers" very well, because his story is similar. He was born in Morelia, Michoacán, and was taken to the U.S. when he was one year old. He grew up there and studied law thanks to the DACA program.

"For us it is very important to resolve this case, and I relate to it personally because I am also protected by DACA and I understand Daniel's worry at the prospect of being deported to a country that is unknown to him," he said.

After taking on Daniel's defense in Washington state, Cortés contacted the Public Counsel firm in Los Angeles, and they in turn contacted the firm Gibson Dunn.

Elizabeth Hawkins joined the group at Cortés's invitation.

"For me it is an honor to be part of such an important group that includes very famous constitutional scholars, although Luis and I are the only ones who specialize in immigration. And that is a key part of the case strategy," she said.

Hawkins, who visited Mexico for academic reasons, said the legal strategy focuses on habeas corpus (a procedure to determine whether the arrest was lawful), since, in her opinion, Daniel's detention violated the U.S. Constitution.

"If they are going to take away his DACA status and his freedom, they must also give him the opportunity to defend himself; and regarding the alteration of his statement, it would not be the first time an official has been sanctioned for actions like this," the attorney stressed.

"Daniel's case is not common, and as lawyers we understand the implications it has. If we are here, it is because we believe this will have positive effects for everyone else," she added.

The legal team: Daniel's defenders are working pro bono (without monetary compensation) and belong to major law firms in the country. The first is Public Counsel, a nonprofit organization recognized as the largest pro bono law firm for low-income people. It has five attorneys on the case: Mark Rosenbaum, Judy London, Kathryn Eidman, Anne Hudson-Price and Elizabeth Hadaway.

For the firm Gibson Dunn, founded in 1890 and with 18 offices worldwide, there are Theodore Boutrous Jr., Katherine Marquart, Jesse Gabriel and Ethan Dettmer.

Barrera Legal Group, a younger firm, contributed three of its litigators: John Barrera, José García and Luis Cortés Romero. The other four attorneys are Elizabeth Hawkins, of Hawkins Law Group; Laurence H. Tribe, of Harvard Law School; Erwin Chemerinsky, of the University of California; and Matt Adams, of the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project.

Desperate and confused: The detention center in Tacoma (Washington), where Daniel is being held, is not a jail but a temporary transit facility; however, the facility is overcrowded because an average of 1,500 people arrive every day because some authority considered their immigration status doubtful.

In addition, 80% of detainees have no legal representation. This happens because the Constitution guarantees a lawyer in criminal cases, but that does not apply to immigration matters. Hence, Hawkins stressed, Daniel is very fortunate.

Of the 16 litigators, the one who visits him most often is Luis Cortés. "The detention center is practically a jail; Daniel has no criminal record and is desperate to get out. But at the same time he feels very strong thanks to all the support he has received," the attorney said. Hawkins has only been able to see him once. "That day he was depressed and very confused, because his situation is traumatic. The cells are shared and the conditions in the centers are not very good."

For now, the group of lawyers asked to cancel the hearing that had been scheduled for this Friday, in which an immigration judge would evaluate the possibility of setting bail to release the "dreamer." Instead, the team opted to ask the federal court in Seattle to rule on accepting jurisdiction over the case. The hearing was set for March 8.

Initially, the lawyers' goal was to keep the case low-profile with the press, which proved impossible given its importance.

"The case is important because, one, it exposes police prejudice against Mexicans through a controversial presidential campaign. And, two, because at the same time it shows that there are many people who will not look away or stay silent when an injustice occurs," Cortés said.

"U.S. courts are saturated with deportation cases, and although under the Obama administration many of these were resolved administratively, that did not relieve pressure on the system. I'll give you an example: for recent immigrant cases my office is handling, the court gave us trial hearing dates as late as 2020," Hawkins concluded.
